studies.applyIt: Think of one instruction you resisted recently where the resistance was really about who was giving it. Do the thing today without renegotiating the terms. Not because the other person was right, and not as a lesson in obedience. Just to find out whether you can separate the task from the standing question underneath it.
studies.explainEasier: God told the angels to bow down to Adam, and they all did. Only Iblis refused. He thought he was too good to bow, and that choice put him with those who reject God.

studies.title: Everything Except One Tree
studies.meaning: The proportions here are the point. A whole garden is opened without limit of place or measure, and a single item is withdrawn from it. The prohibition is also wider than the act it guards, since the instruction is not to eat but not to approach, which puts the boundary at some distance from the thing itself. Early scholars differ over where this garden was, whether above the world or somewhere within it, and over what the tree was. They report the range and note that the passage names neither.
studies.historicalContext: This follows the command to bow and the refusal that answered it. The Quran gives the scene without an occasion of revelation, and the early scholars do not try to supply one. They observe that the surah is unusually brief about the setting and unusually precise about the terms of the permission. That is where their comment concentrates.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness and rest. It describes taking up residence in a place where one can be at ease, and the same root gives the ordinary words for a house and for tranquillity.
Plenty taken without effort or reckoning. The word covers both the quantity available and the absence of anxiety about it, which is a condition the audience for this surah did not know.

The verb concerns proximity rather than consumption. Choosing it sets the limit well before the act, and early scholars note that the Quran uses this construction for the boundaries it means to be kept at a distance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in that audience ate without counting. Grazing depended on where rain had fallen, dates were stored and measured through the year, and water was drawn by the bucket from a well someone had dug and defended. A season of drought reordered everything. So being told to eat freely, wherever you wish, described a state entirely outside their experience. The single exception attached to it would have sounded like almost nothing at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The whole instruction is given in the dual. That is a grammatical form Arabic keeps for exactly two, and English cannot show it. Every verb is addressed to both of them together: dwell, eat, do not approach. Early scholars observe that the surah gives the permission and the limit to the pair jointly, not to one of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Freedom and limit are introduced together here, in a fixed ratio. Almost everything is permitted and one thing is withheld, and that ratio is itself the teaching. A limit set against near-total permission cannot be explained as scarcity, or as restriction for its own sake. The passage also shows that a boundary can be given with no reason attached. That makes trust, rather than agreement, the thing being asked for.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same episode at greater length, including the argument used to talk the two into it.
Adds the warning about an enemy and the promise offered in exchange for approaching the tree.
Repeats the pattern of open permission with one boundary, in the ordinary setting of eating and drinking.

studies.applyIt: Take an inventory today of what is actually available to you, out loud or on paper, before you think about anything you lack. Food, water, a door that closes, people who would answer the phone. It takes four minutes. The ratio in this passage only lands if you have recently counted your own side of it.
studies.explainEasier: God told Adam and his wife to live in the Garden. They could eat from it freely, as much as they liked. But there was one tree they were told not to go near.

studies.title: Words Received On The Way Down
studies.meaning: The vocabulary here is unexpectedly gentle. The verb used is the one for a foot going out from under a person on smooth ground. It is not a word for rebellion, and early scholars keep that distinction. Then the consequence is stated plainly: a departure from one condition into another, with a place to live and provision granted for a limited time. And then the direction reverses. Adam receives words, and the turning that follows is described with a divine name built from the same verb as his own turning.
studies.historicalContext: This completes the surah's Medinan account of the first human being. Early scholars most often identify the words Adam received with a prayer preserved in another surah. In it the two admit having wronged themselves and ask for mercy. Reports on this go back to early authorities, and the identification is widely given. The sources also record other suggestions and do not treat the matter as closed.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a foot sliding on wet or polished ground. It places the event in the category of losing footing rather than of planning a wrong, and the tradition keeps to that register.
A verb suggesting meeting something coming toward you and taking it up. Adam does not compose the words. They arrive, and his part is to receive them and use them.
An intensive form from the verb for turning back, the same verb used of the human being who repents. One root carries both movements, which is why the tradition speaks of a turning that is met.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A settled place, and a stretch of time to enjoy it, were exactly what a person in that world worked for. Nomadic families moved between grazing grounds, and they named the spot they stopped at differently from the road they travelled. Townspeople measured safety in a house, a well and a grove that would still be there next year. Being granted a resting place and a limited term named the ordinary human situation exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic of the second ayah uses one verbal root for both sides of the exchange. The human being turns back, and God turns toward him. The divine name that closes the sentence is built from that same root in its most intensive form. English needs two different words for the two movements, so the connection disappears in translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The remedy is placed inside the account of the fall, not after it. The words are given to the one who needs them, rather than left for him to find. That shows something about the shape of return: it is offered before it is asked for. The passage also refuses to let the first human failure define the human being. The story does not end at the descent, and the last word in it is a name of mercy.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the prayer that early scholars most often identify with the words received here.
Adds that after the turning came both choosing and guidance, continuing the account past this point.
Extends the same opening to everyone, telling those who wronged themselves not to despair.

studies.applyIt: If you have been carrying something without ever putting it into words, borrow words rather than waiting to compose your own. Say a short established prayer of return tonight, exactly as it stands, even if it does not feel like yours yet. This passage has the words arriving first and the feeling following. That is the order most people actually find workable.
studies.explainEasier: Satan made Adam and his wife slip, and they had to leave the Garden. God sent them down to live on earth for a time. Then Adam was given words to say, and God forgave him.

studies.title: A Way Back Given Immediately
studies.meaning: The instruction to go down is repeated from two ayat earlier, and early scholars note that a repetition in the Quran normally carries something new. Here what is new is everything attached to it. The exile arrives with a provision already built into it. Guidance will come, and following it removes two things at once. The pair named covers the whole of a person's time: one word for dread of what lies ahead, one for sorrow over what lies behind. The ayah after it states the other outcome just as plainly.
studies.historicalContext: These two ayat close the surah's Medinan account of the first human being and bridge to the long address that follows. No occasion is reported for them. The early scholars treat them as the hinge of the whole story. Everything the surah goes on to say about scripture, prophets and communities is an instance of the guidance promised here in general terms.

keyTerms.note: A plural command, though only two people have been in the scene. Early scholars read the widening as taking in the whole line to come, which is why the promise attached to it is stated for everyone.
Indefinite in the Arabic: some guidance, any guidance, from Me. The form leaves the shape and the timing open while making the fact of it certain, which is the balance the sentence needs.
Sorrow over what has already happened, distinct from the fear named just before it, which looks forward. The two words together take in both directions of time and leave nothing between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest sanction that world had. A man put out of his clan lost the protection that made ordinary life possible, and could be injured or killed with nobody obliged to answer for it. Readmission needed a mediator and a settlement. So being sent out with the terms of return stated in the same breath was not how any of that worked, and the audience would have heard the difference at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about having no fear and no grief becomes a fixed formula in the Quran. It recurs in surah after surah for those under God's protection. This is its first appearance in the order of the text. It arrives at the very moment humanity is sent out of the Garden, which is the least likely place for a formula of safety to begin.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence and remedy are arranged in an order that matters. Nothing is held back until the descent has been endured, and no gap is left between the loss and the offer. That says something specific about how the relationship is meant to run. The first move is not the human being's to make. The other outcome is stated in the next ayah without softening, so the assurance is a real choice and not a general reassurance.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the formula for the friends of God, with no fear upon them and no grief.
Gives the parallel telling, promising that whoever follows the guidance will neither stray nor be wretched.
Attaches the same assurance to those who say our Lord is God and then remain upright.

studies.applyIt: Write down one thing you are afraid of and one thing you regret, on the same piece of paper, in one line each. Notice that they point in opposite directions in time and that you have been carrying both at once. You do not need to solve either today. Seeing them side by side is what this ayah makes room for.
studies.explainEasier: God told them all to go down from the Garden. But He promised that guidance would come to them. Anyone who follows it will not need to be afraid or sad. Those who turn it down belong to the Fire.

studies.title: Keep Yours And I Keep Mine
studies.meaning: The surah turns to a new audience, and it opens with a memory rather than an argument. Three things are asked in one line: recall what was given, complete what was pledged, and hold God in awe. The middle one is the striking one, since it uses the same verb on both sides. That word is a merchant's term for paying a measure in full. Using it of God as well casts the relationship as an account both parties settle, rather than as a demand made in one direction.
studies.historicalContext: Medina had large Jewish communities that had been settled there for generations. They had a scholarly tradition, palm groves and quarters they could defend. The early agreement of the city included them. Here the surah's long address to the Children of Israel begins, aimed at neighbours with standing and a shared line of prophets. Early scholars read the appeal to memory as resting on exactly that shared past.

keyTerms.note: A singular noun used for a whole history of provision. Early scholars note the singular and read it as gathering many gifts into one continuous act rather than listing them as separate items.
The word a trader uses for completing a measure with nothing held back. It carries the image of a scale that must balance, and it appears on both sides of this sentence.
From a root joining fear to withdrawal and reverence. It names an alertness before something greater than oneself rather than fright, and Arabic uses the same root for a life given over to devotion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Short measure was the classic market fraud, and everyone had a view about it. Grain and dates were sold by volume, in vessels a buyer could not easily check. A trader known for a full measure carried a reputation worth more than a season's margin. Agreements between clans worked the same way. What mattered was whether a party delivered the whole of what had been said aloud, in front of witnesses, at the time promised.
studies.didYouKnow: The address opened here does not close quickly. The surah keeps speaking to this audience, with only brief turns aside, for roughly eighty ayat. It recalls a long sequence of episodes from their history. This is the most sustained address of its kind anywhere in the Quran, and it comes at the front of the longest surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Casting a covenant in the language of trade makes it mutual without making it equal. God is described as paying what He owes. That is a striking thing for a scripture to say about an all-powerful party. The tradition understands it as a debt freely taken on, not one imposed from outside. The order of the clauses matters too. Memory comes first, since a pledge nobody remembers the reason for is not going to be kept.

crossReferences.why: Records the taking of the covenant itself, with the specific undertakings attached on both sides.
States the general principle of fulfilling God's covenant once entered into, and not breaking oaths after confirming them.
Ties gratitude to increase, connecting the remembering asked here to what follows from it.

studies.applyIt: Name three things you were given that you did nothing to earn, going back as far as childhood: a teacher, a language, a place to live. Say them out loud once. Then look at one commitment you made and have been half-keeping. The order in this ayah is deliberate, and remembering first tends to make the second part easier.
studies.explainEasier: God speaks to the Children of Israel and asks them to remember the good things He gave them. He asks them to keep the promise they made to Him. If they do, He will keep His promise to them.

studies.title: Do Not Sell It Cheaply
studies.meaning: The new revelation is introduced as confirming what the audience already has, not as replacing it, and the participle used comes from the root for truthfulness. Then come two warnings. The first is oddly specific: not do not reject it, but do not be the first to. Early scholars read this as weight placed on precedent, since those who could recognise a thing set the terms for everyone watching. The second names a trade, and calls the price small without any reference to its size.
studies.historicalContext: This comes early in the surah's address to the Children of Israel, in the years after the migration. The community had settled among long-established neighbours who held scripture and scholarly standing. The tone is an appeal rather than a verdict. The classical works read it as addressed to a moment of decision, not as a description of a settled outcome.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth in speech, which also gives the word for charity given from wealth. The participle presents the new revelation as certifying what came before rather than as competing with it.
The ordinary word for first in sequence. Its presence changes the warning entirely, making the issue one of who moves first and what follows from that rather than of the position itself.
A price, and an adjective calling it little. Early scholars observe that the smallness is not a measure of the sum but of what it buys, so any worldly return would be described this way.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were no fixed prices in a seventh-century market. Every sale was struck by argument. Everybody knew the shame of a man who had let something good go cheap because he needed cash that week. Selling a she-camel before the season, or a stand of palms to cover a debt, was the sort of thing people remembered about a family for years. The language of a bad price carried all of that.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered as confirming shares its root with two very different Arabic words. One is the ordinary term for telling the truth. The other is the term for money given away from your wealth. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect them through the idea of something proving genuine: a statement, a gift, or here a book measured against an earlier one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The new book is presented as confirming the old, not replacing it. That sets up a continuity running through the whole Quran, where the prophets form one line carrying one message. The ayah then draws a consequence from it. Recognising something is not a neutral event. Whoever is placed to recognise it carries more weight in what they do next. The warning about a small price adds the other half, since recognition can be overridden by interest.

crossReferences.why: States the same relationship, a book sent down confirming what was between its hands already.
Calls the revelation both confirming of earlier scripture and a guardian watching over it.
Has Jesus describe himself as confirming the Torah, the same relation in an earlier link of the chain.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you know to be right and have quietly declined to say, because saying it would cost you standing with a particular group. Name the price to yourself in plain terms today. You do not have to act on it yet. Pricing it accurately is the step most people skip, and it is the step this ayah is about.
studies.explainEasier: God asks them to believe in the new book He has sent down. It agrees with the book they already have. He tells them not to be the first to turn it down, and not to sell His signs for a small price.

studies.title: Reading It And Forgetting Yourself
studies.meaning: The Arabic for mixing truth with falsehood is really a verb for dressing. So the picture is a disguise rather than a dilution: truth put into borrowed clothing until nobody can identify it. Concealment is named beside it, with the aggravating detail that they know. Three practices are then named, the third of them shared rather than private. The question that ends the passage is the famous one, and early scholars are careful with it. It faults forgetting yourself, not the instructing.
studies.historicalContext: Medina's older communities included men whose authority rested on reading and explaining texts. This passage speaks straight to that position, inside the surah's address to those who already held scripture. Early scholars read the last of these ayat as aimed at scholars in particular. They add that dropping the teaching would double the fault rather than remove it.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives the ordinary word for a garment. The instruction is not about blending two substances but about putting the wrong covering on something so that it passes for what it is not.
A wide word for goodness done to others, used in the Quran of kindness to parents and of righteousness generally. It names a whole disposition rather than a particular act.

Ordinary forgetting, and also deliberate setting aside. The choice is exact, since the failing described is not hypocrisy in the sense of pretending but of genuinely leaving oneself out of the account.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cloth announced who you were. A man's dress marked his tribe, his means and often his trade, and disguise was a known device. An unrecognised figure at night was simply someone wearing a cloak that was not his. Traders also knew the practice of dressing poor goods in good wrapping. An audience hearing about truth being clothed in falsehood would have seen the operation, not a metaphor.
studies.didYouKnow: Nearly the same sentence appears again later in the Quran, in another surah and to the same audience. It uses the same verb for clothing truth in falsehood. The two are close enough that early scholars often treat the passages together, and explain both with the same examples.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two failures that usually get merged. Concealing is one thing, and disguising is another and worse, because it leaves something in circulation that looks like the truth. The question at the end then turns the whole reproach inward. It makes reading the text a form of exposure rather than of safety. Knowledge is presented here as raising the standard a person is measured against, never as meeting it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the charge almost word for word, clothing truth with falsehood while knowing what is being done.
States the same reproach in general terms, asking why people say what they do not do.
Returns later in this surah to those who conceal what was sent down after it was made clear.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have said recently that was technically accurate and designed to leave a false impression. Everybody has one. You do not need to correct it publicly. Just identify it, name what the true version would have sounded like, and notice how small the distance between them was.
studies.explainEasier: God tells them not to dress up the truth as something false, and not to hide it. He tells them to pray and to give charity. He asks why they tell other people to do good while forgetting themselves.

studies.title: Two Resources For Hard Days
studies.meaning: Two things are named as sources of help, and both of them are demanding: holding steady, and prayer. The passage then admits the difficulty instead of talking past it. The practice is heavy, it says, except for those who bow. The next line says what makes it lighter, which is that they expect to meet their Lord and to return to Him. So the difficulty is not removed by willpower. It is removed by a change in what a person thinks the effort is for.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this passage sits in a long section addressed to the Children of Israel, recalling favours received and promises made. The address here widens enough that the classical scholars read the counsel as general, and then it narrows again in the third line. The ayat around it rebuke people who preach to others and neglect themselves. That places the advice pointedly: seek the help you have been recommending.

keyTerms.note: Wider than patience in English. The root is used for binding something in place, and for a bitter medicinal plant. So it carries holding fast and swallowing something hard at once.
Used for ground that has sunk down and for a voice that drops. It describes a lowering that is inward before it shows in the body. In that state the weight described stops being felt as weight.

keyTerms.gloss: they expect, they hold as certain
keyTerms.note: Usually this verb means to think or suppose. Early scholars read it here as settled expectation. The same word can slide between guessing and knowing, and the context decides which.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices had a physical cost in that setting. The prayer broke into trade and travel five times a day. A merchant who stopped at midday in a market stopped earning while others did not. Endurance was the desert virtue everyone already respected, praised in poetry as the mark of a man who kept his word under pressure. Naming the two together took a familiar tribal ideal and tied it to something that cost time in public.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of steadfastness and prayer appears twice in this surah, within a hundred ayat. It comes here, and again later in almost the same words. The second time the address narrows to those who believe, and adds that God is with the steadfast. Early scholars treat the repeat as deliberate, since the second use answers the difficulty the first one admits.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Help is offered here as a practice, not as a rescue, and that sets the tone for how the Quran treats hardship generally. The one thing said to make the practice bearable is a belief about where a life is heading. So what a person holds about the end reshapes how the middle feels. And by admitting that the counsel is heavy, the passage refuses to pretend that faith removes strain. It redirects it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same counsel to believers and adds the promise that God is with the steadfast.
Instructs the Prophet to keep his household in prayer and to be patient with it himself.
Contrasts human anxiety under pressure with those steady in prayer, the same diagnosis and remedy.

studies.applyIt: The next time something goes wrong in your day, notice the gap between the news arriving and your first reaction. Put one small thing in that gap: two minutes of stillness, or the next prayer brought slightly forward. You are not trying to feel better. You are practising the order these lines set out, help first and response second, at a scale small enough to keep.
studies.explainEasier: When life is hard, God says to get help from two things: staying patient and praying. That is not easy. It gets easier for people who remember that one day they will go back to God.

studies.title: Four Exits, All Closed
studies.meaning: Four denials come in one sentence. Each one names an institution the audience actually used. Nobody pays off another person's account. No pleading is accepted from a soul, no matching payment is taken, and no group comes to the rescue. On the third of those, the word usually rendered ransom is a term of balance and exchange. On the second, early scholars read the denial alongside passages elsewhere about speaking up for someone by God's leave. What is refused here is any claim made as of right.
studies.historicalContext: This comes in the surah's address to those who held earlier scripture, following two ayat that recall a history of favour. The early scholars note that the ayah is repeated almost exactly later in the same surah. They treat both places as closing off an assumption widespread in that world. Standing, lineage or connection would count for something when the account was finally settled.

keyTerms.note: The verb for settling a debt or standing in for an obligation. It names the specific act of one party covering what another owes, which is exactly what is being ruled out.
From a root meaning even or paired. The one who intercedes joins himself to the one pleaded for, so where there was a single petitioner there are now two. The image is of company, not influence.
From the root for balance and justice. Here it names a compensating weight offered to level a scale, which is why the word for fairness and the word for a payoff are the same word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every one of these was a working part of Arabian life. A killing was settled by a payment in camels agreed between clans, and captives taken in a raid were released for a price. A weak man in trouble was spoken for by someone stronger, and if all else failed his tribe rode out to help him. A person's security was the sum of those four things. The ayah takes them away one at a time.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah returns later in the same surah with two of its clauses swapped. What is refused second here is refused third there. Early scholars noticed the switch early and discuss it. Both places fall inside the same long address, which is one reason the pair is usually read together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lists four mechanisms instead of making a general statement. Answering for what you do is not simply something nobody has taken over. It is something nobody can take over. What can be shared in this life cannot be shared there. This does not present God as unwilling to relent, since the surah says a great deal elsewhere about mercy and pardon. It shows instead that mercy comes from one direction only, and cannot be arranged sideways between creatures.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same point in family terms, saying no father will discharge anything on behalf of his child.
States it as bare fact, a day on which no soul possesses anything at all for another.
Supplies the other half, describing intercession that occurs only by God's own permission.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you are relying on someone else to carry for you. A decision, an apology, an awkward talk you have quietly handed to a family member. Take the smallest part of it back today and do that part yourself. This ayah is about a limit that already exists, and it is easier to meet it early.
studies.explainEasier: Be ready for a day when no person can help another at all. Nobody will be allowed to speak up for you. No payment will be taken to set you free. No one will come to help.

studies.title: Sons Killed, Daughters Spared
studies.meaning: The memory here is deliberately unsoftened. The verb for what was done to them first describes driving animals out to pasture. So the cruelty is pictured as steady herding rather than as separate acts. The policy itself is named exactly: sons killed, women left alive. That is how a people is ended without ending its use. The word that closes the ayah carries two settled senses. Early scholars read it either as naming the ordeal a trial or as naming the rescue a signal favour, and they record both without choosing.
studies.historicalContext: This opens the surah's run of recollections addressed to the Children of Israel. Each one begins with the same formula, and remember, and each takes up a single episode. This first one goes back before the exodus, to the condition the rescue was from. Early scholars note that this is the necessary starting point, since the favour cannot be weighed without the state it interrupted.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of driving livestock out to graze. Applied to people it carries relentlessness and direction, a condition imposed continuously rather than a set of separate cruelties.
Built on the root for life, so the word is literally about letting live. In the same surah a different form of this root carries the sense of shame, which is one root serving two distant meanings.
The word covers testing and also a conspicuous benefit conferred. Early scholars divide over which is meant here, and the ambiguity leaves the sentence pointing at both the ordeal and the rescue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Slavery was ordinary in seventh-century Arabia, and everyone knew how it worked. Captives taken in raids became household labour. Status passed to children born into it. Adult men were the security problem, while women and children were taken into the household. An Arabian audience did not need the policy in this ayah explained. They knew at once what it was meant to do and how long it would take.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sparing the women here and the word for feeling shame used earlier in this surah come from the same three letters. The early Arabic dictionary writers list both senses under one root. They connect them through the idea of holding back. It is holding back from killing in one case, and holding back out of modesty in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is presented here as something to be recalled, not merely believed, and the recollection is made to include the injury. A rescue described without its danger becomes a pleasant fact instead of a debt. The passage also refuses to leave the suffering unnamed or made spiritual. What happened is stated in plain words first, and only then is the word for trial placed over it. That order keeps the trial from explaining the pain away.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same policy with its motive, describing a ruler who divided the population and weakened one part.
Has Moses himself recall this deliverance to his people in almost identical terms.
Repeats the recollection in another surah, again closing on the word for a great trial.

studies.applyIt: Think of one hard stretch you came out of. Describe it to yourself in the order this ayah uses. The difficulty first, in accurate detail, and only then the way out. Most of us tell it the other way round, or skip the difficulty entirely. Then the relief goes thin, because there is nothing behind it.
studies.explainEasier: God reminds them that He saved them from Pharaoh's people. Those people treated them very badly, killing their sons and letting the women live. That whole time was a huge test for them.

studies.title: A Road Through The Water
studies.meaning: One short ayah holds a rescue and a drowning, and puts the same people in front of both. The Arabic construction is unusual: the sea is parted by you or for you, and early scholars note the wording, reading the deliverance as happening on their account rather than merely near them. Then comes the part that matters most. They were watching. Nothing here was inferred, reported or taken on trust, which is what makes the episodes that follow in this surah so difficult to explain.
studies.historicalContext: This is the second in the surah's run of recollections, given in Medina. The account is compressed to a single line here, while other surahs give it at length with dialogue and pursuit. Early scholars treat the brevity as deliberate, since the audience knew the story thoroughly. The surah is not narrating but recalling, item by item, a list of things already granted.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for dividing one thing into two. Three ayat later the same root names the criterion given to Moses, so a single set of letters covers both the parting of water and the separating of truth from falsehood.
From a root suggesting raising to high ground out of danger. It is the word used across the Quran for prophets brought out of destruction, and it implies extraction rather than escape.
Simple watching, in the present tense, so the clause places them inside the moment rather than remembering it. The grammar makes them witnesses in real time rather than inheritors of an account.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabs of the Hijaz were not a seafaring people. The Red Sea was the edge of the world they moved in. The crossing to Abyssinia, which some of the earliest Muslims made to escape persecution, was a real undertaking. Water on that scale was the final barrier, the thing that ended a route rather than continuing it. So a sea that opens into a road was the image of a way out where there plainly was none.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for parting the sea shares its root with the word for the criterion. That word appears a few ayat later, as one of the things given to Moses. So the Quran's name for a book that tells true from false is built on the same three letters. Those letters also name an act of physically dividing water.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting rescue and destruction in one sentence keeps them from being two separate lessons. The same event that saved one group ended another. That is how the Quran generally describes deliverance, not as harm avoided but as a division made. The watching matters for what comes next. If seeing were enough to settle a person, the rest of this section of the surah would have nothing to report.

crossReferences.why: Tells the crossing at length, including the moment the people believed they had been overtaken.
Gives the instruction to strike out a dry path and describes what then covered the pursuers.
Records what Pharaoh said as the water closed, and the answer he was given.

studies.applyIt: Recall something you personally witnessed that ought to have changed you and did not, or not for long. Not a failure of belief, just of retention. Write one sentence about it and keep the sentence somewhere you will see it. This whole section of the surah turns on how quickly seeing wears off, and noticing your own version is the honest way in.
studies.explainEasier: God reminds them how He split the sea open for them and saved them. He drowned Pharaoh's people. All of it happened while they stood and watched it with their own eyes.

studies.title: Forty Nights And A Calf
studies.meaning: Forty nights of absence, a substitute made in the meantime, and then a pardon. The verb for that pardon has a striking background. Its root describes wind blowing over tracks in sand until nothing can be followed, so the word does not mean overlooking but erasing. The stated purpose of the pardon is gratitude rather than mere relief. Early scholars then differ over the last of these ayat, reading the Book and the Criterion as two names for one thing or as two distinct gifts.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's Medinan run of recollections. Another surah describes the appointment of forty nights as thirty completed by ten. Early scholars read the two accounts together rather than as alternatives. The calf episode is given at length elsewhere in the Quran. That telling includes the detail that the image was made from ornaments the people were carrying. Here it is compressed to a clause.

keyTerms.note: The period is counted in nights rather than days, which was the ordinary Arabian reckoning. Months began with the sighting of a crescent after sunset, so a span of time was naturally measured from dark to dark.
The root is used of wind wiping out footprints and of a ruin returning to bare ground. Pardon in this word is not a decision to ignore something but the removal of the trace itself.

From the verb for dividing one thing from another. It names whatever draws the line between truth and falsehood, which is why early scholars can read it as the scripture itself or as something given alongside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a genuine skill in that world. A man could read from prints in sand who had passed, how many, how heavily loaded and how long ago. Disputes over stolen camels were settled by people who could follow a trail for days. The one thing that defeated them was wind. When the sand had shifted, the trace was not faint but gone, and that is the word this passage uses for pardon.
studies.didYouKnow: The two things given to Moses in the last of these ayat carry two names. One is a word for scripture, and the other is built on the root for splitting. That second root has already appeared in the surah two ayat earlier, for the parting of the sea. So the same letters carry a physical separation and a moral one within a few lines of each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of events in these three ayat is the argument. Failure comes after an appointment, pardon comes after failure, and the giving of scripture comes after pardon. Nothing is held back pending improvement. That shows something about how the relationship is understood to work. The stated aim of the pardon confirms it: gratitude is presented as the intended result of mercy, not as its price.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same appointment as thirty nights completed with ten, making the count forty.
Gives the calf episode in full, including the confrontation when Moses returns to find it.
States the consequence for those who made the calf, and what followed for those who turned back afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you were forgiven that you have kept in your own records anyway. Still filed, still consulted. The word used in this passage is about a trace that is genuinely gone. Try that standard once today, on something someone did to you that you have officially let go of but not actually erased.
studies.explainEasier: God called Moses away for forty nights. While he was gone, the people began to worship a calf, which was very wrong. But God still pardoned them, and He gave Moses the Scripture to guide them.

studies.title: Turn Back To Your Maker
studies.meaning: Moses addresses them as his own people first. Then he names the wrong exactly, and locates the injury in themselves rather than in God. The name he uses for God twice is unusual and pointed: the Originator, the one who brings a thing into being distinct and without flaw. It is set against an image they had shaped with their hands. The instruction that follows belonged to that community in that moment. The classical works record more than one account of what it involved and how far it reached. What resolves the ayah is the turning God then makes toward them.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's Medinan recollections. The episode of the calf and its aftermath are told across several surahs. The accounts of what happened next differ in the classical commentaries, which set the reports side by side rather than smoothing them together. What all of them share is the ending given here: the turning was accepted. Early scholars concentrate their comment on the two divine names that close the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be free of defect and clear of something. It names the maker who brings a thing into existence distinct and whole, which is a pointed choice in a passage about a shaped image.
The verb is simply to return. Repentance in Arabic is not primarily an emotion or a confession but a change of direction, which is why the same word can be used of God turning toward a person.
From the root that also gives the word for a womb. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect the two, reading the divine name as a mercy that is sustaining and continuous rather than occasional.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In that society, blame ran through the group rather than around single people. An offence by one member exposed his whole clan to a claim, and clans often punished their own to head off a wider reckoning. Here the order goes to a whole people, and it asks the people themselves to act. That fitted a world where a wrong was never just private and a settlement was never just personal.
studies.didYouKnow: The name for God used twice in this ayah is rare in the Quran. It appears again in a run of divine names near the end of another surah, and almost nowhere else. A reader working through the text will meet it here, in a passage about a made image, and then hardly again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are settled by the wording rather than stated outright. The wrong is described as done to themselves, which places the damage of turning to a made object in the one who turns, not in the one turned away from. And the ayah closes with mercy in the strongest form the language has, right after its hardest sentence. The tradition reads that placement as the point. The passage ends where it does on purpose.

crossReferences.why: Places the same rare name for God among the Creator and the Fashioner in a list of divine names.
Records Aaron's warning during the episode and the answer his people gave him.
Describes what followed for those who made the calf and for those who turned back afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you name your own wrongs to yourself. Most of us describe them by their effect on other people, or by how they looked. This passage names one by what it was and says who it damaged, in that order and without softening. Try writing one sentence about something in that shape, and stop before adding the explanation.
studies.explainEasier: Moses told his people that they had wronged themselves by worshipping the calf. He told them to turn back to their Maker. They did, and God accepted their turning and forgave them.

studies.title: Until We See Him Plainly
studies.meaning: The demand is not for evidence but for one particular form of it. The word used means openly, to the eye, the way an object in front of you is seen. Belief in the messenger is then made to depend on that. What follows is a blast and then a revival. Early scholars divide over whether the word for their death is literal, or describes a stunning that emptied them of awareness. The purpose given for the reversal is the same purpose given for the pardon a few lines earlier.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the run of recollections given in Medina. Another surah connects the demand with a group chosen from among the people to go with Moses for an appointed meeting. The classical commentaries read the two passages together. The episode is also recalled elsewhere in almost the same words. That is one reason early scholars treat the wording here as fixed, not as a loose summary.

keyTerms.note: From a root for what is out in the open, used of a voice raised aloud as well as of something visible. It specifies a mode of perception, which is what makes the demand a demand about method.

The same word used earlier in this surah for what the people in the storm parable put their fingers in their ears against. It covers both a lightning strike and any blast that empties a person of sense.
The Quran uses this one verb for raising the dead and for dispatching a messenger to a people. Both are a sending out, which is why the language of resurrection and the language of prophecy overlap.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Direct sight was the gold standard of proof in Arabian dispute. A man who had seen a thing himself outranked any number who had heard about it, and testimony in an assembly was weighed by how close the witness had stood. Applying that standard was not stupid; it was correct procedure everywhere else in their lives. The passage does not fault them for wanting evidence. It answers a demand for the wrong kind.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for reviving them is the one the Quran uses for raising the dead on the last day. It is also the verb for sending a prophet to a community. Arabic makes no distinction between the two dispatches. So a reader meets the same word describing a messenger being sent and a body being brought back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Whether and how God may be seen has been discussed at great length in the tradition, and that discussion is not settled here. What this passage shows is narrower and firmer. Making belief depend on a chosen form of proof puts the condition where it does not belong. The rest of the sentence answers that on its own terms. The reversal of death that follows was itself witnessed, and it still did not work as the guarantee they had asked for.

crossReferences.why: Recalls the same demand in nearly identical words, calling it a request for something greater still.
Records Moses asking to see, and what happened to the mountain when it was shown.
Names the group chosen for the appointed meeting and describes what overtook them.

studies.applyIt: Identify one condition you have quietly attached to trusting something. A sign you are waiting for, a proof you have decided would settle it. Say it out loud in full, as a sentence beginning with the word until. Hearing your own condition stated completely is usually enough to show you what you have been doing.
studies.explainEasier: They told Moses they would not believe him until they saw God with their own eyes. A blast struck them while they watched. Then God brought them back to life so they might be thankful.

studies.title: Cloud, Manna And Quail
studies.meaning: Three provisions arrive without labour: shade that travels with them, and food of two kinds sent down. Early scholars differ over what exactly the first food was. Some describe a sweet substance found in the morning, and others treat the word as a general term for whatever came as a gift rather than as a crop. Then the sentence turns. Halfway through, the address changes from you to they, and the naming of the wrong is spoken about them rather than to them.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's recollections of what was given during the years in the wilderness. Another surah pairs the same two foods with the twelve springs and the tribal divisions. Early scholars gather the accounts into a single period rather than treating them as separate incidents. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It belongs to the run, not to an event.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cover over. The same three letters give the ordinary Arabic word for grief, understood by the early Arabic dictionary writers as what covers the heart, so covering is the shared idea.
Shares a root with the words for a favour bestowed and for reminding someone of a favour given. Early scholars split between a particular substance and a general term for what arrives unearned.
The plural of a word meaning pleasant, clean and agreeable. It describes food by its quality rather than by its category, and the same root is used of good speech and good land.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade was the scarce commodity, more than food. A day's travel was planned around where cover would be at midday, and a single acacia or a rock overhang on a route was known by name and argued over. Caravans halted through the worst hours and moved at the edges of the day. To describe a cloud that stayed above a moving people was to describe something more extravagant to that audience than any meal.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah begins by addressing the audience directly and ends by speaking about them in the third person. The switch happens in the middle of a sentence, at exactly the point where the wrong is named. Arabic rhetoricians have a term for this kind of pivot, and they treat it as a deliberate device. Early scholars note this ayah as an instance of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The last words of the ayah correct a natural guess about what is at stake when a gift is treated badly. Gratitude adds nothing to God, and its absence takes nothing from Him. So the damage of ingratitude falls wholly on the one who is not grateful. That makes thanks a matter of getting things right, not of good manners. The passage also shows provision arriving before it is earned, which is the pattern this whole section keeps repeating.

crossReferences.why: Pairs the same two foods with the springs given for the tribes, in a fuller telling.
Repeats the provision with a warning attached about going too far in what has been given.
Puts the same instruction generally, to eat of good provision and be thankful for the favour.

studies.applyIt: Eat one meal today that you did not choose, cook or pay for, if such a meal comes your way, and say something specific about it to whoever provided it. If no such meal appears, name the last one that did. The passage is about noticing provision that arrives without your arrangement, and most of it goes past unremarked.
studies.explainEasier: God gave them clouds for shade in the desert. He sent down food for them, and told them to eat the good things He had provided. When they went wrong, they only hurt themselves.

studies.title: One Word At The Gate
studies.meaning: Entry is granted, food without limit is granted, and two conditions are attached to the manner of arriving. The word they were given to say is remarkable. It comes from the verb for lifting a load down off a camel's back at the end of a stage, so what they were asked to pronounce was a request to be unburdened. Early scholars do not name the town, and neither does the Quran; they record several suggestions and leave it. The ayah then adds something nobody asked for, an increase for those who do well.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the recollections. The episode appears again in another surah in nearly the same words, and early scholars read the two together. They differ on which town is meant. They also differ on whether the order about the gate describes a posture or an inward state. Most settle on lowered bearing rather than any set physical form, and they do not press beyond what the text says.

keyTerms.note: A single word from the verb for setting a load on the ground. Given as something to say, it makes the request itself the act: asking that a weight be taken off rather than describing one.
A plural form describing how they were to enter. Early scholars read it as lowered bearing rather than a specific posture, since the instruction concerns the manner of arriving at a place.
From a root meaning both good and beautiful. It names doing a thing well beyond what was asked, which is why the increase promised to them is placed outside the terms already stated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: At the end of a day's march the camels were couched and the loads lifted off. The word for that unloading is the word this passage puts in their mouths. Anyone who had travelled with goods knew the specific relief of that moment, when the animals stopped shifting and the weight was on the ground. It is the plainest possible image for asking that something be taken off you.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about eating plentifully wherever you wish appears in this surah once before. It comes in the instruction given to the first human being in the Garden. The same wording is used here at the gate of a town, so a reader working through the surah meets an unmistakable echo. A spoken word is required in the second case, where a tree was withheld in the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is asked at the gate costs nothing material. The conditions are a bearing and a single word, and against them stand an open town and unlimited provision. That ratio makes the terms of pardon a matter of posture rather than of payment. It fits how the surah has described forgiveness elsewhere. The addition at the end goes further, promising increase to those who do well, so the arrangement is not merely a settling of accounts.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction about the gate and the word, in nearly identical wording.
Uses the same phrase about eating plentifully wherever you wish, in the Garden rather than at a gate.
Recalls the covenant and the instruction to enter the gate bowing, among other undertakings.

studies.applyIt: Find the shortest true sentence for something you have been carrying and say it once, out loud, when nobody is in the room. Not an explanation and not a full account. One short line. The passage puts a single word at the gate, and there is something in the brevity that longer versions of the same thing keep losing.
studies.explainEasier: God told them to enter the town and eat from it as much as they liked. They were to go in through the gate humbly and ask to be forgiven. He promised to forgive them and to give more to those who do good.

studies.title: A Different Word Entirely
studies.meaning: One word was given, and another was said in its place. That is the whole of the offence, and the Arabic keeps it precise: a saying other than the one that was said to them. The sentence then names the wrongdoers a second time instead of saying they, so the consequence is tied to that group again by name. Early scholars point out that this narrows the scope rather than widening it. Nobody else at the gate is swept into it.
studies.historicalContext: This follows directly on the instruction at the gate. The same pair of ayat appears in another surah, again with the changed word named and the consequence following. Early scholars report various accounts of what was said instead, and of what the scourge consisted of. They are cautious here. They generally note that the Quran specifies neither, and decline to fill in more than the text does.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to put one thing in the place of another. It is not about mishearing or forgetting. The word describes a swap made, which requires knowing what was there to begin with.
Indefinite in the Arabic, so the offence is not a specific alternative formula but any saying that was not the one given. The vagueness is the point, since only one thing had been asked for.
A word used in the Quran for various visitations sent upon a people. Early scholars pass on several accounts of what it was here and generally leave the question where the text leaves it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a mostly unwritten world, passing things on word for word was a trained skill and a serious duty. Clans sent messages by men chosen for exact memory, poems were passed on line by line, and family lines were recited without change. Everybody also knew the man who improved a message in the retelling. Changing a word given to you was a known failure, and people could name what it cost.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic would ordinarily use a pronoun for the second mention of a group already named in the same sentence. This ayah does not. It repeats the full phrase instead. Early scholars treat the repetition as deliberate. They read it as confining the consequence strictly to those who changed the word, and not to everyone who was present at the gate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a word as a thing that can be held in trust. That makes accuracy in passing it on a moral matter, not merely a technical one. What was asked for at the gate cost nothing, so the change cannot be explained by difficulty. That leaves it as a small act of self-assertion: altering what you were given in order to stay the author of it. The surah locates a great deal of trouble in exactly that impulse.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same substitution and consequence in another surah, in almost identical wording.
Describes words being displaced from their proper places, and speech twisted with the tongue.
Speaks of hearts hardening and words being moved from their positions after a covenant was broken.

studies.applyIt: Repeat one thing today exactly as it was said to you, rather than in your own words. A message from one person to another, an instruction, a piece of news. Notice how strong the pull is to adjust it slightly, and let the adjustment go unmade. The pull is the thing worth observing here.
studies.explainEasier: Some of them changed the word they had been told to say and said a different one instead. Because of that, God sent down a punishment on the ones who had done wrong.

studies.title: Twelve Springs From One Rock
studies.meaning: Moses asks for water on behalf of others, and the Arabic verb carries exactly that. It is a seeking of something for someone else. What comes is more specific than what was asked for. It is not simply water but twelve outlets, one for each group, so that every party knew where to drink without dispute. Early scholars note that a different verb is used in the parallel account elsewhere, a gentler word for water welling up. They read the two as describing different moments of the same event.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the recollections of the wilderness years. The splitting of the people into twelve tribes is stated elsewhere in the Quran and assumed here, which is why the number of springs matches without a word of explanation. Early scholars treat the giving of a drinking place to each group as the telling detail. A large camp sharing one source was the standard occasion for a fight.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to ask for water, and the construction that follows makes clear he asked on behalf of his people rather than for himself. The request is representative from the start.
A verb of sudden splitting open under pressure. Another surah uses a milder word for the same event, and early scholars read the pair as a first welling followed by full flow.
A noun of place from the verb to drink. It names not the water but the spot at which each group drank, which is what the provision actually settled between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the thing people fought over. Wells were owned, inherited and defended, and a clan's range was defined by which sources it could reach. The order in which herds were watered was a standing occasion for dispute, and feuds that lasted generations began at a watering place. So assigning each group its own outlet was not decoration on a miracle. It removed the most reliable cause of bloodshed in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The parallel account of this event in another surah uses a different verb for the water appearing. That verb means to well up gently rather than to burst out. Early scholars noticed the difference early on. They generally read the two words as catching successive moments, first the seepage and then the full flow, rather than as two versions of one description.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given exceeds the request in a particular direction. What was asked was water. What came was water plus an arrangement that headed off the fight the water would otherwise have caused. That suggests something about how petitions are met. The granting can address a need the asker had not named. The instruction that closes the ayah confirms it. A provision that arrives with a warning about ruin attached assumes the receivers know what they are capable of.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same episode with the tribes named as twelve and a gentler verb for the water.
States the general principle behind this scene, that God is near and answers the one who calls.
Grounds the whole matter, making every living thing from water as a sign for those who deny.

studies.applyIt: Ask for something today on behalf of someone else, by name, without mentioning yourself in it. That is the shape of the request in this ayah and it is a different exercise from praying for yourself. Notice whether you can hold the other person clearly in mind for the length of the asking.
studies.explainEasier: Moses asked God for water for his people. God told him to strike the rock with his staff. Twelve springs burst out of it, one for each tribe, so everyone knew where to drink.

studies.title: Cucumbers, Lentils And Onions
studies.meaning: The complaint is about monotony, and it comes itemised. The reply turns on one word: would you exchange what is lower for what is better. That word for lower also means nearer at hand, so the sentence names the trade exactly, the immediate against the excellent. Early scholars divide on details here. They differ on whether one of the vegetables is garlic or wheat, and on whether the place named is Egypt in particular or any settled town. The ayah ends by attaching a consequence to particular acts, and then naming them.
studies.historicalContext: This closes the surah's run of wilderness recollections. Early scholars read the statements at the end as describing what followed for the generation whose acts the ayah names. They do not read them as a permanent description. They note that the surah goes on almost at once to say that reward belongs to whoever believes and does good, from whatever community.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning nearness. The word carries both senses at once, so the exchange being questioned is not simply bad for good but the close and available for the genuinely better.

One of the few words in the Quran where the early Arabic dictionary writers record two settled readings. Translations still divide between them, and the classical commentaries pass on both without forcing a choice.
From a root meaning to be brought low or made tractable, used of an animal broken to the yoke. It names a condition of reduced standing rather than an emotion felt about it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The list is farm produce. Cucumbers, lentils and onions grow on watered ground that someone tends through a season, and none of it travels with a moving camp. Life away from farmland meant a narrow diet: dates, milk, bread when grain could be got, and meat now and then. Families in Arabia moved between settled and nomadic living often enough that this longing for the food of the fields was entirely familiar.
studies.didYouKnow: One of the vegetables in the list has never been settled. The early Arabic dictionary writers record it as garlic and also as wheat, tracing the word to different origins. English translations still divide between the two readings today. It is a small, honest case of the commentary tradition keeping a disagreement instead of solving it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange being questioned is not between something good and something evil. That would be easy to see. It is between the better and the merely nearer. That is the harder call, and the one people get wrong again and again, because what is close to hand feels like an argument. The passage also ties its consequence to named acts rather than to who someone is. That is how the surah handles such statements generally, and how the classical commentaries read this one.

crossReferences.why: Describes a town secure and provided for that denied the favours, and what was then laid on it.
Attaches a warning about going too far to the same wilderness provision described just before.
Follows shortly after in this surah and states that reward turns on belief and action, not on community.

studies.applyIt: Notice one choice today where you take the nearer option over the better one, knowing the difference. The coffee instead of the sleep, the message instead of the call. Do not fix it. Just say the trade out loud in the terms this ayah uses, naming both sides, and see whether you still make it.
studies.explainEasier: They got tired of eating the same food and asked Moses for vegetables instead. He asked them why they would swap something better for something worse. They were told to go down to a town and find it there.

studies.title: Reward Measured By Deed
studies.meaning: Four communities are named, and then the sentence turns on a condition: any who believe in God and the Last Day, and act righteously. The reward is attached to that condition, not to the label. Scholars differ sharply over how far it reaches. Many early scholars read it as describing those who followed their own prophets faithfully, before the final message reached them. Others read the condition as standing on its own terms. The Quran states the test and does not list the cases.
studies.historicalContext: This line sits inside a long Medinan address to the Children of Israel. That address recalls rescue from Pharaoh, the springs in the desert, and covenants broken again and again. Here it interrupts the record of failure with a statement of principle. The Sabeans are named only three times in the Quran, and early scholars already found them hard to identify. They record several proposals without settling on one.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary trade word for a worker's pay, not a gift. It means something earned and owed at the end of a job. That is why the passage attaches it to acting rather than to belonging.
From a root meaning to be in good repair, or fit for use. It is the opposite of the word used for spoiling. Right action here is work that holds together, not work that impresses.
Grief over what is already past. The same clause sets it apart from fear, which looks forward. Together they cover the two directions worry travels, and both are lifted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was religiously mixed in a way Mecca was not. Jewish tribes had been settled there for generations, farming and trading alongside the Arab clans, and Christian merchants and monks were familiar figures on the northern routes. Questions about who stood where before God were not abstract in that town. They came up between neighbours, in-laws and business partners, which is the setting in which this line was heard.
studies.didYouKnow: Nearly the same sentence appears twice more in the Quran, in surahs five and twenty-two. Each time the communities are listed in a slightly different order, with small changes in wording. Early scholars noticed the variation and discussed what each ordering brings out. It is one of the clearest cases of the Quran restating a principle rather than simply repeating it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test given is conduct joined to belief in God and the coming reckoning, and it is stated without reference to which community you belong to. That puts the decision about any one person beyond human reach. Nobody can audit another's belief, or how far the message ever reached them. The passage also refuses despair as a settled state for the faithful. Neither fear ahead nor grief behind will have the last word.

crossReferences.why: Restates the same principle with the communities listed in a different order.
Names the same groups and says God will decide between them on the Day of Resurrection.
Gives the condition in its shortest form: whoever submits to God and does good.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you place someone in a category and stop thinking about them. It might be a colleague of another faith, or none. Try holding the question of where they stand before God open rather than closed, and let your dealings with them run on what they actually do. That is the discipline this line asks for, and it is easier to hold than to start.
studies.explainEasier: God lists several groups of people here. Then He says what really counts: believing in God and the last day, and doing good. Anyone who does that gets their reward, and will not be afraid or sad.

studies.title: Take It With Strength
studies.meaning: A pledge is recalled together with the setting it was made in, a mountain raised above the people who were making it. Two instructions follow, and they are not the same. The first is about grip: take what has been given with strength, a word the early scholars gloss as resolve and seriousness rather than physical force. The second is about holding on: remember what is inside it, which they read as continued study rather than a single act of recall. The stated aim is a guarded, mindful life.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's recollections. Another surah describes the mountain raised as though it were a canopy, and early scholars read the two accounts together. They report differing details of the scene and are restrained about them, focusing instead on the two verbs. The same pair of orders appears elsewhere in the Quran, given with other scriptures and to other people.

keyTerms.note: The Quran's name for the mountain associated with the revelation to Moses. It is used as a proper name rather than as the ordinary word for a hill, and a whole surah later carries it as a title.
Power, but in the sense of a firm hold and settled determination. Early scholars gloss it as taking something seriously and holding to it, not as exerting force on anyone else.
From a root meaning to shield or guard against. The word describes putting something protective between yourself and harm, so the state it names is watchfulness rather than fright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements in Arabia were tied to places and to physical acts. Parties clasped hands, dipped them together in perfume or blood, and swore at a named landmark that anyone could point to afterwards. The location did the work that a signature does now, because a pledge with no place attached was hard to hold anyone to. A promise made under a mountain held above the crowd is that practice enlarged past all possibility.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to take the scripture with strength appears more than once in the Quran and not only here. It is given to Moses when the tablets are handed over, and it is given to John as a boy in a single short line. The same two words attach to three different moments of receiving a revealed text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are asked, and they answer different failures. A text can be held without being studied, which produces reverence with no content. It can also be studied without being held, which produces information with no grip. Naming both makes the relationship to scripture an active one on two fronts at once. The setting adds a third point, since a pledge made under an overwhelming sign was still, in the event, a pledge that could be turned away from.

crossReferences.why: Describes the mountain raised above them as though it were a canopy, with the same instruction following.
Gives the identical phrase to John as a child, told to take the Book with strength.
Uses the same words when the tablets are handed to Moses, with an instruction to hold to what is best in them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one passage you already believe and read it once as though you were checking what is actually in it, with a pen. Underline anything that surprises you. Holding a text and knowing its contents are separate activities, and most of us do the first much more often than the second.
studies.explainEasier: God reminds them of the promise they made to Him. The mountain was lifted over their heads. He told them to hold tight to what He had given them. He told them to remember what was in it.

studies.title: What Kept You From Loss
studies.meaning: The turning away is stated in four words. Then favour and mercy cut in, and the sentence never reaches the loss it was heading toward. That interruption is the whole point of the first of these ayat. What follows recalls a group who broke a boundary, and what became of them. Early scholars divide over the change, most reading it as an outward one, some as a description of what their conduct had already made of them. The last of the three ayat names the purpose: a restraint for others, and a counsel.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's Medinan recollections. The episode of the boundary broken by a coastal community is told at length in another surah. That account also records that people among them had spoken against the wrongdoing and were delivered. Early scholars read the two passages together. They note that the Quran itself limits who was affected, both in that fuller telling and in the wording here.

keyTerms.note: The verb for turning your back on someone, from the same root that gives the words for an ally and for turning toward. Direction is the whole of its meaning, which is why it can face either way.
From a root naming a hobble or fetter. A punishment called by this word is defined by its effect on those watching rather than by its severity on those it falls upon.
Advice that works on the heart rather than on the fear, from a root suggesting softening. Placing it beside the harder word gives the episode two audiences and two different effects.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was kept alive in verse. A tribe's disgrace or a famous settlement was turned into poetry and recited at markets and gatherings for generations. So a single episode could hold people in check long after everyone involved was dead. Calling something a restraint for the people before it and the people after it named a real thing in that world. Everyone present knew a story that was still doing that work.
studies.didYouKnow: The fuller account of this episode in another surah records something more. A group among the same community had objected to the wrongdoing. They were asked why they bothered warning people who would not listen. That surah states plainly that those who forbade the wrong were delivered. The shorter recollection here leaves the detail out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first of these ayat shows something about how consequences are described. A turning away is named, and then an outcome is named. Between them a mention of mercy keeps the second from following the first. That is the Quran's usual account of why any community continues. The passage also gives a punishment a purpose beyond itself, since a restraint and a counsel are both aimed at people who were not involved.

crossReferences.why: Tells the episode at length, including the objection raised by some and their deliverance.
States the general principle, that immediate reckoning for wrongdoing would leave no creature on earth.
Says the same thing again, that God defers rather than taking people to task for what they earn.

studies.applyIt: Think about something that did not happen to you, a consequence that was available and did not arrive. A near miss, an error nobody noticed, a habit that could have cost far more than it did. Name one, precisely. Gratitude usually attaches to what came, and this passage attaches it to what was withheld.
studies.explainEasier: After all that, they still turned away. God says that His kindness and mercy are the only reason they were not lost. He reminds them of the ones who broke the Sabbath and what happened to them.

studies.title: Do You Take Us Lightly
studies.meaning: An instruction is delivered, and the response is an accusation of mockery. What Moses says back is the striking part. He seeks refuge from being among the ignorant, and the Arabic word he uses does not mainly mean uninformed. In classical usage it stands opposite forbearance as much as opposite knowledge. It names rashness, and the readiness to treat people carelessly. So mockery is classed here not as rudeness but as a failure of restraint. He distances himself from it rather than defending the instruction.
studies.historicalContext: This opens the episode that gives the surah its name, set during the years in the wilderness. It is told only here in the Quran, unlike most of the recollections in this section, which appear in other surahs too. Early scholars note that the surah gives the exchange in dialogue, which is unusual for this stretch of recollections.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for slaughtering an animal, used throughout the Quran without special ceremony attached. Nothing in the word itself signals a rite, which is part of why the instruction seemed so unaccountable to them.
Not the act of mocking but the thing mocked. The accusation is that they are being made into a joke, which is a charge about their standing rather than about the instruction's content.
In classical Arabic this word stands opposite forbearance as much as opposite knowledge. It names unrestrained, headlong conduct, which is why it fits an accusation of mockery so exactly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cattle were not the usual wealth of the Arabian interior, where camels and sheep carried a family's value. Cows belonged to settled farming, to the watered oases and the farming south, where they pulled ploughs and turned the wheels that lifted water. A cow was a working asset with a known price, not a beast anyone kept casually. So an order to destroy one had an obvious cost.
studies.didYouKnow: This episode gives the surah its name. The longest chapter of the Quran runs to two hundred and eighty-six ayat and covers law, history, prayer and creed. It is called The Cow, after an incident that fills seven of them and is never mentioned again. The Quran's surah names are often drawn from such passing details.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The response models something specific. Faced with an accusation, Moses neither argues the point nor claims his authority. He states what he seeks refuge from, and that turns the exchange into a question about character rather than about who is right. The passage also shows that an instruction can arrive without its reason attached. The absence of a stated reason is not itself grounds for treating it as unserious.

crossReferences.why: Warns against asking about matters which, if made plain, would trouble those asking.
