Refers later in this surah to questioning a messenger in the way Moses was questioned before.
Records another ill-judged request made to Moses immediately after the sea was crossed.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you meet an instruction whose reason you have not been given, at work or at home, and watch for the impulse to treat it as unserious. You do not have to comply without thinking. Just separate the question of whether it makes sense from the question of whether you are being taken lightly.
studies.explainEasier: Moses told his people that God had ordered them to sacrifice a cow. They thought he was joking and asked if he was making fun of them. He said he would never be so foolish.

studies.title: Neither Old Nor Young
studies.meaning: This is the first of three requests for more detail, and the answer narrows the field without explaining anything. Two ages are ruled out and a middle range is named, in the words a livestock buyer would use. Then the reply points them back to where they started, telling them to do what they were told. Early scholars pass on a remark often repeated about this exchange. Any cow would have met the first order, and each question made the task harder.
studies.historicalContext: This sits inside the surah's only telling of this episode. The Quran gives the exchange as a run of questions and answers rather than as a summary, which is unusual for this stretch of recollections. Early scholars treat the tightening detail as the point of the story. They note that the return to the original instruction at the end of this ayah is repeated in effect at each stage.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning the space between two things. To make something clear in Arabic is to separate it from what it might be confused with, which is exactly what they are asking for here.
A specific term for an animal too old to breed. Arabic had precise vocabulary for livestock at every stage, and the words in this ayah come straight from the language of buying and selling.
An animal that has bred once and is in its prime. The word marks a stage rather than a number of years, and it names exactly the range left after the two exclusions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock ages were graded finely in Arabic, and the vocabulary was common property. A camel had a different name at each year of its life. Buyers examined teeth and argued over which stage an animal had reached, because the answer set the price. Anyone hearing this ayah knew the register at once. The question had been answered in market language, exactly and without a word of explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: This exchange is one of the most cited in the whole commentary tradition for a point about questions. Early authorities are quoted as saying that any cow at all would have counted, had the people simply taken one. The detail tightened only because they kept asking. The remark is repeated across the classical works almost as a formula.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two kinds of asking. Seeking to understand is not what happens here. None of the answers give a reason, and the questioners never ask for one. What is sought is more detail, and detail works as a delay. The reply treats that as the issue by returning them to the instruction unchanged. Clarity was never what was missing.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same habit directly, warning about questions whose answers would prove burdensome.
States the principle that limits any such burden, since no soul is charged beyond its capacity.
Shows the same people making another request that Moses answers by naming their ignorance.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself once today asking for more information about something you already know enough to begin. The extra detail that will not change what you do is the tell. Notice it, and then do the first small part of the thing instead of asking the next question.
studies.explainEasier: They asked Moses to find out from God which cow they should use. The answer was that it should not be too old or too young, but in between. Then they were told to do as they were told.

studies.title: Yellow, And Bright With It
studies.meaning: The second request asks about colour, and the answer supplies more than a colour. It gives an intensifier, a word Arabic keeps for yellow alone. Then it adds a clause that has nothing to do with identifying an animal: she gladdens those who look at her. Nothing in the narrowing so far has been decorative, so a purely visual detail is worth pausing on. Early scholars note the phrase and read it as crediting real delight to the sight of a colour.
studies.historicalContext: This is the second stage of the narrowing, in the surah's only account of this episode. The story is told nowhere else in the Quran, so there is no parallel version to check the details against. Early scholars work from the wording itself. Their comment on this ayah centres on the two additions: the intensifier, and the phrase about the effect on onlookers.

keyTerms.note: The feminine form of the ordinary colour word. Arabic colour terms take this shape, and the same root gives words for a coat turning pale and for the season when leaves change.
An intensifier used only with yellow. Arabic assigns each basic colour its own such word, so a different term would be required for a deep black, a pure white or a strong red.

From the root that gives the word for joy and also for something kept secret. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect them through the idea of what is held inside, since gladness of this kind is felt before it is shown.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Colour was expensive. Bright yellow came from saffron and similar dyes that had to be traded in, and cloth of a strong, even shade showed means. Herders knew animals by their markings, so a beast of one clean colour with no patches was both unusual and easy to describe. The narrowing was moving, without saying so, toward an animal that would be very hard to find and costly to buy.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic keeps a separate intensifying word for each of the main colours, and they are not interchangeable. The one used in this ayah belongs to yellow alone; black, white and red each have their own. The classical dictionaries list these pairings as fixed, so the ayah is using a term that could not appear with any other colour.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A phrase about something being pleasant to look at sits inside a set of technical details. That treats beauty as a real property of a created thing, not just as a reaction in the viewer. The Quran describes creation this way again and again, listing colour and variety among the signs alongside use and provision. The detail also complicates the episode. The animal being described so warmly is the one about to be slaughtered.

crossReferences.why: Lists streaks of colour in mountains and the varying colours of people and animals among the signs.
Names the variety of human languages and colours as a sign for those who know.
Points to what God has produced on earth in differing colours as a reminder for those who reflect.

studies.applyIt: Find one colour today that you actually enjoy looking at, and look at it for longer than you need to. A wall, a fruit, the sky at a particular hour. This ayah puts pleasure at a colour into a passage that had no other reason to include it, which suggests the noticing is worth doing on purpose.
studies.explainEasier: They asked again, this time about the colour of the cow. The answer was that she should be bright yellow. It was a colour that pleased everyone who looked at her.

studies.title: If God Wills, We Will Find It
studies.meaning: The third request repeats the first word for word, with a reason added: the cows all look alike to them. Then something new appears at the end of the sentence. For the first time in this exchange they attach their intention to God's will, and say that with it they will be guided. Early scholars note both the lateness of the qualification and the fact that it works. The answer that follows is the last one, and after it the search ends.
studies.historicalContext: This is the third and last stage of the questioning, in the surah's only telling of this episode. Early scholars treat the phrase added at the end of this ayah as the turning point of the whole story. Everything up to here had been a request for more detail. Here, for the first time, the questioners refer the outcome to someone other than themselves.

keyTerms.note: From the root for likeness. The same root appeared earlier in this surah describing the fruit of the Garden brought in resembling forms, where the resemblance was a pleasure rather than a problem.
A conditional clause attached to a statement about the future. It has been the ordinary Arabic qualifier for anything not yet done ever since, used in speech far outside religious settings.
A form of the verb meaning to find the way, with an emphatic particle attached. The confidence in the word sits oddly beside the condition preceding it, and the pairing is the sentence's whole shape.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anyone who kept cattle in an oasis would recognise the complaint. Cows of the same stock look alike at a distance. Herds mixed at the watering places and had to be sorted out again, which is why owners cut marks into ears or dyed patches of hide. Telling one animal from another was a practical daily skill. Saying they all look the same was, in that setting, an admission as much as an excuse.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase these questioners add is one the Quran elsewhere tells a person never to leave off. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is told not to say of anything that he will do it tomorrow without adding it. That instruction comes with a reported occasion of its own. The phrase has been ordinary Arabic speech ever since.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Referring an outcome to God's will is shown here as the thing that unblocks a stalled search, and its placement matters. It arrives at the end of a third repeated question, after the demand has already become expensive. So it is not the confident opening of a person who expects things to go well. The passage suggests the phrase is available late and still works. That is a modest but genuine comfort.

crossReferences.why: Instructs directly that nothing be said about tomorrow without attaching this same qualification.
Has Abraham's son use the phrase at the hardest possible moment, saying he will be found steadfast.
Uses the same root for resemblance earlier in this surah, of fruit given in the Garden.

studies.applyIt: Attach the qualification to one plan today, out loud, and mean it rather than saying it as a habit. Not a large plan. Something you fully expect to happen this afternoon. Notice what it changes about how tightly you are holding the outcome, which is the whole content of the phrase.
studies.explainEasier: They asked one more time which cow was meant, since the cows all looked the same to them. This time they said that if God willed it, they would find the right one.

studies.title: Now You Have Brought The Truth
studies.meaning: The last detail rules out an animal that has ever worked, and adds that it must carry no mark at all. A cow's value in that world lay in ploughing and drawing water, so this describes something rare and expensive. Their reply concedes the point. Then the account adds a short clause that reads like an aside: they nearly did not do it. The next ayah supplies what the whole sequence was for, a killing and a dispute over who was responsible.
studies.historicalContext: This closes the questioning and turns to the reason behind the order. The Quran holds back the occasion until this point, so a reader meets the demand, the resistance and the rising cost before learning what any of it was about. Early scholars note the ordering. They read the hidden motive as the key to the episode, since a slaughtered animal was about to expose what a community was covering.

keyTerms.note: Used of an animal trained to the yoke. Its root also gives the word for lowness used earlier in this surah, so the same letters describe a beast made docile and a condition of reduced standing.
From the root that gives the words for peace, safety and submission. Applied to an animal it means delivered whole and unimpaired, with nothing missing and nothing wrong.

A spot of contrasting colour in a coat. Herders used exactly such markings to tell their animals apart, so requiring the absence of one made the beast both unusual and difficult to identify by ownership.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An unsolved killing was the most dangerous thing an Arabian community faced. A body found with no known killer put suspicion on everyone. It could open a feud between clans that outlasted the people involved, since blood claims were inherited. There were ways of settling blame by sworn oath when evidence ran out. They existed because the alternative was a war nobody had chosen.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the animal as broken to work shares its three root letters with the word for humiliation used ten ayat earlier in this surah. Both describe being brought low and made easy to handle. One is a beast under a yoke, the other a people's condition. The pairing is visible only in the Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The story is arranged so that the cost of delay is felt before the purpose is revealed. What began as a plain order became an expensive one entirely through the questioning. The aside about nearly not doing it records how close the whole thing came to failing. The next ayah then names the real subject, and it is concealment. A community was holding something back, and the elaborate procedure existed to bring it out.

crossReferences.why: Tells of another killing and a body concealed, with a bird sent to show how to bury it.
States earlier in this surah that God knows what is disclosed and what is being held back.
Describes people hiding from others what cannot be hidden from God, who is with them as they plan.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you delayed by asking for more information. Price the delay honestly: what it cost in money, in time, or in the thing itself getting harder. Do it for one case, in writing. This passage lets the reader feel that cost before explaining anything, which is a good order for reviewing your own.
studies.explainEasier: The last answer was that the cow had never been used for work and had no mark on her. They said that now the truth was clear, and they killed her, though they almost did not.

studies.title: Struck With Part Of It
studies.meaning: The instruction is brief and the outcome is left unstated: strike him with part of it. What the ayah reports instead is the meaning of what happened, and it gives two. A killing is resolved, and a demonstration is provided of how God gives life to the dead. The instrument is worth noticing. Life is restored by means of a slaughtered animal, so the sign is built out of the very thing that had been so expensive to obtain. The ayah ends by naming reason as the faculty being addressed.
studies.historicalContext: This closes the episode that gives the surah its name. The Quran does not narrate the moment of revival or report what was said. It moves straight to the general statement. Early scholars pass on various details of what followed. They are aware that the text itself supplies none of them, so they keep what the ayah says apart from what the reports add.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for striking, addressed to the community rather than to an individual. The same verb is used across the Quran for setting forth a parable, which is a separate and much discussed usage.
A form meaning to cause to live, from the root behind the word for life itself. The Quran uses it of reviving dead earth after rain as often as of raising human beings.
One word covers a natural sign, a miracle and a verse of the Quran. A reader meets it here as a token shown, having already been reading the same word as a name for the text itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An unknown killer was the one problem Arabian custom handled worst. Payment could settle a killing that someone admitted to. Oaths could share out blame when a body was found among a known group. But a real unknown left every family open to suspicion. Communities lived for years with such cases unsettled. Something that named the killer outright ended the danger of the whole situation.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's word for a sign is the same word it uses for one of its own verses. So a person reading this ayah meets the term twice over. It is the token being described, and it is also the unit of text they are reading it in. The double use runs through the whole Quran and is never marked by a different word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One event serves two purposes at once. It settles a particular dispute, and it stands as evidence for a general claim. That is how the Quran usually presents signs, as ordinary events carrying more than their occasion. What the ayah asks for at the end is the notable part. Having described something entirely outside experience, it asks for reason rather than awe. That assumes the step from a single revival to a general rising is one a person can follow.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham asking to see how the dead are given life, and being shown with birds.
Points to earth revived after its death as the pattern for how the dead will be raised.
States the conclusion directly, that God is the Truth and gives life to the dead.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing today that has come back after appearing finished. A plant after cutting, a friendship after silence, energy after illness. Notice that you accept this without difficulty on a small scale. The argument in this ayah asks you to follow that acceptance one step further, using reason rather than feeling.
studies.explainEasier: God told them to strike the dead man with part of the cow. That is how God brings the dead back to life. He shows people signs like this so that they will use their minds.

studies.title: Harder Than The Stones
studies.meaning: The comparison is graded rather than absolute. Hearts became like stone, the ayah says, or harder, and it then proves that qualification by listing three things stone does. Rivers burst out of some of it. Others split along a seam and water comes through. Others come down out of awe. Early scholars differ over the third item, some reading it plainly and others as a way of speaking, but the point holds either way. Three degrees of yielding are named, and the heart in question is placed beneath all of them.
studies.historicalContext: This comes right after the account of a dead man restored in front of witnesses, and the placement is the argument. Early scholars read the hardening as following directly on a sign of the most unanswerable kind. They note that the surah has by this point recorded several such sequences. Something extraordinary is seen, and the response to it fades within a few lines of text.

keyTerms.note: The verb used of stone and of ground baked hard. Applied to a heart it describes a physical change of texture rather than a decision, which is why the ayah answers it with more physical description.
An intensive form of the verb for cleaving, suggesting splitting along a seam rather than shattering. The word allows for a rock that yields under pressure without ceasing to be a rock.

The early Arabic dictionary writers distinguish this from ordinary fright: it is a fear grounded in knowing what is before you. The Quran attaches it to those who know, which is why it can be ascribed to stone here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: All three of these are things people in Arabia actually saw stone do. Springs emerged from rock faces and fed the wells that settlements were built around. Cliffs seeped after rain, and water was collected from the seams. Rockfall down a wadi side, sudden and heavy, was a known hazard of travelling through gorges in the wet season. The list is observation, not invention.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not simply call the hearts stony. It says like stones, or harder, and then spends the rest of its length arguing that even the comparison was generous. Three separate ways in which rock yields are set out one after another, so the passage concedes its own image and then withdraws it as insufficient.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardness is described here as a condition, not a verdict, and that matters for what can be done about it. Something hard has a texture, and a texture can change. This is why the Quran speaks elsewhere of hearts being opened and softened. The passage also puts responsiveness in unlikely places. If stone can yield in three distinct ways, then the absence of yielding in a person is not explained by the stuff they are made of.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether the time has not come for hearts to soften, warning against the hardening that followed earlier scripture.
Contrasts a breast opened to submission with hearts hardened against the remembrance of God.
Says a mountain would have split from awe had this Quran been sent down upon it.

studies.applyIt: Notice something today that used to move you and does not any more: a passage, a piece of news, a person's difficulty. Do not manufacture a feeling about it. Just register the change accurately, and note roughly when it happened. Hardening is gradual and almost always goes unnoticed at the time.
studies.explainEasier: After seeing all that, their hearts went hard, like rocks or even harder. Some rocks have rivers bursting out of them. Some split open and water comes out, and some fall down in awe of God.

studies.title: After They Had Understood It
studies.meaning: The address turns to the believers and lowers an expectation. The sentence is carefully limited: a group of them, not all, and used to, in the past. The verb for what that group did comes from the word for the edge of a thing, so the picture is of turning something until it is no longer seen straight on. Early scholars divide on whether this describes altering wording or altering the sense given to it, and both readings are standard. What carries the weight comes at the end: they had understood it first.
studies.historicalContext: This sits in the section addressed to those who held earlier scripture, and it is spoken here about them rather than to them. Early scholars are careful with the limits built into the wording and generally repeat them. They note that the Quran elsewhere in this same surah describes a portion of the same community standing through the night in recitation. The passage is about a practice, not a people.

keyTerms.note: A portion separated off from a larger body, from the root meaning to divide. The word itself does the limiting, and early scholars lean on it when explaining the scope of what follows.
From the noun for the edge of something, and also for a letter of the alphabet. To do this to a text is to turn it onto its edge so that it is no longer being looked at squarely.
The root means to tie or tether, as a camel is hobbled to stop it wandering. Understanding in Arabic is what fastens a thing down, which is why the word also gives the ordinary term for the mind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Where almost nobody could read, whoever could read held a position. A scholar's account of what a passage said settled questions no listener was able to check, and this was true in every scripture community of the region. The gap between a text and the explanation of it was invisible to the audience, by definition. That is not a charge against anyone in particular. It is a description of how authority worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for understanding comes from the verb for tethering an animal so it cannot stray. The ordinary Arabic word for the mind is built from the same root. Reason, in the language of the Quran, is named after the act of tying something down so that it stays where you left it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause about having understood it first is what makes this a serious charge. Misreading is a mistake. Shifting something you have already grasped is a decision. The word for knowingly is added at the end to close off any remaining doubt. It also sets a warning that reaches well beyond its occasion. Understanding a text is exactly the condition needed before anyone is able to bend it.

crossReferences.why: Describes words being displaced from their positions and speech twisted with the tongue while listening.
Connects hardened hearts with words moved from their proper places after a covenant was set aside.
Speaks of a revelation made into sheets, some of it shown and much of it kept out of sight.

studies.applyIt: Take something you know well, a text or a rule or an agreement, and ask whether you have a habitual reading of one part that is convenient for you. Everyone has at least one. Say the plain sense of it out loud once, without your usual gloss attached, and see whether the two versions differ.
studies.explainEasier: Some of them used to hear the word of God and then change it on purpose. They did this even after they had understood it. So do not expect them all to believe you.

studies.title: What Was Opened To You
studies.meaning: This is a scene in two parts, and what they say in private gives everything away. The worry voiced there is that shared knowledge will be used in argument against them before their Lord. Early scholars point out what that concedes: nobody worries about being argued with using something false. The verb for what God has disclosed is the one used for opening a door and for granting a victory. So what they propose to withhold is described as something given to them, not acquired.
studies.historicalContext: This comes in the surah's account of meetings between the young community and its neighbours in the city. Early scholars describe a general pattern of exchanges and do not report one occasion. They note that the passage records private speech, which by its nature is reported rather than seen. The question at the end is put to those speaking, not to the believers named at the start.

keyTerms.note: The verb for opening a door and, across the Quran, for granting a decisive victory. Applied to knowledge it presents what they hold as something unlocked for them rather than earned.

keyTerms.gloss: so they may argue against you
keyTerms.note: From the word for a proof or an argument that stands. The form implies a contest between two parties, so the fear is not of being contradicted but of being out-argued with their own material.
The verb for a space emptied of everyone else. The surah used it much earlier of another group withdrawing into private company, so the same word marks both scenes of a second conversation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge was capital in a society that wrote almost nothing down. A route through open country, the site of a seasonal well, a family line that settled a claim, the words of an old pact: each of these was worth something because few people had it. Keeping such things inside a family was ordinary care, not meanness. The instinct described here was the normal way to handle a scarce asset.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats a pattern the surah used some sixty ayat earlier, about a different group. It uses the same verb for slipping away into private company. It uses the same reported sentence when meeting believers. The echo is close enough that a reader going through the surah in order meets the earlier scene again in a new place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reasoning quoted here contains its own answer, which is why the passage lets it stand without comment and then asks whether they use reason. Someone who fears that a piece of knowledge will count against him before God has already accepted that it is true, and that the reckoning is real. So concealment often runs on belief rather than on doubt. That is a harder position than plain denial.

crossReferences.why: Records the same doubled speech earlier in this surah, with the same verb for private company.
Describes a scripture put on sheets with parts displayed and much of it kept from view.
Says people hide from others what they cannot hide from God, who is present as they plan.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true that you know and have not passed on because it would be inconvenient for you if the other person had it. A piece of feedback, a fact about a shared decision. You do not have to hand it over today. Just notice that your reason for holding it is that it is true.
studies.explainEasier: When they met the believers, they said they believed too. But in private they asked each other why they should share what God had shown them. They did not want it used against them.

studies.title: Knowing The Book By Hearsay
studies.meaning: Two ayat describe two different problems. The first is a question put to those who calculate what to say in public and what in private. It simply names the scope of what is known. The second turns to a much larger group who cannot read the text at all and hold it only as things heard and hoped. The word for what they have is read by early scholars either as wishful notions or as recitations carried without understanding, and both senses are recorded. The verb that closes the passage places them in guesswork rather than in denial.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's account of the groups around the young Muslim city. Few people in seventh-century Arabia could read or write. For most, a scripture existed only as somebody else's recitation of it. Early scholars read the second ayah as a picture of that ordinary state, not as a rebuke. They mark it off sharply from the knowing reshaping described a few ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: Describing a relation to writing rather than a quality of mind. The Quran applies the same word to the Prophet and to the wider Arab population who had received no scripture of their own.
The plural of a word covering both a hope entertained and something read aloud. Early scholars record both senses here, and the two readings describe different failures that often occur together.

The state between certainty and doubt. Arabic gives it its own verb, and the Quran repeatedly contrasts it with knowledge, treating supposition as a poor foundation rather than as a mild form of knowing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was a specialist trade. A small number in Mecca could keep trade records, and the scripture communities of Medina had trained readers who handled texts professionally. For everyone else a book existed as a voice: what a learned man had recited, what an uncle had repeated from him, what everybody knew it said. The distance between a text and the general belief about its contents was not a fault. It was the normal condition.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for those without letters is applied elsewhere in the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself. In another passage it names the community he was sent among. The same term therefore marks both a limit being noted and a circumstance treated as important. That is why early scholars are careful with its tone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat name two ways of being wrong about a text, and only one of them involves any fault. Calculating what to reveal is a choice. Inheriting a book as rumour is a circumstance. Putting them side by side makes access to knowledge a matter of justice as well as of effort, since the second group's position was created by others. The passage also treats guesswork as a real category, neither knowledge nor lying.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind the closing word, that conjecture avails nothing at all against the truth.
Uses the same word for the unlettered, describing the community a messenger was raised among.
Applies the same term to the Prophet, describing him as the unlettered messenger foretold before.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are confident a text says, scripture or otherwise, that you have never actually looked up. Everyone has several. Find the passage today and read it yourself. Most of the time it will say roughly what you thought, and the value is in the small number of times it does not.
studies.explainEasier: God knows what they hide and what they show. Some of them cannot read at all. They only know the Book from what they have heard other people say, so they are left guessing.

studies.title: Written By Their Own Hands
studies.meaning: One act is described with unusual precision. A text is composed, credited to God, and sold for a price. The word of ruin that opens the ayah is then repeated twice more, once for what was written and once for what was earned, so the deed and its proceeds are pronounced on separately. Early scholars divide over whether that opening word names a place or is simply a cry of doom. Most take it as a cry, while recording the other view.
studies.historicalContext: This continues the surah's account of the groups around the young Muslim city. Early scholars read the ayah as aimed at one practice, among some who handled texts for a living. They are careful about the scope, and the ayat around it keep marking off a group from a whole. No single occasion is reported with confidence, and the commentaries mostly decline to name anyone.

keyTerms.note: A cry of doom rather than a curse pronounced on someone. Early scholars differ over whether it also names a particular place of punishment, and most treat it as an expression of ruin.
Grammatically unnecessary, since writing is done by hand in any case. The redundancy is emphatic, insisting on the human origin of something about to be attributed somewhere else entirely.
The ordinary verb for earning a living. Its use here makes the proceeds a separate matter from the act, which is why the ayah pronounces on the two of them one after the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was a paid trade, not a general skill. A small number of men drew up contracts, recorded debts and wrote letters for others, and they charged for it. A name attached also carried a price everywhere. A line of poetry ascribed to a famous poet was worth more than the same line from an unknown. Everyone in that world understood how much an attached authority could add to a text's value.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying they wrote it with their own hands is strictly unnecessary, since nobody writes with anything else. Early scholars noticed the extra words and read them as the point of the ayah. They insist on the ordinary human hand behind something that was then given a different origin when it came to be sold.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two wrongs that would usually be merged. Crediting something to God that did not come from Him is one, and profiting by that credit is another. Each is named on its own. That shows the gain is not merely evidence of the motive. It is an object of judgement in its own right. The ayah also assumes what it does not argue: that texts can be checked and that origins matter.

crossReferences.why: Returns later in this surah to concealing what was sent down and taking a small price for it.
Asks who is more unjust than one who invents a falsehood against God or claims revelation received.
Describes tongues twisting the Book so a hearer takes for scripture what is not from it.

studies.applyIt: Check one thing you are about to pass on today. A quotation, a number, a claim about what someone said. Take the thirty seconds to find where it actually came from. Attribution is the whole subject of this ayah. The everyday version of the problem is repeating something confidently without ever having looked.
studies.explainEasier: Some of them wrote a book with their own hands and then said it came from God. They did it to sell it for a small price. Woe to them for writing it and for what they earned.

studies.title: Only A Number Of Days
studies.meaning: A claim of limited exposure is quoted, and the reply is built as a fork with only two branches. Either a pledge was taken from God, in which case it will certainly be kept. Or something is being said about God without knowledge. The first branch is granted generously, with a parenthesis affirming that God does not break a pledge. That concession is what leaves the second branch standing alone. Notice the verb in the original claim too: the Fire will not touch them, which is the lightest word available for contact.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's account of the assumptions held by communities around the young Muslim city. A nearly identical claim is quoted in another surah, with a comment attached about self-deception. Early scholars pass on differing reports of the number of days being claimed. They note that the Quran itself does not specify it. That is why the reply addresses the basis of the claim rather than its arithmetic.

keyTerms.note: The lightest verb in Arabic for contact, used of a hand brushing something. The claim is minimising in its very grammar, describing not exposure to fire but the possibility of grazing it.
A word used in the Quran for small finite quantities, including the days of the fast. Its presence turns an open danger into a manageable item with a stated length.
A binding undertaking, of the kind sworn before witnesses. The question asks for one in exactly that sense, which makes it a challenge with a procedure behind it rather than a rhetorical flourish.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A claim to hold a guarantee could be tested in that society, and everyone knew how. Who gave it. In what words. Before which witnesses. At what gathering. Agreements were public by necessity, because nothing was written down. So a person claiming protection could be asked to produce the occasion. The question in this ayah is that ordinary social step applied to a claim about God.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply grants the stronger of its two possibilities before ruling it out. It says that if a pledge was taken, God will not break it. That concedes everything the claim would need. Only then does it offer the alternative. Early scholars note the structure, since an argument that first strengthens the position it answers is unusual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the passage objects to is not optimism but a claim made without grounds. A pledge from God would settle the matter completely, and the reply says so. The fault named is speaking about God on the basis of nothing. The Quran treats that elsewhere as a category of its own, apart from denial and from error. Confidence about the unseen is shown to need a source, exactly as any other claim would.

crossReferences.why: Quotes almost the same claim about numbered days and attributes it to something they invented themselves.
States the general rule, not to pursue what you have no knowledge of, since every faculty is questioned.
Meets a comparable claim later in this surah by asking simply for the proof behind it.

studies.applyIt: Take one comfortable assumption you hold about how things will turn out for you, and ask yourself where it came from. Not to dismantle it. Just to find whether it has a source or whether it arrived by itself and has been sitting there unexamined since. Most of us have at least one of each.
studies.explainEasier: They said the Fire would only touch them for a few days. The reply asks whether God ever promised them that. God always keeps His promises. Or are they saying things about God that they do not know.

studies.title: Encircled By What You Earned
studies.meaning: Two outcomes stated as a matched pair. They end with the same words, so the parallel is plain. But the conditions attached to them are not parallel at all. One needs wrongdoing that has closed in all round a person. The verb is one of ringing something, with no gap left. Early scholars read it as a whole state, not any single act. The other needs belief plus good action. The word that opens the passage exists in Arabic only to contradict a denial. So the whole statement lands as a reversal.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering the claim quoted in the ayah just before, about a strictly limited stay in the Fire. Early scholars read these two ayat as the correction to that claim. They put a description of condition where a length of time had been. The pairing also restates in general terms a rule the surah has stated elsewhere. Outcome follows what a person believes and does, not what group they belong to.

keyTerms.note: A particle that cannot answer a positive statement. It exists solely to overturn a negative one, so its presence tells a reader that something just denied is being reasserted.
The verb for a wall going all the way round, used earlier in this surah of God encompassing those who deny. Applied to a person's wrongdoing it leaves no direction open.
From a root meaning to miss a mark, as an arrow misses. The word describes error and offence together, which is why commentators discuss whether it names deliberate wrong or covers both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being surrounded was a military and a travelling fact, not a figure of speech. A camp ringed on open ground. A party caught in a gorge with both ends held. A settlement under siege. In each case what mattered was that no direction of escape remained. The word the ayah uses for wrongdoing that closes around a person carried all of that at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The particle that opens this passage is one Arabic keeps for contradicting a negative statement. It cannot be used to agree with a positive one. English has no single word for it. Translations reach for phrases like on the contrary, or indeed, and the grammatical signal that something is being reversed goes missing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The gap between the two conditions carries the meaning. The second outcome is entered by two ordinary things, belief and good action. The first requires a person to be entirely surrounded by what he has earned. Early scholars press on that difference. It shows that the two are not mirror images. The threshold described for the harder outcome is a whole state, not a count of offences.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle earlier in this surah, tying outcome to belief and action rather than to community.
Rejects reliance on wishes and attaches the outcome to what a person actually does.
Reduces the whole matter to weight, an atom of good and an atom of evil each seen.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between having done something wrong and being surrounded by it. The ayah describes the second, and most self-accusation confuses the two. Take one thing you carry as though it defines you and describe it instead as a thing you did, in one sentence, with a date attached.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who keeps doing wrong until it closes in all around him belongs to the Fire, and he will stay there. Those who believe and do good belong to the Garden, and they will stay there.

studies.title: Speak To People Beautifully
studies.meaning: A covenant is recalled as a list, and the order of the list is the interesting part. It begins with worship directed to God alone. Then it moves outward through decreasing closeness: parents first, then relatives, then orphans, then the destitute. Only after all of that does it name how to speak to people in general, with no limit on who they are. Then two practices. Early scholars observe that the widest instruction in the list is the one about ordinary speech.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, recalling the terms of an earlier covenant within the surah's long address. A closely parallel list appears in another surah, addressed to the community receiving the Quran. It has the same opening and nearly the same order of people named. Early scholars set the two passages beside each other. They treat the shared shape as significant, since the same duties run across different scriptures.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning both good and beautiful. It names treatment that goes past what is owed, which is why grammarians note that the sentence leaves its verb unstated and lets the noun carry the weight.
From the root for stillness and settling. The word pictures a person whom need has brought to a stop, unable to move on their own situation, which is a description rather than a category.

Attached here to speech and directed at people with no restriction attached. Commentators note the absence of any qualifier, and read the instruction as covering everyone a person happens to speak to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every group named in this list was a real position in Arabian society, with real exposure. An orphan lost his protector and often his inheritance, since property passed to whoever was strong enough to hold it. The very poor had nothing behind them at all. Older parents leaned entirely on the household they had raised. Naming these four in order named the people whose safety rested on nothing but duty.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction about speech uses the general Arabic word for people, with nothing added to narrow it. Early scholars have noted the missing qualifier from early on. They read the instruction as covering everyone, inside the community and outside it. That makes it one of the broadest single instructions in this stretch of the surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ordinary speech sits in the middle of a covenant. It stands between the people one owes and the practices one performs. That gives talk the same standing as the rest of the list. It is a strong claim about where a life is actually made. The passage also runs from the vertical to the horizontal without a break. Worship of God alone and kindness to a poor stranger appear as items in one pledge, not as two departments.

crossReferences.why: Gives a closely parallel list, adding neighbours near and far and the traveller to the same sequence.
Expands the clause about parents into its own passage, down to the tone of voice used.
Restates the substance later in this surah, defining righteousness by what is given rather than by direction faced.

studies.applyIt: Take the instruction about speech literally for one day and apply it to the person you are least careful with. Not a stranger, and not someone you are trying to impress. The one whose reaction costs you nothing. Notice how much of your tone with them was running on the fact that it costs nothing.
studies.explainEasier: God made an agreement with them. Worship no one but God. Be good to your parents, your relatives, orphans and the poor. Speak kindly to everyone. Pray, and give to those in need.

studies.title: You Agreed And You Witnessed
studies.meaning: Two undertakings, and the pronouns are what carry them. The Arabic does not say do not kill one another. It says do not shed your own blood, and do not drive yourselves out of your homes, so an offence against a member of the community is described in the grammar as an offence against the self. The closing clause then adds two separate things. They acknowledged the terms, and they were present as witnesses to the acknowledgement, which forecloses any later claim not to have understood.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, recalling a further term of the same covenant. The ayah sets up the one that follows, which describes what happened to these undertakings in practice. Early scholars read the two together. They note that the surah states the terms in full before describing the breach, so a reader has the agreement in hand before the account of how it was handled.

keyTerms.note: The specific verb for spilling blood, not a general word for killing. It names the physical act and its visible result, which is how blood claims were actually described and pursued.
The word covers a house, its enclosure and by extension a whole territory. Losing one meant losing standing, water rights and protection together, so expulsion was never merely a change of address.
From a root meaning to settle or come to rest. An acknowledgement in Arabic is a claim brought to rest, which is why the same root gives the words for a fixed place and for contentment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being driven out was the heaviest penalty short of killing. A man driven from his dwelling lost the protection of his group, his access to a well, and any standing in a dispute. The audience for this surah included people who had been through exactly that. The emigrants in Medina had left Mecca under pressure and arrived dependent on hosts. Nobody in that city needed the second term explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic uses the possessive throughout. The terms read as your blood and yourselves, rather than as one another. Early scholars treat this as deliberate, not as mere idiom. It makes a community a single body in the grammar of the sentence, before anything is said about it in the argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A covenant with two clauses about violence, put in the language of self-harm, makes a community more than a group of individuals. The passage draws a consequence from that in what follows. A body cannot be injured in only one place. The closing detail about witnessing also shows the terms were public. Nothing here was inherited unknowingly or accepted by default. That is what makes the account that follows a breach, not a mix-up.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same construction in the community receiving the Quran, saying do not kill yourselves.
States the principle at full width, one soul taken counting as though all humanity were taken.
Describes those driven from their homes and property, and what is owed to them by others.

studies.applyIt: Think about a group you belong to and one person in it you have quietly written off. Family, workplace, community. The grammar of this ayah treats damage to them as damage to you. Test that today by doing one ordinary thing for them that you would do for someone you liked.
studies.explainEasier: God also made them promise not to shed each other's blood and not to drive each other out of their homes. They agreed to it, and they all stood there as witnesses.

studies.title: Part Of The Book Only
studies.meaning: The undertakings just recalled are set against what was done with them. People of one community fought on opposing sides. They expelled some of their own and backed others against them. Then, when the same people came into their hands as captives, they paid to release them. That last act was itself an observance. It is exactly the arrangement the central question names: holding to part of a scripture while setting aside the part that costs, and doing the first sincerely.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars connect this ayah to conditions in the city before Islam. Its two main Arab tribes were at war, and the settled communities holding scripture were bound by treaty to one side or the other. They fought alongside their allies against people who shared their own scripture and lineage. Afterwards they paid the ransoms their scripture required for captives. The reports on this setting are widely given.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for a back. To do this for someone is to lend them your back, standing behind them in a fight, which makes the word describe alliance in its most physical form.
From the verb meaning to bind. A captive in that world was defined by being tied and by having a price, and the two facts together are what makes the following clause possible.
Shame that others can see, not private regret. In a society where standing was the whole of a person's security, this named a real and measurable loss rather than a feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina before Islam ran on cross-cutting alliances. A group could be bound by treaty to one Arab tribe while sharing scripture and ancestry with a group bound to the other, and when the tribes fought, the allies fought. Everyone in the city had lived through the last war or grown up on accounts of it. The situation this ayah describes was recent memory for the people hearing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The question at the centre of this ayah, about believing in part of a book and rejecting part, has become one of the most quoted lines in the surah. The case it was asked about is worth noting. The selectivity described is not doctrinal. The clause that was kept was the expensive one to perform. The clause set aside was the one that would have prevented the fighting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to let one kept rule offset another that was dropped. And it does so without doubting the sincerity of the one they kept. Paying to free captives was a real act of obedience. Crediting it against the driving out is exactly what the passage will not do. That shows a scripture is taken whole or misused. Partial keeping can look, from inside, like devotion.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who accept some messengers and reject others, seeking to take a way in between.
Speaks of people who made the revelation into portions, taking it in separated parts.
Shows the opposite disposition, hosts preferring others over themselves despite their own need.

studies.applyIt: Identify the part of a commitment you keep easily and the part you have quietly dropped, in the same area of life. Prayer and temper. Generosity and honesty. Diet and sleep. Write both down on one line. The ayah's question works because the two are almost always visible together once you look for the pair.
studies.explainEasier: Yet they killed their own people and drove some of them out of their homes. When those same people were taken captive, they paid to free them. They kept part of the Book and left out part.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: The Present Bought With The Future
studies.meaning: The commercial image the surah has been using returns. Here the goods and the price are named exactly: the present life obtained, the hereafter paid. Two consequences follow, and they are not the same. The punishment will not be made lighter, and there will be no help. So two separate hopes are closed, not one. Early scholars note the first of these particularly. A denial of easing is different from a denial of rescue, and it shuts a door that would otherwise stay ajar.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, summing up the conduct described in the ayah before it. Early scholars read it as the assessment rather than a new charge. They note that the surah has now used the words of buying and selling several times, in different places, always for the same kind of exchange. The audience for these ayat lived in a city whose economy ran on exactly that language.

keyTerms.note: The verb takes what is paid after a small particle, so the present life is what was obtained and the hereafter is the price handed over. Reading the grammar closely reverses the intuitive order.
From the root for lightness of weight. The denial concerns reduction rather than removal, which is a smaller hope than rescue and is closed here separately from it.
The verb for coming to someone's assistance in a fight, and the root behind the Quran's word for victory. It names outside intervention, the last of the four supports denied earlier in this surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravan trade was built on deferred return. Investors laid out money in the spring for a payment that came months later. The whole skill of the business was weighing a distant gain against a present need. Anyone who could not wait sold his share early at a discount, and everyone knew what that cost. The exchange this ayah describes was a familiar and expensive mistake in ordinary trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for buying runs through this surah as a repeated image. It is used for guidance traded away near the beginning, for revelation sold at a low price, and here for the whole of the next life. Early scholars note the repetition. The build-up makes trade the surah's steadiest image for how a person disposes of what they were given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing the choice as a purchase makes it a valuation, not merely a wrong. Something was assessed, weighed against something else, and preferred. So the failure is one of judgement working normally on bad terms. The passage also assumes the hereafter is a possession a person actually holds and can spend. That is a stronger claim than saying it may be lost. What is described is not a forfeiture but a sale.

crossReferences.why: States the misjudgement in its simplest form, preferring the present life while the hereafter is better and lasting.
Describes selling God's covenant and one's own oaths for a small price, and what follows from it.
Asks whether the enjoyment of this life is anything but a little compared with what comes after.

studies.applyIt: Take one hour you spent yesterday and price it in what it displaced rather than in what it contained. Not to feel bad about it. The exercise is simply to practise valuing a distant thing against a near one deliberately, which is a skill and not an attitude, and the ayah assumes it can be learned.
studies.explainEasier: These are the people who bought this life and paid with the next one. Their punishment will not be made any lighter, and no one will come to help them.

studies.title: Messenger After Messenger
studies.meaning: One sentence sums up a long history. God gave Moses the Scripture. He sent messengers one behind another after him. He gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs, and He backed him with the Holy Spirit. Most early scholars say that Spirit is Gabriel. Then the sentence turns. What decided how each messenger was received was not the evidence. The ayah has just called that evidence clear. It was whether the message suited the hearer. The test named here is appetite.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It sits inside the surah's long address to those who held earlier scripture. The ayah packs a whole history of prophecy into one line. Then it asks about the pattern in how that prophecy was received. The classical scholars note that the Quran keeps presenting the prophets as one unbroken line, not as separate new starts. They read the verb used here for sending as making that line plain.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for the back of the neck. To send messengers this way is to send each at the heels of the last, so the succession is described as a relay rather than a series of new starts.
From the root meaning the space between two things. A proof of this kind separates a claim from what it might be confused with, which is why the word is used for evidence rather than for wonders.
The same verb means to fall. Arabic pictures desire as the direction a soul drops in when nothing holds it, which is why the noun from this root is used for unchecked inclination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Messages crossed Arabia by relay. A rider carried word to the next stage and handed it on. The message kept moving, though no single person made the whole journey. Pilgrim routes and trade roads had stopping places set up for just this. The word this ayah uses for sending messengers in a row comes from that world. There, covering distance meant one traveller arriving at the heels of the last.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic switches tense in the middle of the last clause. Calling messengers liars is put in the past. The killing is put in the present form. Grammarians and early scholars note the switch. Most read the present form as a way of making the act vivid in front of the reader, not as a claim about when it happened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grants the strength of the evidence first. Only then does it name the obstacle. That order changes what kind of problem this is. If the proofs were clear and the support was given, refusal is not a position of the mind. It is a preference. So the ayah names what the soul leans toward, not what the mind works out. It also shows prophecy as one unbroken line. Rejecting a messenger is then a repeat, not a new event.

crossReferences.why: Describes messengers sent one after another, each denied in turn by the community he came to.
Recalls the support given to Jesus by the Holy Spirit, alongside the signs he was granted.
Names the person who has taken his own inclination as a god, the failure this ayah describes in general terms.

studies.applyIt: Notice one piece of advice you rejected recently and ask whether you evaluated it or simply did not want it. The two feel identical from inside. A useful test is whether you can state the case for it accurately. If you cannot, you did not assess it, and this ayah is describing the difference.
studies.explainEasier: God gave Moses a book. He kept sending messengers after him. He gave Jesus clear signs and helped him. But when a messenger brought something people did not want to hear, they turned proud and refused him.

studies.title: Our Hearts Are Covered
studies.meaning: An excuse is quoted, phrased as a diagnosis, and the single Arabic word for it is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One reading makes the hearts wrapped in coverings, like a blade left in its sheath. The other makes them vessels already full, with no room for more. Both are preserved and both are used in the commentaries. The reply does not accept the excuse as a fact about their equipment, and its final phrase is measured rather than absolute: they believe little.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars report that some in the city had spoken of an expected prophet before the Quran came. They looked to his arrival as an advantage over those who had no scripture at all. The second of these two ayat turns on that hope. It describes recognition, then refusal. These reports are widely given. The ayah's own wording states the recognition rather than working it out.

keyTerms.note: One written form with two established readings. As coverings it pictures a sheathed blade; as containers it pictures something already filled. Each yields a different excuse, and the commentaries work with both.
From the verb for opening a door, in a form meaning to seek. The Quran uses it for asking a decisive outcome, so the word covers both praying for victory and requesting a judgement.
Recognition of something previously encountered, distinct from learning it for the first time. The verb makes a claim the ayah does not argue for, that what arrived was already familiar to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both pictures behind the disputed word were everyday objects. A sword in its sheath was no use until a man drew it. A waterskin already full could take nothing more, however good the water offered. Anyone hearing the excuse would have seen one picture or the other at once. Either one makes the same claim. Nothing can get in here.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply ends by saying they believe little, not that they do not believe. Early scholars discuss whether this means few of them believe, or that what they hold adds up to little. Either way it is a measure of amount. Even in a passage this severe, the wording stops short of describing an empty hand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An excuse dressed up as a condition is answered here as a choice. That sets a limit on how far a person may call himself unable. The passage does grant something. The reply speaks of a result that follows refusal rather than coming before it. What is refused is the order of events the excuse implies. The state is shown as arrived at, not as the equipment a person was handed.

crossReferences.why: Records a similar excuse, that hearts are within coverings and ears carry a heaviness.
States the sequence the other way round, sealing following on the breaking of a covenant.
Speaks of those given scripture recognising it as surely as they recognise their own children.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the moment you describe an inability that is closer to a decision. I am not a morning person. I am bad at apologies. Pick one such sentence you say about yourself and restate it as something you do rather than something you are. Then leave it there. Naming it accurately is the whole task.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said their hearts were closed, so nothing new could get in. God said that was not true. A book came to them that matched what they already had. They knew it. Then they turned it down.

studies.title: Resenting Another's Portion
studies.meaning: A motive is named here, and it is not disbelief in the message. What they object to is the recipient. They resent that God sends down His bounty on whomever He chooses among His servants. Early scholars gloss the word for that resentment as both envy and overreaching. Its root means to seek beyond your own share. The passage then calls this a sale where the goods and the seller are the same thing. The closing phrase doubles one word rather than reaching for a stronger one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It is the surah's most direct statement of a motive for refusal. The classical scholars link it to objections raised about the messenger's origin rather than about his message. They note that the Quran records like objections elsewhere. One is the complaint that revelation should have come to a man of standing in one of the two great towns. The reports frame the whole dispute as one about who, not about what.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to seek. It slides between wanting what is not yours and going past a limit, so the same word covers envy and transgression without the Arabic having to choose.

The root means what exceeds a measure, what is left over beyond the amount required. Bounty in Arabic is surplus, which is what makes resentment of it a strange complaint about something nobody was owed.
The verb for going back to a place carrying something with you. It pictures a journey home with a load rather than a sentence handed down, so the outcome is described as brought back.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Who got what was the standing grievance of tribal life. A chief assigned water rights, handed out a share of spoils, or arranged a marriage tie. Whoever was passed over remembered it. The poetry of the age is full of such complaints, kept in verse for generations. Resenting another man's portion was no strange vice in that world. It was the daily stuff of politics.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for God's bounty comes from a root meaning what runs over a measure. It is the part beyond what was needed. The same root gives the plain words for a remainder and for something spare. So in the language itself, resenting bounty means resenting extra that was never anyone's to claim.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah splits an objection to a message from an objection to its bearer. That names a refusal no evidence can answer, because the evidence was never the point. It also calls the exchange selling yourself. The usual gap between what a person trades and what a person is closes. And it says God's giving is not bound by merit. That is the very thing being resented.

crossReferences.why: Asks directly whether they envy people for what God has given them from His bounty.
Records the objection that revelation should have come to a great man of one of the two towns.
States the principle plainly, that bounty is God's and He gives it to whom He wills.

studies.applyIt: Notice one person whose good news you found harder to be glad about than you expected. Say something specific and true to them about it today, in one sentence, out loud or in writing. Not a general congratulation. Something that shows you actually looked at what they were given.
studies.explainEasier: These people turned down what God sent down. They did it because they hated that God gave His gift to someone they had not picked. They made a bad trade, and it cost them a great deal.

studies.title: We Believe In Ours
studies.meaning: The position quoted is not that the new revelation is false. It is that it is not theirs, and the sentence says so directly: we believe in what was sent down to us. The ayah then adds two things the speakers have not disputed, that it is the truth and that it confirms what they already hold. The reply that follows does not argue about the new revelation at all. It tests the claim to hold the old one against a record of how those who brought it were treated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It sits within the surah's address to those who held earlier scripture. The classical scholars read the exchange as a general pattern, not a single occasion. They note that the reply reaches back into a history the speakers themselves accepted. That is what makes it an argument from inside their own position rather than a challenge from outside it.

keyTerms.note: One of a small set of Arabic words that carry opposite senses. The dictionaries list it as meaning both what is ahead and what is behind, so the phrase covers everything outside the speaker's own portion.
From a root meaning what is established and rightfully owed. Arabic uses one word for a true statement and for a valid claim, so truth in this language is something with a right attached.

From a root meaning to bring news, or from one meaning elevation, and the lexicographers preserve both derivations. Either way the word describes a function rather than a rank held independently of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a tribal society the first question about any claim was whose it was. Alliances, feuds and standing all ran through that question. Weighing a thing on its merits before you knew its owner was not how disputes worked. The quoted sentence turns that everyday reflex on a revelation. It does not deny the content. It refuses to look at anything that came from elsewhere.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word used here for what lies beyond means both in front and behind. It belongs to a small group of words that carry opposite senses. The early Arabic dictionary writers collected them and studied them as a class of their own. A translator has to pick one direction. In the original the sentence reaches both ways.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply sets out a method rather than winning a point. A claim of loyalty to a source is measured against how what came from that source was treated. Anyone can apply that test. It does not depend on agreeing about the disputed item. The reply also makes ownership beside the point. It grants that the revelation did not start with them, and denies that this bears on whether it is true.

crossReferences.why: Answers a comparable claim by pointing to messengers who came with proofs and were denied anyway.
States earlier in this surah that the revelation confirms what its audience already possessed.
Describes the attempt to accept some messengers and reject others as taking a way in between.

studies.applyIt: Notice a claim you assessed today partly by its source: a news item, an argument, a piece of advice. Ask whether you could state it in your own words accurately. Where you cannot, you sorted it by owner rather than by content, which is exactly the move this ayah is examining.
studies.explainEasier: When people are asked to believe a new message from God, they say they only believe their own. But the new message is true and it agrees with theirs. They are asked why they killed God's prophets long ago.

studies.title: Clear Proofs, Then The Calf
studies.meaning: One short ayah finishes the argument of the one before it. Clear proofs had been given. What followed was not doubt, and not a slow drift. It was the making of a substitute while the messenger was briefly away. The Arabic word for the wrong that closes the sentence comes from a root meaning to put a thing somewhere other than its place. So misplaced worship is named as an object set down in the wrong spot, not as a feeling or an opinion. That is literally what the episode was.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes a short run of arguments in the surah's long address. The calf episode was already recalled earlier in this same surah, and other surahs tell it at length. The classical scholars note that its brief return here serves an argument, not the story. It supplies the counter-example to a claim about believing in what had already been received.

keyTerms.note: Evidence that separates a claim from what it might be mistaken for. The word carries no sense of overwhelming display, which matters here, since the passage is about proofs that were understood and then set aside.
A form of the verb meaning to adopt something as one's own. It implies deliberate acquisition rather than being given or misled into it, which is why the ayah needs no further explanation of motive.
From a root meaning to put something out of its proper place. The same root gives the word for darkness used earlier in this surah, since darkness is light absent from where it belongs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia rested on the man, not on an office. A chief's arrangements held while he was there and often fell apart when he was not. No office carried them in his absence, and rivals moved fast. So a story about what a people did while their leader was away for some weeks made plain sense to that audience. They had watched smaller versions of it again and again.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for wrongdoing shares a root with the word for darkness used in this surah's opening parables. The early Arabic dictionary writers explain both by the idea of a thing out of its place. In the one case, light is missing from where it should be. In the other, an act or an object is put in the wrong spot. English keeps no trace of the link.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names the shortest gap possible between evidence and its failure. Nothing here had faded with time or come down at second hand. The proofs were recent, seen, and not in doubt. The swap happened during a short absence. Placed where it is, the example shows that clear evidence is needed and is not enough on its own. The surah has now made that claim about a sea, a revival and a mountain.

crossReferences.why: Describes the calf made from ornaments, a body that made a sound but could not speak or guide.
Records the moment itself, including the warning given while the messenger was still absent.
Recalls the same episode earlier in this surah, followed there by the pardon rather than by an argument.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you were shown clearly and now act as though you never saw. A test result, a piece of feedback, a pattern someone pointed out. Write the evidence down in one line, exactly as it was given to you. The gap between knowing and acting is the subject here, and writing it plainly narrows it slightly.
studies.explainEasier: Moses showed his people clear signs from God. Then he went away for a short time. While he was gone, they started worshipping a calf instead. The ayah says plainly that they were in the wrong.

studies.title: We Hear And We Disobey
studies.meaning: The opening repeats an earlier ayah of this surah almost word for word. Only the last instruction changes, and here it is simply to listen. The answer quoted takes two halves that belong together and splits them. They heard, and they disobeyed. Then comes the strangest image in the passage. The calf is described as made to soak into their hearts. The verb comes from drinking. Early scholars explain it by the way dye enters cloth and cannot be washed back out.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes this run of arguments in the surah's long address. The classical scholars note the near repetition of an earlier ayah and read the pair as deliberate. The two versions of the covenant scene end differently, and the difference is what each passage goes on to discuss. No separate occasion is reported for this ayah. It belongs to the argument rather than to an event.

keyTerms.note: In Arabic one verb covers hearing a sound and acting on what is heard. The quoted reply splits a word that does not normally divide, which is why the sentence is so jarring in the original.
A passive from the verb to drink. Commentators explain it by dye soaking into cloth: not something held in the heart but something taken up into its fibre, so it can no longer be separated out.
From a root connected to a staff or rod, and to breaking away from a group. Disobedience in the word is departure from a body rather than the breaking of a rule considered on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cloth was coloured by soaking. A garment went into the dye bath and the colour entered the fibre rather than sitting on the surface. That is why a dyed cloth stayed dyed through years of washing and wear. Anyone in that world had watched the process or worn the result. It is the exact image the early scholars reach for, and the ayah reaches for it first.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats an earlier one from this same surah word for word until its final instruction. There the covenant scene ends with remembering what is in the scripture. Here it ends with listening. Early scholars treat the pair as one passage told twice with a different closing verb, and each version builds on the verb it ends on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sentence quoted here has an exact counterpart elsewhere in the Quran. There believers answer their Lord by saying they hear and they obey. The two replies differ by one word, and the Quran keeps both. The pair describes the only two things a person can do with something heard. The passage also treats devotion as something absorbed rather than chosen. What soaks into a heart was taken up before it was decided on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answering form of the same sentence at the end of this surah, hearing joined to obeying.
Describes the response of believers called to judgement as hearing and obeying, in the same two words.
Quotes the same divided reply again, alongside the ambiguous word this surah later tells believers to drop.

studies.applyIt: Notice one instruction today that you heard clearly and set aside without deciding to. Not a rule you disagree with. Something you simply received and did not act on. Say the two halves out loud in sequence, what you heard and what you did. The sentence in this ayah works because it is so ordinary.
studies.explainEasier: God made a promise with them and lifted the mountain over them. He told them to hold on to what He gave and to listen. They said they heard, and then they disobeyed. Their hearts were full of the calf.

studies.title: Then Wish For Death
studies.meaning: A claim to own the next life alone is met with a test, not an argument. If the final home is yours only, then long for it. The challenge is framed on the claimant's own terms. The second ayah reports that the longing never comes. It gives the reason as what their hands have sent ahead. That is the Quran's usual picture for deeds. Baggage is sent forward to a place, so what waits there was already loaded and sent.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It sits within the surah's long address to those who held earlier scripture. A closely matching challenge appears in another surah, put in almost the same words to those claiming a special standing with God. The classical scholars note that the test is offered rather than forced. The passage reports the outcome as a prediction. That is what makes it a claim the Quran is willing to stake something on.
