keyTerms.note: From a root meaning free of any admixture. The Quran's word for sincerity comes from the same root, so a claim of exclusive possession is made with the language of something unmixed.
Related to the word used earlier in this surah for scripture held as mere wishes. It names desire directed at something not yet in hand, which is exactly what a claim about the next life is.
The verb for putting something forward or dispatching it in advance. Deeds in the Quran are repeatedly described this way, as goods sent on ahead of the traveller to a place he has not yet reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travellers and traders sent things ahead. Baggage went forward to the next stage with an earlier party. Goods were sent on to a town before the owner set out. A merchant arriving there found waiting exactly what he had sent and nothing else. The image behind this ayah is not a figure of speech made up for it. It is how anyone moving across that country actually planned a journey.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for sole possession comes from the same three letters as the Quran's word for sincerity. That root means free of anything mixed in. Both words describe something unmixed. So in Arabic the claim being tested is made in the language of purity. That is part of why the reply asks for a matching purity of desire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test proposed treats desire as evidence. If a conviction about the next life were held as firmly as it is stated, a preference would follow from it. The passage says the preference does not follow. That makes what a person actually wants a report on what a person actually believes. It is a harder standard than any form of words. The reason given also places the reluctance precisely, in what has already been sent ahead.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same challenge to those claiming to be God's friends to the exclusion of others.
Meets a related claim later in this surah by asking simply for the evidence behind it.
Describes people asking why fighting was ordained and pleading for a short delay, fearing what they claim to want.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you say you believe about what matters most, and ask what you would prefer if it were true. Not what you would say. What you would choose between two ordinary options this week. The gap between the two answers is small and specific, and it is more informative than any amount of restating the belief.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said heaven belonged to them alone. They were told that if that were true, they would want to go there now. They never did want that. What they had already done was holding them back.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Thousand Years Would Not Help
studies.meaning: The observation is comparative and precise. Not eager for a good life, since the Arabic leaves the word for life indefinite, but eager for any life at all, on any terms. The wish attributed is a thousand years. Then the argument, and it turns on a rare verb meaning to shift something a little to one side. Being granted that span would not budge a person away from what follows, not because the span is short but because length and what comes after it are not measured on the same scale.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It follows the challenge in the ayat just before and explains it. The classical scholars read this ayah as accounting for the reluctance just described, not as a fresh charge. They note the careful comparison it draws. It sets one attachment against another rather than making a flat statement about anyone.

keyTerms.note: The superlative of a word for avid, clutching desire. It describes wanting that has stopped weighing what it wants, which is why the object of it here is left as bare life without qualification.
From the root behind the word for a lifespan, which also gives the verbs for building up and inhabiting a place. A life in Arabic is something constructed and dwelt in rather than merely elapsed.
A rare doubled form meaning to budge something a small distance. The word makes the denial exact: not that long life is insufficient rescue, but that it does not move a person even slightly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long life was genuinely rare and genuinely admired. Infant mortality was high, fevers and raids took adults without notice, and a man who reached great age became a source of history for everyone younger, since he remembered droughts and battles nobody else had seen. Wishing for a very long life was not a strange wish in that world. It was the most reasonable thing a person could want.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives a figure close to this one elsewhere. It says Noah stayed among his people for a thousand years less fifty. So the number wished for here sits just beyond the longest span the Quran records for anyone. The wish looks stated at the outer edge of what could be imagined, not picked at random.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats love of life as evidence, not as a fault. It reads a preference as a report on what a person expects. The argument is then about scale. Stretching a span does not change the relation, however far it goes. The thing stretched and the thing that follows are not measured on one scale. That is why the verb chosen is one of tiny movement. Even a nudge would imply the two sat on a single line.

crossReferences.why: Gives the span of a thousand years less fifty for Noah's time among his people.
Describes the gathering as though they had lingered only an hour of a day.
Has people asked how long they remained on earth, and answering a day or part of one.

studies.applyIt: Work out roughly how many weeks you have been alive. It takes a minute with a calculator and the number is smaller than most people expect. Do not draw a conclusion from it. Just let the figure sit for a moment, since this ayah is arguing about scale and a real number is more useful here than a feeling.
studies.explainEasier: These people cling to life more than anyone else. Each of them would like to live a thousand years. But a long life would not move them even a little away from what is coming.

studies.title: Brought Down Upon Your Heart
studies.meaning: An objection aimed at the carrier of the revelation is answered without any defence of the carrier. The ayah states what he did, adds that he did it by God's leave, and then lists three things about what was brought: it confirms what came before, it is guidance, and it is good news. None of those concerns the messenger. The place of delivery is also worth noticing. Not to the ear or the eye but upon the heart, which is where the Quran consistently locates the receiving of revelation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars report that this ayah answers an objection raised about which angel had brought the revelation. The hostility was aimed at the bearer rather than at the message. The reports vary in detail, and the commentaries usually give the substance without pressing the particulars. The ayah's reply works by turning the question aside rather than by settling anything about the angel himself.

keyTerms.note: Named directly, which the Quran does for only a few angels. Elsewhere the same figure is called the Trustworthy Spirit and the Holy Spirit, and commentators identify all three with one another.
Permission, from a root that also gives the word for an ear. Lexicographers connect the two through listening, so granting leave in Arabic carries the sense of having given something a hearing.

The place the revelation is said to have been brought down to. The Quran uses the same phrase elsewhere for the same event, so the heart rather than the ear is consistently named as the point of arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: That world kept the carrier of a message apart from the one who sent it, and everyone understood the difference. Envoys moved between clans under protection. An envoy could be disliked while his message went unanswered. Ducking a message by objecting to the man who brought it was a known dodge. It was common enough that people could name it when they saw it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran says the revelation was brought down upon the heart. It uses the same wording in another surah for the same descent. Early scholars note that the heart, not the ear, is always named as the place where it arrives. That is why revelation is described throughout as something settled inside a person rather than handed to him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply refuses to treat an angel as a party of his own who could be hated in his own right. What it states instead is the errand. He brought it, by leave, from the one whose leave it was. That shows how the Quran presents the unseen servants of God. They are never described as having interests of their own. The three descriptions that close the ayah then move the talk back to the content.

crossReferences.why: Describes the Trustworthy Spirit bringing the revelation down upon the heart in clear Arabic speech.
Attributes the same descent to the Holy Spirit, sent down in truth to make the believers firm.
Describes the bearer as a noble messenger, possessed of power, obeyed and trustworthy.

studies.applyIt: Notice one message you brushed off this week because of who brought it. A colleague you find tiresome, a family member you have stopped listening to. Split the two apart once, on purpose. Write down what was actually said, with the person left out, and read it back.
studies.explainEasier: Some people were angry at the angel Gabriel. But Gabriel only brought the message down, and God told him to. The message agrees with the books that came before it, and it brings good news.

studies.title: Tossed Aside Every Time
studies.meaning: Three ayat, each narrowing something. The first gathers God, His angels, His messengers and two named angels into one object of hostility. It will not let opposition strike a part and spare the rest. The second says the signs sent are clear, so refusal cannot be blamed on them being hard to see. The third turns from one event to a pattern. It asks whether every time a covenant is made, some of them throw it away. Even there the wording holds back. A group of them, not everyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. These follow the answer to an objection about which angel brought the revelation. The classical scholars read the three as that answer widening out. It moves from one angel to the whole chain, then to a record of promises made and thrown away. By this point the surah has recalled several covenants. So the question at the end already has a string of specific cases behind it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to run past or overstep. An enemy in Arabic is one who goes beyond a boundary toward you, which makes hostility a movement rather than a state of feeling.
The verb for throwing away something judged worthless, casually and without looking. It appears again in the next ayah of the surah, where what is thrown is described as landing behind their backs.
A word of proportion rather than of totality. The surah uses such limiting terms repeatedly in this section, and commentators lean on them when explaining how far any of these statements reach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Treaties between clans were public. They were spoken before witnesses and could be renewed. A group that broke one did it in the open, because there was no other way to do it. Everybody in a region knew whose word held and whose did not. That knowledge decided who would trade with them, marry into them, or stand beside them in a dispute. Throwing away an agreement was a visible act, and people remembered it for a long time.
studies.didYouKnow: Gabriel and Michael are named one by one right after the general phrase for His angels, though both are already covered by it. Arabic rhetoric knows this move. You name a particular right after a general term to single it out for stress. Early scholars point to this ayah as a standard case of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gathers God, the angels and the messengers into one object. That treats revelation as a chain nobody can break one link at a time. Objecting to one link counts as objecting to the whole. It is why the answer to a complaint about one angel comes in this form. The third ayah adds a point. One broken promise is an event. A pattern of them is a settled habit, and the question is put about the pattern.

crossReferences.why: States the believing counterpart at the end of this surah, making no distinction between any of His messengers.
Describes accepting some messengers while rejecting others as an attempt to find a way in between.
Names those who break their covenant every time one is made, without any wariness about it.

studies.applyIt: Look at agreements rather than intentions. Pick one small commitment you have made repeatedly and dropped repeatedly, to a person or to yourself. Do not renew it today. Instead write down how many times the cycle has run. A pattern counted is different from a pattern felt, and the counting is the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Being against God's angels and messengers means being against God himself. The signs He sent are clear. Even so, every time these people made a promise, some of them threw it away.

studies.title: Thrown Behind Their Backs
studies.meaning: The verb from the ayah before returns, and now it is given a direction. Thrown behind the back. That is the ordinary Arabic gesture for dropping something as worthless. Early scholars differ on which book is meant. Some read it as the scripture they already held, others as the one that had just arrived. Either reading works, since the ayah has just called the second a confirmation of the first. The last clause is the careful one. Not that they did not know, but that they acted as if they did not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It continues the account of how the arrival of a new revelation was received among communities that held an older one. The wording again limits the scope to a faction, as the ayat around it keep doing. The classical scholars read the passage as describing a response, not as fixing a permanent character. They note that the same phrase about throwing something behind the back appears elsewhere in the Quran.

keyTerms.note: Throwing away what has been judged worthless. The word carries no anger, which is what makes it worse than a rejection: something is not argued with but simply dropped out of the hand.
A fixed Arabic idiom for putting something out of consideration. The gesture behind it is real, a thing tossed over the shoulder without turning to see where it lands.
A particle of comparison, not of statement. It says they behaved in the manner of people who did not know, which quietly keeps the knowledge in the account rather than removing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Throwing something over the shoulder was a real gesture with a settled meaning. A broken tool, a stone turned up while digging, a thing not worth carrying went behind you without a look. Arabic poetry used the phrase for treating advice as nothing. Anyone hearing this ayah saw the movement. They saw that it is done without argument and without a second glance.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not say they were ignorant. It says they acted as though they were, using a particle of comparison. Early scholars lean on that particle when they explain the passage. It matters because the ayat around it have kept insisting that recognition was there. A plain statement of ignorance would clash with what has just been settled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A show of ignorance is treated here as its own condition. It is neither not knowing nor disputing. Knowledge placed behind a person is still knowledge, and the grammar keeps it on the account. The passage also ties the two scriptures together in a specific way. The new one is described as confirming the old. So discarding either comes to the same act, which is why early scholars can read the ayah both ways without changing its sense.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about throwing a covenant behind the back and taking a small price for it.
States earlier in this surah that what arrived confirms what its audience already possessed.
Says those given the Book recognise it as surely as they recognise their own children.

studies.applyIt: Find something you know perfectly well and have arranged your life not to look at. A bill, a result, a conversation you owe someone. The ayah's gesture is throwing it behind you without argument, which is exactly how this works. Take it out and look at it once today, without acting on it yet.
studies.explainEasier: A messenger came to them from God with a message that matched the book they already had. Some of the people who had that book threw it behind their backs. They acted as if they had never known it.

studies.title: Solomon Did Not Disbelieve
studies.meaning: The ayah's first move is a denial on Solomon's behalf, clearing a name before explaining anything. What follows is unusually hedged at every turn. The two at Babylon warned each person before teaching, saying they were a trial. Nothing learned could cause harm except by God's leave. What was acquired is described as harming its holders and benefiting them in nothing, and they are said to have known this already. Early scholars record differing accounts of the details and generally keep close to what the wording states.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars report that stories tying sorcery to Solomon's reign were going around, and read the ayah as answering them head on. That is why the denial comes first. Babylon was a real name to that audience. It was a ruined ancient city on the northern trade route with a long name for old learning. The commentaries differ on the details of the two figures named and are careful about going past the text.

keyTerms.note: From a root suggesting the turning of a thing from its reality. The same letters give the word for the last hour before dawn, when shapes are present but cannot be made out clearly.
Originally the assaying of gold by fire to see what is genuinely in it. A trial in this sense does not create a quality; it brings out what was already there and makes it visible.
A person's allotted part of something. The Quran uses it for a share in the hereafter, so the phrase denies a portion rather than describing a punishment inflicted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Charms and knot-tying were widespread across the region. A great deal of it aimed at exactly what this ayah names: splitting a husband and wife, or joining them. Those who did it were paid, and clients came to them in private with troubles at home. The Quran speaks elsewhere of those who blow on knots. That was a known technique, not an image, and everyone who heard it knew so.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning sits inside the account rather than being added by later scholars. The two at Babylon are described as teaching nobody until they had said that they were a trial. They told the person not to lose his faith. So the passage records a caution given first, every time. Readers often miss the detail, because the ayah is long and moves fast.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Every clause takes something away. A prophet is cleared. A warning is recorded. Harm is placed under permission. The learners are said to have known the cost. What is left is a picture in which nothing works apart from God, including what looks like a power in its own right. The passage also returns to the surah's trading image. It states the exchange in its harshest form, with the sellers and the goods being the same.

crossReferences.why: Names seeking refuge from those who blow on knots, the practice this ayah describes people learning.
States that whatever a practitioner of such arts contrives, he does not succeed wherever he comes.
Describes what Solomon was actually given, knowledge and understanding, and his response of gratitude.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you have been drawn to that you already know does not help you. Not a vice, necessarily. A conversation you keep re-entering, a feed you keep opening. The ayah says twice that they knew. Say the sentence about your own case out loud, in the past tense: I knew this did not help.
studies.explainEasier: Solomon never did anything wrong. It was others who taught people magic while he ruled. Two angels at Babylon warned every learner first that this was only a test. People learned it anyway. It could not hurt anyone unless God allowed it.

studies.title: Change The Word, Not The Tone
studies.meaning: The first of these says what would have been better. The second gives a very small instruction with a well attested background. A word the community used to ask for the Prophet's attention could be heard two ways in Arabic. One sense was respectful and the other was demeaning. Some were using the second while keeping their cover. The remedy given is not a telling-off about tone or intention. It is a replacement word with no second meaning on offer, followed by the instruction to listen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It is one of the passages where the classical scholars do report a specific occasion, with fair agreement. They describe a term in ordinary use among the believers that a slight shift could turn into an insult. They record that the alternative supplied here closed the gap. The same word is mentioned again in another surah, in a passage about speech being twisted.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for tending a flock, so the plain sense is a request for care and attention. A nearby form of the same letters carries heedlessness, which is the second reading that made the word usable as an insult.

keyTerms.gloss: look at us, wait for us
keyTerms.note: The replacement offered. It asks for exactly the same thing, a moment of the listener's attention, and carries no second sense that could be exploited by anyone saying it.
From a root meaning to return, which also gives the ordinary word for a garment, understood as cloth returning to its shape. A reward in Arabic is what comes back to you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic culture prized double meaning and paid for it. Poets built reputations on lines that wounded while staying defensible. A phrase that insulted deniably was a known tool, not a rare trick. In a society where a direct insult could open a feud between clans, the double-edged form was the safer weapon. Everyone present could hear it working without being able to name it.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction given is a change of vocabulary, not a correction of attitude. The community is not told to be more respectful. It is told to stop using a word that had become open to misuse, and to use a different one meaning the same thing. That is a strikingly practical way to handle a problem of intention.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Blame for a double meaning is placed on the speaker, not on how a hearer chooses to take it. That is an unusual place to put it, and it has a consequence. A word that has been turned is a word to set down, whatever any one speaker meant by it. The passage also shows a broad principle handled by a small, specific remedy. That is a pattern in how the Quran deals with friction inside a community.

crossReferences.why: Mentions the same word again, in a passage about speech twisted with the tongue while listening.
Addresses the community about mockery and offensive nicknames, the same terrain at a different scale.
Instructs believers to say what is best, since ambiguity is exactly where discord is sown between them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a phrase you use that has become loaded between you and one particular person. It may have started harmless. Replace it with a plainer one for a week and see whether the exchange changes. This passage suggests that swapping the word is a real remedy and not merely a cosmetic one.
studies.explainEasier: Faith and good deeds would have brought them a better reward. Then believers are told to drop a word that could be twisted into an insult. They should use a clear, polite word instead, and listen.

studies.title: God Singles Out Whom He Wills
studies.meaning: A wish is reported, then stepped around rather than argued with. See how total the Arabic makes that wish. An indefinite word for good is placed inside a negation. In Arabic that sweeps a whole category. So what is described is not the holding back of some great favour. It is the holding back of any good at all. The reply does not deny that the wish exists. It points out that the wish is addressed to a party with no part in the handing out. Then it closes on a name meaning overflow.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The wording again limits its subject. It names those who disbelieve among the People of the Book rather than the whole, alongside those in Mecca who set others beside God. The classical scholars note the qualifier, which the surah uses steadily in this section. They read the ayah as describing an attitude found among some in both groups toward the young community in Medina.

keyTerms.note: An indefinite noun inside a negation, which in Arabic makes the denial cover the entire category. The construction is a standard way of making a negation total rather than partial.
From a root meaning particular as opposed to general. The verb describes picking something out for a specific recipient, which places the distribution wholly with the one doing the picking.
What exceeds a measure, the part beyond what was required. The same root gives the ordinary words for a remainder and for something spare, so bounty in Arabic is by definition surplus.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a world of hard limits, one party's good season often was another's loss. Grazing, wells, caravan routes and market share were finite. A rival's strong year really did shrink your own. The sense that another's gain costs you something was not foolish there. It described the economy accurately. What this ayah answers is that sense applied to something which does not work that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic construction here makes the denial absolute. Put an indefinite word for good after a negative and it sweeps the whole category. So the sentence says they wish no good of any size to reach its recipients, not that they begrudge one blessing. Grammarians treat this construction as the standard way of making a denial complete.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is described as singled out by God's will. That puts the handing out beyond anyone's preference, the recipients' included. It is the answer the passage gives. It is not comfort about outcomes but a statement about who decides. The closing name then reframes the whole exchange. Bounty in Arabic means an overflow, and an overflow given to one party is not taken from another.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same statement, that God singles out for His mercy whomever He wills, in a similar setting.
States that the People of the Book may know they hold no power over any of God's bounty.
Asks whether they envy people for what God has given them of His bounty.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you treat someone else's good fortune as arithmetic, as though a fixed amount were being handed out. Most of us do this without ever forming the thought. Pick one person doing well in an area you care about and say something specific and true about their work today.
studies.explainEasier: Some people did not want anything good sent to you from your Lord. But God chooses who gets His mercy. Nobody else has a say in that. God gives out of more than enough.

studies.title: Better Than It Or Like It
studies.meaning: A rule is stated with a guarantee attached. What replaces is better or equal, never less. Early scholars differ widely here. They differ over whether the word for what is replaced means a verse of scripture or a sign given to a prophet. The second verb is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One means to cause something to be forgotten. The other means to put it off. How far all this reaches has been discussed at great length, and the range of classical views is genuinely wide.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It answers objections about a revelation arriving in instalments over years, with later guidance sometimes replacing earlier. The classical scholars tie the ayah to that general situation rather than to a single occasion. They note that a second question opens with the same words right after it. They read the pair as one argument: the first about power, the second about ownership.

keyTerms.note: The verb means both to cancel something and to copy it out. The ordinary Arabic word for a manuscript copy comes from this root, so one word holds replacing and transcribing together.

The same word covers a natural sign, a miracle granted to a prophet and a unit of the Quran. Commentators divide over which is meant here, and the ayah's reach differs considerably depending on the answer.
The lower limit of the guarantee. Better or equal exhausts the options offered, so the sentence rules out replacement by something lesser as a matter of the rule itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world was learned in stages from a person. A boy learned a trade, a route or a set of poems by being given as much as he could hold, then more. A teacher's later instruction routinely replaced an earlier simple version, and nobody thought the first had been a mistake. The community hearing this ayah had been receiving guidance in instalments for well over ten years.
studies.didYouKnow: The second verb in this ayah is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One reading means to cause something to be forgotten. The other means to defer or put off. Both are kept in the standard works on recitation. Early scholars explain the ayah with each reading. The difference between them is a single vowel.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers an unsettling idea by attaching a guarantee to it. Replacement is not loss. What arrives is equal or better by the terms of the rule itself. It also closes on power rather than on knowledge. Early scholars notice that. The objection being met is not whether God knows what to send. It is whether He may change what He has already given. The closing question treats that as settled by what God is.

crossReferences.why: Describes one sign put in the place of another, and the accusation of invention that followed.
States that God effaces and confirms what He wills, with the source of the Book held with Him.
Notes that the Quran was divided into portions to be recited to people gradually, sent down in stages.

studies.applyIt: Think of an instruction you were given that was later revised, by a teacher, a doctor, a manager. Notice whether you experienced the revision as the first version having been wrong. Usually it was not. It was as much as you could use at the time, and the revision is evidence of attention rather than of error.
studies.explainEasier: God says that when He sets aside one of His verses, or lets it be forgotten, He always brings one that is better or just as good. He can do anything.

studies.title: No Guardian Besides Him
studies.meaning: This is the second of two questions in a row that open with the same four words. The first tied its question to power. This one ties it to ownership. The pair is one argument in two steps: what God can do, and what God holds. Then it draws a result that does not follow from ownership on its own. Two supports are named, and both are denied. One stands behind a person. One comes to his aid. Between them they covered everything a person in that world leaned on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It follows the statement about replacement at once and completes its argument. The classical scholars treat these two ayat as a unit, since the repeated opening formula joins them in the Arabic. The ayah is addressed in the singular. They read that as directed to the Prophet and, through him, to anyone reading. Its second clause then switches to the plural.

keyTerms.note: The same root gives the words for a king and for possessing something outright. Ownership and rule are not distinguished in it, which is why the sentence can move from holding to protecting without a step in between.
From a root meaning nearness. A person of this kind stands close enough to act on your behalf, which in that society was a formal position rather than an affectionate description.
From the verb for coming to someone's assistance in a fight, and the root behind the Quran's word for victory. It names intervention from outside rather than a standing relationship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone needed a protector and everyone knew who theirs was. A clan answered for its members. A patron stood behind a client. A stranger arriving in a town sought someone's protection before doing anything else. Without it a person could be wronged and the wrongdoer paid no price. The two words used in this ayah name the two things such an arrangement actually gave you.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it begin with exactly the same four words in Arabic. They form a matched pair that translation tends to hide. Early scholars read them as two halves of one argument, not as separate statements. The first rests on what God is able to do. The second rests on what belongs to Him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Joining sovereignty to protection is a real move and not a truism. Owning everything does not by itself mean that nothing else can shelter a person, and the ayah asserts both in one sentence so that the second reads as following from the first. Using the exact vocabulary of the social order also matters. The passage does not say protection elsewhere is inferior. It says the position does not exist.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this ayah almost word for word, adding that He gives life and causes death.
States that you cannot escape on earth, and have no guardian or helper apart from God.
Places the same sovereignty of the heavens and the earth beside God's power over all things.

studies.applyIt: Write down who you would actually call if something went badly wrong tomorrow. Three names at most. Then notice that the list is short, that it has changed over the years, and that you did not build it deliberately. The ayah is not asking you to value them less. It is asking you to see the list clearly.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. He rules all of it. Apart from Him, you have no one to protect you and no one to come to your help.

studies.title: Questioning Your Own Messenger
studies.meaning: The warning points to a precedent instead of describing one. That assumes the reader has just been given it. This surah has supplied two. One is a rising series of questions about an animal that turned a simple instruction into an expensive one. The other is a demand to be shown God plainly. The closing clause then names the risk in the words of trade. It calls it an exchange, not a drift. The result is leaving a road the Arabic calls level.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing this stretch of the surah before it turns to other matters. The classical scholars link the warning to the episodes already recalled in this same surah, not to a particular incident in Medina. They read the questioning in view as the kind that seeks to delay or to test rather than to understand. The surah has just shown both kinds at work.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for asking, with no negative sense of its own. The Quran elsewhere instructs people to ask those who know, so what is warned against here is a use of the act rather than the act.
A form meaning to take one thing in place of another. It makes a change of position a transaction with two sides, so something is handed over as well as received.
Built on the root for evenness. A level road in that country was one a loaded animal could take without unloading, so the phrase was navigational before it became a way of speaking about conduct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Routes were graded by ground. A level way could be taken by a loaded camel at pace, while broken country meant unloading, longer days and real risk of loss. Guides were paid for knowing which was which, and the difference between the two showed up in the arrival date and in what was still intact when you got there. Straying from the level way was an expensive mistake before it was ever a metaphor.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the level way is built from three letters that show up twice already in this surah. Near its start, warning and no warning are said to stand equal for certain listeners. Later the heavens are described as brought into proportion. Evenness is the shared idea in all three. Once it is a comparison, once a making, and here a road.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage tells apart questions that seek understanding from questions that work as resistance. It draws the line by pointing at cases rather than by defining terms. That is a practical choice. The two are hard to separate in a description and easy to spot in an example. Naming the risk as an exchange matters too. It implies that nobody arrives at a new position empty-handed.

crossReferences.why: Warns about questions whose answers would burden the asker, and notes that people before asked them.
Records the demand to be shown God plainly, one of the two precedents this ayah points back to.
Instructs those who do not know to ask the people of remembrance, which shows what kind of asking is meant.

studies.applyIt: Sort your next few questions into two piles as you ask them: the ones whose answers will change what you do, and the ones that will not. Only the first pile is enquiry. Doing this once, for an afternoon, is usually enough to show you which pile you have been filling.
studies.explainEasier: People are asked if they want to question their messenger. Moses was questioned that way long ago. Anyone who trades faith for disbelief has walked off the straight, level road.

studies.title: Pardon And Turn The Page
studies.meaning: A hostile wish is reported, its motive is located inside those holding it rather than in anything done to them, and the truth is conceded to have been clear. Then, having built the least sympathetic case available, the passage instructs pardon. Two verbs are used and they are not synonyms. The first is to give up a claim; the second, built on the word for the flat side of a thing, is to turn away from the matter so it is not brought up at all. Early scholars treat the second as the wider of the two.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to a community under real pressure in the years after the migration. The instruction comes with a horizon attached: until God brings His command. The classical scholars discuss at length what that phrase points to and when it was met. Their views differ a good deal. The commentaries set them out rather than settling on one, so the clause is best read as the text leaves it.

keyTerms.note: The word for wanting a good thing to leave someone else. The phrase after it places the source inside the people themselves, which rules out the reading that they had been provoked into it.
The root describes wind wiping out tracks in sand. Pardon in this word is giving up a claim so completely that nothing remains to be followed, rather than deciding not to press it for now.
From the word for the broad flat side of something, and later for a page. To do this is to present your side rather than your face to a matter, and to stop raising it altogether.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds ran on the duty to answer. A slight left unanswered was read as weakness. Poets recorded which clans had replied and which had not. A family's safety rested in part on being known to answer. This ayah tells a community to pardon and then leave the matter unmentioned. That community was outnumbered and under pressure, and the instruction cut straight against the machinery everyone lived inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs of pardon in this ayah are not a doubling for emphasis. Early scholars separate them carefully: the first gives up the claim, while the second stops the matter being raised at all. A person can do the first and still bring something up, which is why the second is described as the more demanding of the pair.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is placed after every softening factor has been removed. The motive is named as envy. The knowledge is granted. The wish is described as active. So restraint is asked for in the hardest case available, and that is arranged on purpose. The horizon attached matters too. The passage frames the restraint as an interval rather than a verdict, and it closes on power rather than on patience.

crossReferences.why: Uses the second of these two verbs on its own, instructing an overlooking that is gracious.
Tells believers to forgive those who do not look forward to the days of God, with a similar horizon attached.
Describes repelling with what is better, and the enmity that turns into warm friendship as a result.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between letting something go and stopping yourself from mentioning it. Pick one grievance you have officially forgiven and count how many times you have raised it since. Then try the second thing for a week: not raising it at all. Most people find the second harder and more useful.
studies.explainEasier: Many people wanted the believers to give up their faith. They wanted it because they were jealous, even though they knew the truth. Believers were told to forgive them and let it go until God decided.

studies.title: You Will Find It Waiting
studies.meaning: Two practices are named and then something is said about all good generally, using an image of dispatch. Whatever you send forward, you find with God. The phrase for whose benefit it is sent is the one to notice: for yourselves. Nothing here is presented as a service rendered upward. The passage describes a deposit lodged for later collection rather than a payment made, and it closes with a name of seeing rather than of receiving, so the one who is watching is not the one being paid.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It comes straight after the instruction to pardon. Restraint toward others is followed at once by an instruction about your own practice. The classical scholars note that the surah keeps pairing these two acts. They also note that the image of sending good ahead appears in almost the same words in another surah. That is why they read the two passages together.

keyTerms.note: The verb for standing something up so that it stays standing. Applied to prayer it describes maintaining a thing in place over time rather than performing it on a given occasion.

From a root meaning both to grow and to be pure, used of a plant thriving. One word therefore carries increase and cleansing together, which is a claim about the remainder as much as about the portion given.
Putting something forward in advance. The surah has already used this verb for deeds sent ahead in a passage about reluctance, and here the same image is turned the other way round.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were no banks and no way to carry value safely over a long road. A merchant left goods with a trusted agent in a town he expected to reach. Or he sent them ahead with an earlier caravan and found them waiting when he arrived. The whole arrangement ran on reputation. Saying you will find it with God uses exactly that vocabulary, of something lodged and later collected.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic name for what is given away comes from a root meaning to grow and to be pure at the same time. The same root is used of a plant thriving. Neither sense comes from the other. The dictionaries list both as primary, so increase and cleansing are held together in the word itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The phrase saying that good is sent ahead for yourselves moves who benefits. In this ayah God is described only as seeing, never as receiving. So nothing here is a trade with Him. That makes the practices named an investment in the person doing them. It also explains the image chosen. A deposit is picked up by the one who left it, not handed to someone else.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same clause almost word for word, adding that what is found is better and greater in reward.
Contrasts wealth put out to increase through people with what is given seeking God's face.
Describes the same movement later in this surah as a loan advanced and multiplied on return.

studies.applyIt: Give something small away today that you will not see again and will not be thanked for. Money, an hour, a thing you were keeping. Do not tell anyone. The image in this ayah is a deposit lodged ahead of you, and the exercise is simply to have made one deposit you cannot check on.
studies.explainEasier: Keep up your prayer, and give to those in need. Any good you send on ahead is really for you. You will find it waiting with God. He sees everything you do.

studies.title: Produce Your Proof
studies.meaning: A claim about who gets in is quoted, called a wish, and met with one instruction. Bring your evidence. The reply makes no counter-claim at all. It applies a standard, and that standard runs in every direction. It runs back at anyone else who states who gets in and who does not. The word used for the claim is the one the surah used earlier for scripture held as things merely hoped for. That quietly sorts the statement before the demand for proof is even made.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's long address. The ayah right after this one gives the Quran's own answer to the same question. It states a condition anyone may meet rather than a name anyone may hold. The classical scholars read the two together. A demand for evidence about entry only makes sense if the test offered in its place is one that can be checked.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for something hoped for, used earlier in this surah for scripture held as hearsay. Applying it here classifies the claim before any argument about it begins.
One of a small group of Arabic verbs that exist only as commands. There is no past tense of it, which gives the demand an abrupt conversational quality that translations tend to smooth away.
A word for conclusive evidence rather than a supporting reason. It later became the standard term for a formal demonstration in Arabic philosophy, and it carries that weight already here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in that society were settled by evidence and then by oath, in a fixed order everyone knew. The claimant produced witnesses. If he could not, the matter passed to the other party's oath. So demanding a proof was not a flourish. It was the opening move of a real process. Every person hearing this ayah knew exactly what came next when none was produced.
studies.didYouKnow: The command used for produce your proof belongs to a small set of Arabic verbs that exist only as commands. Grammarians call these defective. They have no past tense and no ordinary present. In speech the word works as plainly as hand it over. That makes the demand sound closer to talk than to argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering a claim with a demand for evidence, rather than with a rival claim, sets a standard that binds whoever uses it. Anyone who states the boundaries of the next life is asked for grounds. So the ayah after this one offers a test in place of a label. That is the shape of the argument. Not a different group named, but a condition stated that anyone may meet or fail.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the answer immediately after, stating a condition rather than naming a community.
Uses the identical demand for proof after a series of questions about who creates and provides.
States earlier in this surah that reward follows belief and good action rather than membership.

studies.applyIt: Take one confident claim you made this week and ask what would count as evidence against it. If nothing would, you were not making a claim about the world. Doing this once, on something small and low stakes, is the cheapest way to learn the difference between a conviction and a wish.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said that only their own group would get into heaven. The Quran calls that a wish, not a fact. Then it asks them for proof, if what they say is true.

studies.title: The Condition Stated In Full
studies.meaning: The line answers a claim made two ayat earlier that Paradise belongs to one group alone. It replaces the claim with a condition in two parts, and both are required. The first is inward, surrendering yourself to God, which the Arabic renders as handing over your face. The second is outward, being a doer of good. Reward is then attached to the person rather than the label, and the sentence ends by lifting both fear and grief.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits in a stretch dealing with disputes between the town's religious communities. Each side made claims about who alone could be saved. The ayat just before quote such a claim and answer it by asking for proof. Early scholars tie this line to no single reported occasion. They read it as the surah's own reply to the argument it has just recorded.

keyTerms.note: The verb shares its root with peace and with wholeness. It carries handing something over intact and undamaged. So the surrender described is a giving over, not a defeat.
In Arabic the face stands for the person and for their direction of attention. Surrendering the face means the whole of you turned one way, not a part of you kept back.
The root joins beauty and benefit. It describes work done well and generously, not merely correctly. So the second condition asks for quality, not only compliance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The gesture behind the wording was familiar. You handed over a thing with both hands, face turned to the person taking it. That is how a debt was settled in front of witnesses. It is also how a surrender was made. Turning your face toward someone in a crowded gathering marked who you were talking to, and whose judgement you accepted. The phrase borrowed a public act to describe something inward.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause that closes this ayah says they have nothing to fear and will not grieve. It comes back more than a dozen times across the Quran. Each time it is attached to a different group. The steadfast, those who give without wounding, those who declare God their Lord and hold to it. Early scholars treat the repetition as a deliberate refrain. It gathers those descriptions into one promise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pairing inward surrender with outward good refuses two shortcuts at once. Sincerity without action is one. Action without direction is the other. The passage also removes group membership from the sum, which is the argument the surrounding ayat are having. What remains is a standard anyone can be measured against and nobody can inherit. The promise is stated in the negative: two specific fears will not survive.

crossReferences.why: States the same criterion at greater length across several named communities.
Uses nearly the same phrase, surrendering the face to God while doing good, of Abraham's way.
Repeats the image of handing the face over and calls it grasping the firmest handhold.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you did well this week and ask which half of this line it satisfied. Was it good work aimed at nobody in particular, or was it turned toward God without much care taken over the work itself? Most of us lean one way. Spend this week strengthening the side you lean away from, in one ordinary task, and see whether it changes how the task feels.
studies.explainEasier: You do not get into heaven by belonging to the right group. You get there by giving yourself to God and doing good to people. Then your reward is safe, and you have nothing to fear.

studies.title: Both Of Them Read Scripture
studies.meaning: Two communities are quoted dismissing each other in identical words, an Arabic idiom meaning to have no ground at all to stand on. The clause that follows is the aggravating one: both of them recite scripture. Then the sharpest line. People with no book at all said the same thing, which flattens the very distinction the disputants were relying on, since the form of the dismissal turns out not to require a text. The passage does not adjudicate. It names a day and a judge and stops.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Several religious communities lived side by side in that city. Disputes of exactly this shape could be heard in ordinary talk. The classical scholars describe the setting in general rather than reporting one exchange. They note the ayah's closing clause, which puts the matter off rather than settling it. The Quran does the same in several other places where communities differ.

keyTerms.note: An idiom meaning to have no standing whatever. It is a total dismissal, not a criticism of a position, which is what makes the two quoted sentences mirror images of each other.
One verb means both to read aloud and to come along behind. Reciting in Arabic is following a text word after word, in the way a person follows a track across ground.
From a root meaning to come after or to take another's place, so difference in Arabic is pictured as two parties standing in succession rather than as an opposition of views.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Claiming first place and denying it to others was a known literary form. Every tribe kept a poet who boasted of his own people and said a rival had nothing. No line worth naming, no standing worth counting. Crowds at the seasonal markets came to hear exactly this. What is striking in the ayah is that it puts the same form in the mouths of people who read scripture.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah observes that people with no scripture at all made the same statement. The remark does not answer either party. It notes that the form of their argument does not need a book to produce. That removes the one thing both sides had been treating as the ground of their case. Early scholars generally read it as the sharpest line in the passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a third position. It neither judges between them nor pretends the two are the same. It names the difference as real, names a judge, and names a day. Then it declines to fill the interval with a verdict. That stance returns wherever the Quran describes communities in dispute, and it shapes how the interval is meant to be spent. Settling the matter is not what is left to people in the meantime.

crossReferences.why: States the same deferral, that God will judge on the Day concerning what they used to differ about.
Says each community was given a law and a way, and directs them to compete in good instead.
Sets out earlier in this surah the criterion by which the deferred judgement will actually be made.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you describe a group's position as having nothing to it. That phrasing is a signal, not an assessment. State the strongest version of the position instead, in one sentence, and see whether the dismissal survives your own summary of it.
studies.explainEasier: Two groups each said the other stood on nothing at all. Both of them read scripture. People with no book said the same thing. God will settle what they argued about on the last day.

studies.title: Who Empties A House Of Prayer
studies.meaning: The question is put in the Quran's strongest form, which it saves for a small number of offences. Here it is aimed at blocking worship, not at any belief held. Two acts are named together. One is stopping God's name from being remembered in places of prostration. The other is working toward their ruin. The second follows from the first. A building emptied of its use is already on the way down. Early scholars propose several historical episodes for the ayah and set them side by side without choosing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentaries offer more than one setting for this ayah. One is the shutting out of the believers from the Sacred Precinct at Mecca. Another is an ancient destruction of a place of worship far to the north. They set the proposals out and generally decline to choose. The wording is plural and ties the ayah to no one building, city or community.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a noun of place from the verb to prostrate. It names any spot where a person lowers himself in worship, which is why nothing in the word restricts it to a particular structure.
The word for a building falling to ruin, which in Arabic covers emptying as well as demolishing. A house nobody uses is described with the same term as one that has been pulled down.

A plural participle describing the state in which they would enter. The clause is a statement about their position rather than an instruction, and commentators read it as describing what became the case.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sanctuaries were real institutions across the peninsula and their protection was widely honoured. Inside the Sacred Precinct at Mecca, blood feuds were suspended and men who would have fought outside could trade. Other tribes kept their own sacred places on the same understanding. Getting in the way of access to such a site was seen as a grave breach, whatever the person doing it believed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word here is a plural. Nothing in the ayah limits it to one community's buildings. Another surah says so plainly. It names monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques together as places where God's name is much mentioned. It says they would have been pulled down had God not held some people back by means of others.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The offence named is not a belief but a blocking. That puts it in a different class from most of what this part of the surah describes. Emptying a place of worship and working toward its ruin are treated as one act. So neglect and knocking down sit on the same line. The strongest form of the question then sets the weight, since the Quran uses that form sparingly.

crossReferences.why: Names several kinds of house of worship together and says restraint alone keeps them from being destroyed.
Describes who is fit to maintain the places of worship, tying it to belief and to practice rather than to lineage.
Concerns those who barred access to the Sacred Precinct while not being its rightful guardians.

studies.applyIt: Do one small thing for a place where people gather to pray. Sweep something, fix something, pay for something. Or simply turn up when the room is nearly empty. The ayah joins emptying a place to ruining it. Turning up is itself a kind of upkeep.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody does more wrong than a person who stops God's name being said in a place of worship. Such a person also helps that place fall apart. People like this should enter only in fear. Shame waits for them here, and worse waits later.

studies.title: Whichever Way You Turn
studies.meaning: Two claims sit side by side. The first is that no direction is outside God's reach, so turning anywhere still faces Him. The second denies that God has taken a son. It answers that with ownership rather than argument: everything in the heavens and the earth already belongs to Him. Only someone who lacked something would need offspring. Early scholars read the pairing as one point. God is neither held in by place nor extended by family line.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines come shortly before the change of prayer direction toward Mecca, which the surah announces a few ayat later. Several occasions are reported for the first line. One is prayer on a journey, when the direction cannot be fixed. The classical sources record these without agreeing on which is primary. The setting is a community whose neighbours were disputing its standing and its direction.

keyTerms.note: Early scholars read it as His presence, His direction, or what is turned toward the worshipper. They are careful to add that the term carries no bodily sense and no place.
From a root for roominess and space, used of land wide enough to hold everyone. It answers the worry about direction by saying there is no edge to run past.
It describes standing in service over time, not a single act of obeying. Applied here to everything that exists, it makes obedience the ordinary state of creation, not a human achievement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Direction mattered enormously to people who navigated by stars and landmarks. Caravans crossed open country by reading the sky, and getting east and west wrong could cost lives. The two words also named the two halves of the known trading world, Syria and Persia one way, Abyssinia and the sea the other. Saying both belonged to God claimed the whole map a merchant could picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The denial that God has taken a son comes with a distinctive marker here. It is one of the few statements followed by the word for glorification used as an exclamation. That is a short interjection rather than a sentence. Early scholars note that the passage does not argue the point at length here. It answers with a single word and a statement of ownership.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting these two lines together separates God from the two ways people usually locate a thing: in space, and in a family. He is not somewhere. He is not descended from anyone, and nobody carries Him on. What replaces both is ownership and knowledge that covers everything. For a community about to be told to face a particular building, the order matters. The reminder that no direction holds God comes before the instruction about which way to stand.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction to turn toward the Sacred Mosque, which these lines prepare the ground for.
Answers the same claim about offspring by defining God entirely through denial.
States nearness from the other side: God is closer to a person than their jugular vein.

studies.applyIt: Next time you pray somewhere unfamiliar and are not sure of the direction, notice the small worry that rises before you settle on one. Face your best guess and let the worry go without arguing with it. These lines were given, among other things, for exactly that moment. The ease they offer is meant to be used rather than admired.
studies.explainEasier: Every direction belongs to God, so wherever you turn, He is there. Some people said God had a son. The answer is simple: everything in the sky and on earth is already His.

studies.title: Be, And It Is
studies.meaning: A name, then a sentence. The two say the same thing in different keys. The name means originating with nothing to copy. Not making something well, but making something first of its kind. The word stands apart from every Arabic term for shaping material that is already there. The sentence then removes the process, as the name removed the material. A decree that needs only a word. Early scholars are careful about an address to what does not yet exist. Most read it as a picture of speed rather than a report of an event.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It answers a claim about God taking a son, which the ayah before reports and rejects. The classical scholars read this ayah as the ground of that rejection rather than as a separate statement about creation. A being who originates with no model and produces by decree has no need of the tie being claimed. No separate occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to do something with no model in front of you. The same root gives the ordinary Arabic word for an innovation, something brought about that was not there before in any form.
The verb for bringing a matter to completion and closing it, used also of a judge giving a decision. It implies finality rather than intention, so what is decreed is already concluded.
The bare imperative of the verb to be, two letters in Arabic. It is the shortest possible command in the language, and the ayah pairs it with a verb of becoming built from the same root.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything a person in that world made was made from something. A potter had clay dug from a bank. A smith had ore carried in from a mine. A weaver had wool from an animal he could name. A builder had stone from a quarry. No craft anywhere in that life produced from nothing and on no model. That is why the word chosen here has no match among human trades.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name opening this ayah shares its root with the ordinary Arabic word for an innovation. The connection is the absence of a precedent in both cases. So the name does not say that the heavens and the earth were well made or made powerfully. It says specifically that they were made without anything to copy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two halves work together to describe a making unlike any a person has seen. Originating with no model removes the need for a pattern. A decree of a single word removes the need for a process. The ayah's placement then does the arguing. A being described this way needs nothing to complete Him, and that is the claim the passage before was rejecting. The reply is made by definition rather than by dispute.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing as a general rule about His command whenever He wills a thing.
Uses the same divine name in the same argument, about a claim of offspring.
Applies the identical phrase to the announcement made to Mary about a birth without a father.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you made and trace what you started from. The materials, the tools, the instructions, the person who taught you. Follow it back four or five steps and notice that you never reach a beginning. That is the ordinary case, and this ayah is naming the exception to it.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth from nothing at all. He had no model to copy. When He decides that something will happen, He only says be, and it is.

studies.title: Their Hearts Resemble Each Other
studies.meaning: A request is quoted. Let God speak to us directly, or let a sign arrive. The answer does not take up the request at all. It notes that earlier people said the same words. Then comes the line that carries the ayah. Their hearts resemble one another. The subject has moved from evidence to temperament. The same demand keeps coming back across centuries and communities. So it belongs to the person making it, not to a gap in what has been given.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The phrase for those who do not know is usually read as naming people who had received no scripture at all. The classical scholars tie the demand to requests recorded elsewhere in the Quran, where a much longer list of specific signs is set out. They read this ayah as answering a pattern rather than one occasion. The middle clause says so directly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for likeness, which the surah has already used of fruit given in the Garden and of cattle indistinguishable to their owners. Here the resemblance is between hearts separated by centuries.
Left indefinite in the request, so what is asked for is not a particular proof but some sign, any sign. The vagueness of the demand is part of what the answer is responding to.
From a root carrying the sense of something settling until it becomes clear, as water clears when it stops moving. Certainty in the word is a condition arrived at rather than a conclusion reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Requests of this kind were made and recorded. Another surah keeps a much longer list put to the Prophet. Make a spring gush from the ground. Produce a garden with rivers running through it. Bring the sky down in pieces. Produce angels. Own a house of gold. The way that list climbs tells you something the single demand here does not. No item on it was the real condition.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran keeps the escalated version of this demand in another surah, where five or six specific signs are named one after another. Each is more extravagant than the last. The list grows rather than settling on one item. That is itself telling, since a person who really had a condition in mind would have stated it once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause runs in a direction most readers do not expect. It says the signs have been made clear for people who are certain. It does not say signs are given in order to make people certain. Early scholars discuss that order at length. What it shows is that evidence and reception are not separate things. The same material can be clear or cloudy, depending on what a person brings to it. The surah has been showing this for a hundred ayat.

crossReferences.why: Records the escalated version of this demand, listing several increasingly extravagant signs in succession.
Answers the request for an angel to be sent down by describing what would follow if one were.
Notes that each of them wants to be handed scrolls of his own, spread open before him.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what would actually change your mind about something you are undecided on. Write the condition down in one line. Then notice whether it is a real condition you could recognise if it arrived, or whether it moves whenever you approach it. The ayah is about the second kind.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said they wished God would speak to them, or that a sign would come. People long before them said exactly the same words. Their hearts are alike. The signs are already clear for anyone who is sure.

studies.title: Not Answerable For The Outcome
studies.meaning: A role is set out by two jobs, and then a third thing is ruled out. Good news and warning are the task. Between them they cover both directions a message can run. The closing clause lifts away responsibility for how any of it lands. The final phrase is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One makes it a statement that he will not be questioned about them. The other makes it an instruction not to ask about them. Both are kept in the standard works.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It arrives after a long stretch of the surah describing refusal, dispute and demands for signs. The classical scholars read it as comfort placed where comfort is needed. They note that the two titles used here are among the Quran's most frequent descriptions of the prophetic role. No specific occasion is reported, though the placement itself is treated as telling.

keyTerms.note: From the root that also gives the word for skin. Lexicographers connect them through news that shows in the face, which is why the word cannot be used for ordinary information.
From a verb meaning to give notice of something coming. A warning in this sense is advance information rather than a threat, which is why the two titles form a matched pair rather than a contrast.
From a root describing a fire kindled to intensity, with the flames massed together. It is one of several distinct names the Quran uses, each drawn from a different aspect of burning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A herald went ahead of a caravan or an army to announce its coming. His job was to deliver, clearly and audibly, and then to withdraw; nobody held him accountable for what people did with the news. Tribes also sent criers to proclaim a truce, a market or a death. The two words this ayah uses name exactly the two kinds of announcement such a man carried.
studies.didYouKnow: The last clause of this ayah is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One reading makes it a statement, that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) will not be questioned about those people. The other makes it an instruction, that he should not ask about them. Both are preserved in the standard works and the commentaries explain the ayah with each.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting out a role by two jobs, then naming a third that lies outside it, draws a limit rather than adding a duty. Announcing is the task. Outcomes are not. That lifts a weight the passage assumes was being carried. It also says something that reaches well past prophecy. Nobody answers for a response they were never able to produce. The comfort works by making the job smaller.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit plainly, that the task is reminding and not exercising control over people.
Divides the responsibilities explicitly: upon you the delivering, and upon Us the reckoning.
Asks whether he would compel people to believe, when belief is not something produced that way.

studies.applyIt: Name one place where you are carrying the weight of another person's response instead of your own conduct. A talk you keep rehearsing. A result you are trying to steer. Write down the part that is actually yours to do. Do only that part this week.
studies.explainEasier: God sent His messenger with the truth. His job was to bring good news and to warn people. He will not be asked to answer for the ones who end up in the Fire.

studies.title: God's Guidance Is The Guidance
studies.meaning: The subject is the terms on which approval is offered. Approval is described as conditional on adopting another community's way, and the sentence at the centre answers by defining rather than arguing: God's guidance is the guidance. What follows names the price of the exchange in the same two words the surah used a few ayat earlier for what a person has apart from God. Notice what is not disputed. The approval on offer is treated as real, and the objection is to what it costs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It is addressed to the Prophet in the singular, during years of pressure from several directions in the city. The classical scholars read the ayah as being about the condition attached to approval. They do not read it as a general description of anyone. They note that the Quran elsewhere describes an upright community among the people of earlier scripture. Those people recite God's signs through the night and prostrate.

keyTerms.note: A community's defining path. The surah uses the same word a few ayat later for the way of Abraham, which was itself the disputed question, so the vocabulary already contains the reply.
From the root for contentment and acceptance. It describes settled approval rather than agreement on a point, which is why the condition attached to it is a whole way rather than a position.
The plural of a word whose verb also means to fall. Arabic pictures desire as the direction something drops in, and the plural here sets many inclinations against a single guidance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging was everything in that society, and belonging had terms. A person outside every group had no protection, no standing in a dispute and no share in anything. Falling in with a group's way was the ordinary price of acceptance. Everyone paid it, and it rarely felt like a bargain, because there was no other choice. The pressure described here was that machinery turned on a messenger.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for their way is the same word the surah uses shortly after for the way of Abraham. Several communities claimed that inheritance. The surah is about to spend a long passage on the question. So this ayah's wording already points ahead to the answer. What was in dispute was exactly whose way Abraham's really was.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The central sentence is a definition placed between a description of pressure and a statement of cost. It does not argue that God's guidance is better than the alternatives. It identifies guidance with it. That is a different kind of claim, and weighing options cannot meet it. The passage also treats approval as a real good being offered. That is what makes it a temptation rather than a threat. And it names what would be handed over in return.

crossReferences.why: States the same exchange later in this surah and answers it by naming the way of Abraham.
Describes an upright community among the people of earlier scripture, reciting God's signs in the night.
Tells each community to compete in good works rather than to seek one another's approval.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place where you have adjusted a position to keep someone's approval. Not a compromise you decided on, but a drift you have not examined. Name the approval and name what it cost in one line each. Seeing the two written side by side is usually enough.
studies.explainEasier: Some people will only be happy with you if you follow their way. But God's way is the right one. Follow what they want, and you will have no one to guard you. No one will come to help you.

studies.title: As It Deserves To Be Recited
studies.meaning: A positive statement sits in the middle of a long and often severe address, and early scholars note where it falls. Those who recite the Book as its recitation deserves are said to believe in it. So belief comes from proper reception, not from membership. The Arabic phrase for that recitation is glossed as following the text properly. Reading it, understanding it, and acting on it. The verb for reciting is also the verb for coming along behind. The second ayah then returns to a call made much earlier.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the surah's long address to the Children of Israel. The classical scholars differ on who is meant by those given the Book here. Some read the earlier communities, some the recipients of the Quran, and they set the readings side by side. The second of these two ayat repeats an earlier one almost word for word. That is how the section's boundary is usually marked.

keyTerms.gloss: they recite it, they follow it
keyTerms.note: One verb covers reading aloud and coming after. Reciting in Arabic is following a text word behind word, which is why the same root gives both senses without any sense of metaphor.
Literally the right that its recitation has. Commentators gloss the phrase as reading, understanding and acting together, since a text has a claim on the person carrying it.
From the root meaning what exceeds a measure. The word describes a portion given beyond the ordinary share, which is why the surah pairs it here with a call to remember rather than with a title.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Texts travelled by voice, so the quality of a transmitter mattered enormously. Everyone in a scholarly community knew who could be trusted. A man who reproduced sounds accurately without understanding them was known and discounted. So was one who understood but altered as he went. Anyone who handled texts for a living would have recognised the standard this ayah names at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat repeats an ayah from about seventy-five earlier in this same surah, word for word. The pair forms a bracket around the whole address to that audience. It opens and closes with the same call to remember. Early scholars use the repeat to mark where the section begins and ends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a plainly positive statement here matters more than its content. After a hundred ayat of refusal, distortion and dispute, the surah pauses. It says that those who receive the text as it deserves believe in it. It does not qualify the group or name it. That makes the standard open to anyone rather than assigned. The closing repeat then ends the section where it began, on memory rather than on a verdict.
