crossReferences.why: Opens the long address with the identical call to remember, which this passage repeats to close it.
Gives the same positive assessment elsewhere, describing an upright community reciting through the night.
Says the reward of those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer is not allowed to be lost.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of scripture three times today: once for the sound, once for what it says, once for what you would do differently if you took it seriously. Five minutes in total. The phrase in this ayah is usually explained as those three things together, and doing them separately makes the difference visible.
studies.explainEasier: People who read the Book the way it should be read really do believe in it. Those who turn it down lose out. Then God tells the Children of Israel to remember the good He gave them.

studies.title: The Warning Said Again
studies.meaning: This warning appeared once before in the surah, and the second telling is not a copy. Two of its clauses have changed places, and one has changed its verb. Where the earlier version said that pleading on a soul's behalf would not be accepted, this one says it would not benefit. The first denial concerns whether such a plea is received; the second concerns whether it would do any good. Taken together the two versions close the same door from opposite sides.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the long address that the earlier version of this warning opened, so the section is bracketed by the same day named twice. The classical scholars note the repeat and the reordering, and read the pair as deliberate rather than as a duplication. Elsewhere the Quran speaks of pleading that takes place by God's leave. The commentaries read the denials here alongside those passages.

keyTerms.note: The object of the verb is a day rather than a person. Guarding oneself against a stretch of time is an unusual construction, and the surah uses it in both versions of this warning.
The verb for something being taken and admitted. In this version it governs the ransom, whereas in the earlier telling it governed the plea, which is the exact point where the two differ.
To be of use to someone. Denying benefit is a wider statement than denying acceptance, since something can be admitted and still change nothing, and this version chooses the wider word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a world without books, important things were repeated on purpose, and audiences expected it. A poet returned to his central line. A speaker said a warning again in different words, so the second hearing did not slide past. A message carried between clans was said twice before the messenger left. Repeating on purpose, with small changes, was a skill of speech. It was not a slip.
studies.didYouKnow: The two versions of this warning in this surah are not identical. The clauses change places. The verb attached to speaking up for someone changes from being accepted to being of benefit. Early scholars noticed the difference at once. The effect is that a reader who has met the first version cannot let the second pass as something already known.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repetition with a change keeps a warning from hardening into a formula. That is a general feature of how the Quran restates things. The change of verb here also does real work. It moves the denial from process to effect, and leaves no version of the hope intact. Placing the second telling at the end of the section the first opened then frames everything between them with the same day, named twice.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first version of this warning, with two of the clauses in the other order.
States that no plea and no ransom would be accepted from those who let their faith become a game.
Describes the pleading that does occur, taking place only by the permission of the one who grants it.

studies.applyIt: Notice a warning you have heard so often that you no longer hear it. From a doctor, a friend, a text you know well. Say it back to yourself in different words, your own, once. The surah changes its own wording for exactly this reason, and the second version is what gets through.
studies.explainEasier: Watch out for a day when no person can do anything for another. Nobody can pay a price to get out of it. Nobody can speak up and make a difference. No help will come.

studies.title: Leadership Earned Under Test
studies.meaning: Abraham is tested with words. He completes them, and God then appoints him a leader for humanity. He asks at once whether the appointment reaches his descendants. The answer allows it, but shuts out those who do wrong. Early scholars differ over what the words were. Some say the rites of pilgrimage, some the trials of his life, some commands that are not named. What the passage fixes is the order: testing first, appointment second, and no inheriting the office by blood alone.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line opens the surah's long treatment of Abraham, the Kaaba, and whose claim to him holds. It sits in a section arguing with communities in Medina that traced their standing to descent from him. The passage answers that argument at its root, without naming anyone. Early scholars read the exclusion in the last clause as the whole point of the exchange.

keyTerms.note: The root is used for wearing something out through use, as a garment wears. Testing here shows what a person is made of through repeated strain, not through a single exam.
From a root meaning to go in front. The word describes someone others take their bearings from, so the office is defined by who follows rather than by who commands.
A binding agreement between two parties, the ordinary word for a treaty between tribes. Using it here makes the appointment a contract, with terms a party can fall outside of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian leadership ran through the family line. A chief's standing passed to his sons. A man's worth was recited through his ancestors before anything else was said about him. Genealogists were respected professionals, and disputes over rank were settled by tracing descent. Against that background, an appointment a father cannot pass to a wrongdoing son was not a mild condition. It cut across the main way that society handed out authority.
studies.didYouKnow: Abraham is called a leader for humanity here. Elsewhere in the Quran he is described as a community in himself, one man standing where a whole people would stand. He is the only figure the Quran gives both descriptions. Early scholars connect them: the office given at the end of his testing is one he first had to hold alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes standing before God something you cannot hand on. A covenant can run through a family, but it does not run past wrongdoing. So descent secures nothing on its own. It also sets a shape for authority in the Quran generally. Those who lead have first been tried, and the trial is what qualifies them. Abraham's question is granted and limited in the same breath, which is the Quran's usual way of answering hope honestly.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same request continuing as prayer while he builds, asking for a community rather than a dynasty.
Describes Abraham as a community in himself, devoted and upright before God.
Narrates the hardest of the trials, and the ransom that ends it.

studies.applyIt: Consider something you expect to pass on: a business, a reputation, a set of values in your family. Ask what in it can actually be handed over and what has to be earned again by whoever receives it. Then tell one person honestly which is which. Abraham asked the same question and was given an answer that was kinder for being limited.
studies.explainEasier: God tested Abraham and he passed. So God made him a leader for everyone. Abraham asked if his children would lead too. God said yes, but not the ones who do wrong.

studies.title: A Place People Come Back To
studies.meaning: The House is named twice over. First as a place people return to, then as a security. The order is worth noticing. Return comes before safety. So the building is defined by people coming back, not by what happens once they arrive. What follows is an instruction to keep it fit for that. It is addressed to Abraham and Ishmael. It names three ways of being present, not one: circling it, staying in it, and lowering oneself in it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It falls in the surah's long passage on Abraham. That passage comes straight after the address to earlier communities, and answers whose heir he is. The classical scholars name the standing place mentioned here. They report differing details about it. They also note that the sanctuary worked as a safe place long before this revelation, and that the whole peninsula honoured it.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to come back. The same root gives the ordinary word for a garment, understood as cloth returning to its shape, and the word for a reward, understood as what comes back to a person.
Safety, from the root that also gives the words for belief and for entrusting. What is named is a condition of the place itself rather than a feeling in the people who come to it.
From a verb meaning to hold persistently to a place and not leave it. It names presence without motion, set here between those who circle and those who bow.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inside the sacred precinct a blood feud was suspended. Men who would have killed one another on the road could stand and trade a few paces apart. The sacred months spread the same truce across the peninsula's main travelling seasons. The whole yearly pattern of trade rested on it. Calling the House a security named a working arrangement, not a hope for one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a place of return in this ayah shares its root with the ordinary Arabic words for a garment and for a reward. The early Arabic dictionary writers link all three through the idea of coming back. Cloth returns to its shape. A reward returns to the one who earned it. A person keeps returning to a place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming three postures rather than one lets the House hold several kinds of presence at once. None is described as better than the others. Moving around it, staying in it and lowering oneself in it are given as three ways the same place is used. The passage also puts the instruction to keep it fit before any account of rites. So upkeep is presented as the first duty attached to a sanctuary.

crossReferences.why: Names it the first house appointed for people, and says whoever enters it is secure.
Records the same charge to Abraham, to purify the House for those who circle and pray there.
Continues the account in this surah with Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations and praying.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place you return to and have stopped noticing. A room, a route, a table. Do one small act of upkeep on it today, and notice that returning is what makes a place matter rather than anything that happens there. That is the order this ayah puts them in.
studies.explainEasier: God made the House a place people come back to, and a safe place. He told Abraham and Ishmael to keep it clean and ready. It is for people who walk around it, stay in it, and bow down there.

studies.title: The Condition He Added
studies.meaning: Abraham asks for two things. Security for a place, and fruit for its people. Then he narrows the second request to those of them who believe. The reply widens what he narrowed. Whoever denies is granted enjoyment too, for a while, before a separate outcome. Early scholars treat that correction as the point of the exchange. They read it as one of the clearest statements in the Quran that what people are given in this world is handed out on terms that have nothing to do with approval.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's passage on Abraham. A closely matching prayer appears in another surah, made for the same valley and calling it land without crops. The classical scholars read the two together and note the setting. It was a place with no farming of its own, ringed by bare hills. Its people ate what was carried in and lived on what the sanctuary brought.

keyTerms.note: Security named as a property of the place rather than of its people. The word for the town covers a settled area with its surroundings, so what is requested is a condition attached to ground.
From the word for the provisions a traveller carries and uses up on the road. What is granted is named as supplies for a journey, which builds a limit into the giving.

keyTerms.gloss: I will drive him, compel him
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning necessity and being left no alternative. The verb describes being brought to something by the closing off of every other direction rather than by force applied directly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The valley in question grew nothing. It sat among bare hills with no field, no river and no orchard, and everything eaten there arrived by camel from somewhere else. Its whole economy rested on the sanctuary and the seasonal traffic that came for it. A prayer asking for fruit in that place was asking for something the ground could not produce and only trade could deliver.
studies.didYouKnow: The request was made with a condition and the answer removed it. Abraham asked for provision for those of the people who believe. The reply extends enjoyment, for a time, to whoever does not. Early scholars single this exchange out. It settles plainly a question people keep asking, about whether doing well means anything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange separates two things that are constantly merged. What people are given in this life is described as broadly handed out and openly temporary. What follows it is stated on its own. So neither wealth nor its absence can be read as a verdict on anyone. It is also striking that a scripture records a prophet's request being answered and corrected in one breath. The correction is a widening, not a refusal.

crossReferences.why: Gives the parallel prayer for the same valley, describing it as a place without cultivation.
Warns against being impressed by the movement of the denying through the land, calling it a brief enjoyment.
Says that were it not for one danger, houses of silver and gold would be given to those who deny.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you have quietly read as a sign of approval, yours or someone else's: an income, a health, a run of good luck. This exchange says plainly that provision is given on other terms. Hold the thing you named and separate it from the verdict you had attached to it.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asked God to make the town safe and to feed the people who believe. God said He would feed the others too, for a while. After that, a hard end waits for them.

studies.title: A Prayer Said While Building
studies.meaning: Father and son are raising the walls of the House and praying at the same time. The prayer is about the work, not about themselves. They ask first that the labour be accepted, which assumes it might not be. Then they ask for surrender in themselves, and a surrendered community from their descendants. Then for teaching in how to worship, and last for their repentance to be accepted. Early scholars note the order: acceptance, then character, then knowledge, then pardon.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines sit in its account of Abraham, Ishmael and the sanctuary at Mecca. They were given while the young community was being told to face that building in prayer. The Quran does not date the building itself, and the classical scholars discuss the foundations without settling the history. What the passage supplies is the intention behind the structure. That is what the surah's argument needs.

keyTerms.note: The word for what sits at the bottom and carries the load, from a root meaning to sit. Raising the foundations names the least visible and most decisive stage of the work.
A form of the verb that means to receive something willingly and gladly, not merely to take it. That strengthening is what makes the request humble rather than routine.
It refers to the acts of worship at the sanctuary. Asking to be shown them admits that the right way to approach God is taught, not invented, even by a prophet building His House.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Building in Mecca meant carrying stone by hand from the surrounding hills in a valley with no timber and little water. Work of that kind took months and was done in family groups, an older man setting courses while a younger one hauled. Anyone in the audience had seen a wall raised that way. The picture of two men praying while lifting rock was ordinary labour, not ceremony.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places in the Quran where a prayer is quoted while the person praying is in the middle of physical work. The request that follows in the next ayah asks for a messenger to be raised from their descendants. Early scholars connect that request directly to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). That makes the passage a prayer the audience was hearing answered.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Effort and dependence are shown together rather than in sequence. The two are working hard and asking for acceptance in the same breath, which rules out both idle waiting and self-satisfied labour. Asking to be taught the rites concedes that worship is received rather than designed. And the closing name, the one who turns back to those who turn, ends a prayer of the righteous on repentance rather than on merit.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same prayer, asking for a messenger raised from their own descendants.
Describes the sanctuary's purpose and the call to pilgrimage that followed Abraham's work.
Gives Abraham's longer prayer over the same valley, for safety, provision and steady worship.

studies.applyIt: Take something you are in the middle of building, a project, a home, a friendship, and ask for it to be accepted rather than for it to succeed. The two requests feel similar and are not. One is about the outcome and the other about the offering. Say it once, during the work rather than after it, and notice how it changes your grip on the result.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham and his son are building God's House. While they work, they pray. They ask God to accept what they are doing, to help them obey Him, and to teach them how to worship.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among Them
studies.meaning: This is the last request in Abraham's prayer, and it asks for four things. Someone to recite the signs, to teach the Book, to teach wisdom, and to purify. None of the four is protection, victory or wealth. What is asked for a community that does not yet exist is an education. The messenger is named as coming from among them rather than to them. The prayer closes on two names. One can grant such a request. The other names what is being asked to be taught.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It completes the prayer Abraham and Ishmael make while raising the foundations of the House. The classical scholars read the request as answered in the mission of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They note that the Quran itself makes that link elsewhere. It describes a messenger raised among the unlettered with the same four tasks listed.

keyTerms.note: The same verb the Quran uses for raising the dead. One word covers both dispatches, so sending a messenger to a people is described with the language of bringing something back to life.
From a root that also gives the word for a horse's bridle. Wisdom in Arabic carries restraint and the placing of each thing where it belongs, so it is practical before it is theoretical.
From the root meaning to grow and to be pure at once, the same root behind the word for the purifying due. Purification here implies increase rather than reduction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An outsider carried no authority in tribal Arabia. A man who spoke for a people had to be of them. He had to be known by line and by his conduct since boyhood. A stranger with the same message would simply not have been heard. The prayer asks for exactly this, someone from among them. That very closeness later produced objections of its own.
studies.didYouKnow: The four tasks named in this prayer appear again in two other places in the Quran describing what was actually sent. In both the order is different. Purification comes last in the request. It is placed before the teaching in the accounts of what came. Early scholars have discussed the switch for centuries without settling it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prayer made for descendants asks for formation rather than for advantage. That says something about what a founder is understood to be able to leave. None of the four requests can be inherited as a possession. Each has to be received again by every generation. The closing pair of names then matches the content exactly. Might is what can grant such a thing. Wisdom is what is being asked to be handed on.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same four tasks as a favour conferred, with the order of two of them reversed.
States the fulfilment again, naming a messenger raised among the unlettered with these same functions.
Repeats the list later in this surah, addressed directly to the community that received it.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you actually want for the people who come after you, and write down three things. Then check how many of them are conditions and how many are capacities. This prayer asks only for the second kind, which is worth noticing, because conditions can be arranged for and capacities have to be taught.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asked God to send these people a messenger from among them. That messenger would read God's words to them. He would teach them the Book and teach them to be wise. He would make them clean.

studies.title: One Word, Answered At Once
studies.meaning: A question makes leaving this way the thing that needs explaining, not following it. The phrase for the person who leaves is the same word the surah used far earlier of people who called others foolish. Then comes the exchange. One word, answered by two. No question is asked and no term is haggled over. The answer also gives more than the command required. It names the one submitted to. Early scholars read that addition as the substance of the reply.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's passage on Abraham. That passage follows straight on from the long address to communities that claimed him. The classical scholars read these two ayat as setting out what his way actually consisted of. Then the surah turns to the dispute over who inherits it. They note that the answer given here names no community at all.

keyTerms.note: The verb reverses with its preposition. With one small word after it the verb means to desire something; with the one used here it means to want nothing to do with it, and the verb itself stays neutral.
From the word for the clearest part of a liquid, what is poured off above the sediment or skimmed from the top. Choosing in this verb is taking the finest portion rather than picking among options.
A completed act rather than a promise, from the root that gives peace, safety and handing over. The form states the thing as already done, which is why no interval appears in the exchange.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Anyone who kept animals knew what the verb for choosing describes. Milk left standing separates, and the clear part is taken off the top. Water settling in a skin leaves its sediment below. Taking the choicest portion was a daily job with a name. It meant letting something rest until the best of it could be lifted away clean.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic verb for turning away in the first of these ayat becomes its exact opposite when a different preposition follows it. With one particle it means to want something. With another it means to want nothing to do with it. The verb carries no direction of its own. The whole meaning rests on a two-letter word placed after it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply expands the command rather than just accepting it. Told to submit, the answer names the one submitted to. That turns an act of going along with something into a statement of who is being obeyed. The difference matters. Submission with no object named would be obedience to a voice. The first ayah then flips where the burden of explanation lies. The way itself is the ordinary case, and leaving it is what needs a reason.

crossReferences.why: Asks who is better in religion than one who submits and follows the way of Abraham, inclining to truth.
Uses the same verb for choosing, naming the families God selected above all peoples.
Records Abraham turning his face to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, upright.

studies.applyIt: Notice the gap between being asked to do something and doing it, in one small case today. Not a difficult request. Something ordinary that you would normally hold for a moment, weigh, or answer with a question. Close the gap once, deliberately, and see what the closing costs you.
studies.explainEasier: Only a person who fools himself would turn away from the way of Abraham. God picked Abraham in this life, and he will be among the good ones later. God told him to submit, and he said at once that he had.

studies.title: What A Father Leaves
studies.meaning: The verb used is the one for making a will. So what follows comes as a bequest, not as advice. Then a sentence that cannot mean what it plainly says. Do not die except while submitting is, in the grammar, an instruction about dying. Nobody chooses that hour. Early scholars read it from the start as an instruction about living. The moment cannot be picked. So the only way to meet the condition is to be in that state all the time. The wording makes the point without saying it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's Abraham passage. The ayah joins two generations in one sentence. Jacob is named alongside Abraham as giving the same charge, and the scene of Jacob doing so follows right after. The classical scholars read the pair as setting up a line of handing down. That matters, because the surah is about to say what does and does not pass along it.

keyTerms.note: The verb behind the ordinary Arabic word for a will. It names the instruction a person leaves for after his death, which in that society was the most binding kind of speech there was.
The same verb used two ayat earlier of Abraham himself. There a person is chosen, here a way is chosen for people, which quietly makes the two selections parts of one act.
A participle describing a state in progress, not an act completed. The grammar is what turns the instruction from something about a moment into something about a condition maintained.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A deathbed will was the most serious speech there was in that world. It divided property, named guardians for children, settled debts and gave instructions on blood claims. It was spoken before witnesses who would repeat it exactly. What a man said in that hour outweighed anything he had said in life. Families remembered the wording for generations, because so much rested on it.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction cannot be obeyed as it stands, since nobody picks the hour of his own death. Early scholars noticed this at once. They read it as a statement about a lasting condition rather than about a final moment. The Quran uses the same construction elsewhere. In each case the point is that a state must already be held when the unscheduled thing arrives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Casting this as a will makes what passes between generations a way rather than a possession. The surah is about to say, very shortly, that what an earlier community earned does not transfer. Those two claims sit together without clashing. A practice can be handed on while its credit cannot. The difference between them is exactly what the ayat that follow are arranged to show.

crossReferences.why: Shows the scene itself, with Jacob putting the same charge to his sons as death approaches.
Instructs enjoining prayer upon one's household and being steadfast in it oneself.
Records Joseph asking to be caused to die submitting and joined to the righteous.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you would want to say to the people closest to you if you had one sentence and no chance to explain it. Write the sentence down. Then notice whether anything in how you live this week would let them work it out for themselves, which is the harder half of the same question.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham left his sons a last instruction, and Jacob left the same one. God has chosen this way for them. They should still be giving themselves to God on the day they die.

studies.title: What Will You Worship After Me
studies.meaning: The ayah opens by asking who was in the room. That turns a dispute about what ancestors believed into a question about evidence. Then the scene itself. A dying man asks his sons a single question. It is not about property, standing or carrying on a name. The answer they give names his God and the God of his fathers, and lists them. Then it adds two things the question had not asked for. That this is one God, and that they are submitted to Him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's Abraham passage, right after the ayah describing the charge given to sons. The classical scholars read the opening question as aimed at those making claims about what the patriarchs believed. They note how the ayah answers. It does not point to a rival tradition. It points to the absence of any witness on either side, apart from what revelation supplies.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both being present and giving testimony, since in that society the two were the same thing. Asking whether they were witnesses is asking whether they were physically in the room.
The ordinary verb for arriving somewhere and being there. Death is its subject here, so the Arabic describes it as something that turns up in a room rather than as something that happens to a body.
An addition the question did not ask for. Having named their father's God and their forefathers', the sons collapse the list into a single object, which is the whole content of their answer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deathbeds were public. A dying man lay surrounded by his household and often by much of his clan. Many heard his last words and repeated them afterwards. Inheritance disputes were settled by what witnesses agreed they had heard. The question this ayah opens with uses that custom exactly. Asking who was present was the ordinary first move in any contested claim about what somebody said.
studies.didYouKnow: The sons name Ishmael among their fathers. He was Isaac's brother, so he was their great-uncle rather than a direct ancestor. Early scholars note that Arabic often stretches the word for father to cover an uncle, or any forebear in the line. This ayah is the standard example given for that use.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question a dying man asks is about worship, and it comes right after a will. So what is handed on is a direction rather than an estate. The sons' answer then does something the question did not require. It gathers several generations into one object of worship. That is the claim the whole passage is making. The line is single because what it worshipped was single.

crossReferences.why: Gives the charge itself, with Abraham and Jacob enjoining the same thing on their sons.
States plainly that Abraham belonged to neither of the later communities but was upright and submitting.
Has Joseph name the same line of fathers when explaining what he follows, in a prison cell.

studies.applyIt: Ask someone older than you what they hope you keep. Not what they achieved, and not advice. Just that question, in those words. Most people are never asked it and most have an answer ready. It takes one conversation, and the answers are almost never what you would have guessed.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody saw Jacob on the day he died. He asked his sons what they would worship after he was gone. They said they would worship his God and the God of his fathers. One God, and they gave themselves to Him.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: That Community Has Passed
studies.meaning: An account is closed. A community is described as having gone by, using a verb that means to become empty, and everything it acquired is assigned to it. The word for what it acquired is the ordinary term for earning a living, which the Quran uses throughout for deeds, so a life's record is a set of earnings rather than a status held. Then the final clause turns the same principle around. If their credit does not reach you, neither does their liability.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It comes straight after the deathbed scene in which sons name the God of their fathers. The placement is deliberate. A passage setting up a line of handing down is followed at once by a statement of what does not travel down it. The classical scholars read the ayah as addressed generally rather than to one audience. They note that it comes back word for word a few ayat later.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to become empty of people. The surah has used the same root for withdrawing into private company, so what is described is a space vacated rather than merely time elapsed.
The plain word for earning a living. Using it of deeds makes a record something accumulated by work, and earnings in that society were precisely the kind of thing that did not pass on intact.
A passive form, so no one is named as the questioner. The construction leaves the sentence as a statement about liability rather than as a description of a scene.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance in Arabia carried far more than property. Alliances passed down, and so did feuds and blood claims. A man could be pursued for a killing his grandfather had done. He could be owed for one done against his line. The duties were real and could be enforced across generations. In that world, being told you will not be questioned about what they did was a release, not a truism.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a community comes from a root that also gives the plain Arabic words for a mother and for one who leads from the front. The early Arabic dictionary writers link them through aim and origin. A community is a body moving toward something. It is named from the same idea as the one who goes first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah is usually read as a rebuke to anyone leaning on ancestry, and it is. But its closing clause is a relief. Cutting the passing on of credit cuts the passing on of debt in the same stroke. That society was built around inherited claims of both kinds, so this was a substantial thing to say. It leaves a person holding only what he has earned himself. That is the only portion he can still add to.

crossReferences.why: States the principle at its widest, no bearer carrying another's load and a person having only his own striving.
Says every soul earns only against itself, and no bearer of a burden bears the burden of another.
Adds that a heavily laden soul calling for help will have nothing of its load carried, even by a relative.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you take credit for that was actually handed to you: an education, a name, a start someone else paid for. Say what it was, plainly, once. This ayah is not asking you to be ashamed of it. It is separating what you were given from what you have done, and most of us keep those in one pile.
studies.explainEasier: Those people lived and are now gone. They keep what they earned. You keep what you earn. Nobody will ask you to answer for the things that they did.

studies.title: Neither, But Earlier
studies.meaning: An invitation is put as a choice between two. The reply refuses the frame rather than the options. It does not offer a third party. It moves the question back in time, to a figure who came before both and whom both claim. It describes him with a word already in use in Arabia. That word named people who held to one God outside either community. The final clause then closes the one reading that would make the answer a compromise. It says what he was not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the middle of the surah's Abraham passage. The setting is a city where both scriptural communities were present. There, which of them a person should join was a live and practical question. The classical scholars note that the word used here for Abraham was current in Arabia before Islam. It was applied to individuals remembered for keeping to belief in one God without belonging to either.

keyTerms.note: A plain command to enter a category. The invitation is not to accept a claim or to change a practice but to take on a name, which is what the reply then declines to do.
A community's defining path, the whole shape of how a people lives before God. The surah used the same word a few ayat earlier for what was being demanded as the price of approval.
Commentators gloss it as turning away from every deviation toward what is straight. The word was in circulation in Arabia for those who kept to one God outside both scriptural communities.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were men in Mecca before Islam who had rejected the idols without joining either scriptural community. They were remembered for it, and the word used in this ayah was the term applied to them. To that audience it was not an old word. It named a position some of their own relatives had held within living memory. That is part of why the reply lands as an answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran here takes a term its audience already used and attaches it to Abraham. That is why the reply works as an answer rather than as a third claim. It does not invent a new category to escape a forced choice. It names one that already existed and that everyone present understood. Then it identifies the figure both parties were claiming with it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply turns a dispute about preference into a dispute about inheritance. The figure both sides claim came before both of them. So the question is not which community to join. It is which of them carries on from him. The surah spends the ayat that follow on exactly that, asking who was present and who knows better. The last clause matters too. It rules out reading the answer as a middle position between the two.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing directly, that he belonged to neither community but was upright and submitting.
Records the same pressure a few ayat earlier, approval offered on condition of adopting a way.
Describes him as a community in himself, upright, and instructs following that way.

studies.applyIt: Notice a question you have been answering inside a frame someone else set. This side or that. One label or the other. Write the question out as it was handed to you. Then write what you would actually want to say, if you were not picking between the two on offer.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said you would only be guided if you joined their group. The answer went further back. Follow the way of Abraham, who came before both groups. He believed in one God and never worshipped idols.

studies.title: One Line Of Messengers
studies.meaning: This is a statement of belief, given as words to say. It names what was sent down to this community. Then it reaches back through Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, then to Moses and Jesus, then to all the prophets without listing them. The decisive clause is the refusal to divide between any of them. Accepting one messenger while rejecting another is ruled out. The sentence closes by naming the speaker's own position: surrendered to God.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits in a passage arguing with communities that traced their faith to particular prophets and disputed the claims made for others. The ayat before it record Jacob questioning his sons at his death. They also record a demand that the community become Jews or Christians to be guided. This line is the reply they are told to give. Early scholars treat it as a formula for the whole community, not an answer to one person.

keyTerms.note: Used for the twelve tribes descended from Jacob's sons. The root suggests something stretched out in a line, like a spreading branch. So the word carries continuity rather than a fixed number.
The verb means to split apart or separate into pieces. What is forbidden is not comparing the prophets but dividing them into a group you accept and a group you set aside.
From the same root as peace and wholeness. Here it names a posture before God rather than a community label, and the Quran applies it to Abraham and to Jacob's sons in the same passage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Medina, Jewish and Arab clans shared markets, wells and treaties. The question of which prophets a person owned was a live boundary marker. It was worked into arguments at the date market as readily as into formal debate. Reciting a list that included everyone else's founders, and refused to rank them, was a public act with a social cost. It gave away an advantage both sides had been using.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names twenty-five prophets. It also states plainly that messengers were sent whose stories were never told. Jesus appears here in a list that Muslims recite as their own creed. He is named in the Quran more often than the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is named directly. Early scholars note this without treating it as a ranking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is shown as one long act with many deliveries. So believing the latest does not mean throwing out the earlier ones. Rejecting any prophet breaks the whole chain. It is not a small local quarrel. The words also settle who you are by direction, not by descent. The speaker ends not with a tribe or a family line, but with a bond: surrendered to the one who sent them all.

crossReferences.why: Puts almost the same declaration in the mouth of the Messenger and the believers together.
Warns against believing in some messengers and rejecting others, and names it a middle way that fails.
Says the same religion was enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus alike.

studies.applyIt: Say this list slowly once today, out loud, and stop at the name you know least about. Most people have one. Read a short account of that prophet this week rather than promising yourself a longer study later. The line you recite claims them all equally, and it is worth having at least a sentence of your own about each of them.
studies.explainEasier: Muslims say they believe in God and in every prophet He sent, from Abraham to Moses to Jesus. You cannot pick some and turn down the others. They all came from the same God.

studies.title: Whose Colour Are You Wearing
studies.meaning: A condition, then its alternative, and then an image. If they believe in the like of what you believe, they are guided. That sets the standard as content, not membership. If they turn away, the word used pictures two parties on opposite sides of a split. The promise that follows is stated as enough rather than as victory, using a verb meaning to suffice. Then the second ayah answers a question about belonging with a colour. It does so in a fragment with no verb at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes a passage in which the community is told what to say about the prophets it shares with its neighbours. The classical scholars explain the image of colouring in two ways. One is the nature God gave every human being. The other is a reply to practices in which a community marked its members on the body. They record both readings, and the two do not clash.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for cleaving something in two. It pictures parties standing on either side of a crack rather than in conflict, so the word describes position more than it describes hostility.
Built on the verb meaning to suffice. What is promised is sufficiency rather than triumph, which is a smaller and more precise assurance than the translations usually make it sound.
The word for dye taken into cloth rather than a mark applied to a surface. Commentators read it as the constitution God gives, which goes all the way through and is not put on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Colour identified people at a distance. Cloth was dyed once and permanently, and across the region what a community wore told you who they were before anyone spoke. Dye entered the fibre rather than sitting on it, which is why a dyed garment stayed dyed through years of wear. The question of whose colouring a person carries was, in that world, a question about visible belonging.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about colouring stands in the accusative in Arabic with no verb in front of it. Grammarians handle that by supplying one, either hold to or this is. So the words arrive as a fragment, not as a sentence. That abruptness is part of how the ayah reads in the original, and it vanishes in translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard set in the first ayah is the content of belief, not the name of a community. That fits how the surah has answered such questions throughout. The image in the second ayah then puts identity in something that has gone all the way through a person. It is not a mark applied to the outside. Between them they describe belonging as a matter of what someone is made of.

crossReferences.why: Names the natural constitution God made people upon, which commentators connect directly to the colouring here.
Asks whether God is not enough for His servant, using the same verb of sufficiency.
Gives the same assurance in another setting, that He is sufficient against those who mock.

studies.applyIt: Think about what identifies you to other people at a glance, and then about what would still be true if none of those markers were visible. Not as an exercise in modesty. Just to find out how much of what you would name is applied to the outside and how much has gone through.
studies.explainEasier: If they believe the same thing you believe, they are on the right path. If they turn away, they have split off. God will be enough for you against them. We take our colour from God alone.

studies.title: Do You Argue About God
studies.meaning: Three clauses, and together they take the argument apart rather than winning it. A shared Lord is stated. That rules out the idea that the two sides are talking about different things. Deeds are then handed to each side separately. That rules out settling the matter by group. What is left is sincerity, named by a word meaning unmixed. Nobody can check that from outside. The reply turns down the contest itself. In a culture built on public debate, that was a clear and unusual move.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It follows the passage on Abraham and the prophets held in common. A nearly identical sentence appears in another surah, at the end of a statement about differing communities. The classical scholars read this ayah alongside the instruction elsewhere to dispute with the people of earlier scripture only in the best way. They treat the two as describing the same stance.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a proof that stands. The form implies a contest between two parties, and the surah used the same verb earlier of people afraid of being out-argued with their own material.
Assigned twice in the same sentence, once to each side. Repeating the noun rather than using a pronoun makes the separation explicit, so neither party's record is available to the other.
From a root meaning free of admixture. The surah used the same root earlier for a claim of exclusive entitlement, so the language of unmixedness serves twice with very different results.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public debate was a skill people trained in and crowds turned out for. Arguments over lineage, rank and old claims were held before witnesses, with known moves, known ways of pressing an advantage and known ways of giving in. Refusing to enter a contest at all, rather than making a move inside it, was a visible and deliberate act. Everyone present would have noticed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sincerity here shares its root with the word used earlier in this surah for a claim of sole entitlement to the next life. Both mean unmixed. One describes a possession nobody else may share. The other describes devotion with nothing hidden underneath. The Arabic keeps the two plainly related.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply grants what is shared and separates what is not. The residue it reaches is deliberately out of sight. Sincerity cannot be produced in an argument or checked by an opponent. Naming it as the last item ends the dispute by moving it somewhere no dispute can reach. That is not a dodge. It is a claim about where the question was always going to be settled.

crossReferences.why: Repeats almost the same sentence, adding that there is no argument between us and you.
Instructs disputing with the people of earlier scripture only in the best way, saying our God and yours is one.
Ends a whole surah on the same separation, each side left with what is theirs.

studies.applyIt: Leave one argument today that you could win. Not by conceding the point and not by walking off. Say what you actually hold, once, without pressing it, and let the exchange end there. Notice how strong the pull is to add one more sentence, and do not add it.
studies.explainEasier: Believers are told to point out that they share the same Lord with the people arguing. Each side has its own deeds. And the believers say they are honest with God, all the way through.

studies.title: Do You Know Better
studies.meaning: A claim about what named ancestors believed is met with a question about sources, not with a rival history. The figures listed all came before both of the communities claiming them. So saying they belonged to one requires knowledge nobody has, and the reply asks where it came from. Then a second and different charge is added. Holding back a testimony you actually have is a different failing from stating something you do not. The ayah names it in the Quran's strongest form.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It falls where the surah's Abraham passage turns from stating what his way was to disputing who may claim it. The classical scholars differ on what testimony is meant here. Some read it as knowledge of a coming messenger. Some read it as the truth about the way of Abraham itself. They set the readings out and generally leave the question open.

keyTerms.note: The descendants of Jacob's sons, taken as the ancestral lines rather than as individuals. Naming them extends the claim being questioned across several generations rather than resting it on one figure.
The verb for holding something in so it cannot escape, used of stopping water or sealing a wound. The surah used it far earlier of what the angels were holding back unspoken.
From the same root as being present. A testimony is what a person who was there can supply and nobody else can, which is exactly what makes withholding it consequential.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the machinery of justice, since almost nothing was written down. A witness who stayed silent did not merely fail to help. He made a judgement impossible, because there was no other route to the facts. Everyone knew that the whole method of settling disputes rested on people saying what they had seen. A man known for holding back was known for it for good.
studies.didYouKnow: The strongest form of question used here, asking who does greater wrong, appears a limited number of times in the Quran. Each time it is attached to a small set of offences. Concealing a testimony is one of them. Making up a lie against God is another. Blocking places of worship, which this same surah named a few ayat earlier, is a third.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering a claim about history with a question about knowledge sets a standard rather than winning an exchange. The question applies to anyone making such a claim in any direction. The second half then names an offence of leaving something out. It gives that the same weight the Quran gives to the gravest offences of speech. So silence stands alongside speech as something a person can answer for.

crossReferences.why: States the answer to the question directly, that he belonged to neither of the later communities.
Says later in this surah that whoever conceals testimony has a heart that is sinful in doing so.
Uses the same superlative question of one who invents a falsehood against God or denies His signs.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you know that would help someone and that you have not said, because saying it would be awkward or would cost you an advantage. Not a secret you were entrusted with. Something you simply have. Decide today whether you are keeping it for a reason you could state out loud.
studies.explainEasier: Some said Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and their sons belonged to their own group. They are asked whether they know better than God. And nobody does worse than someone who hides a true thing God gave him to tell.

studies.title: Said Twice In Eight Ayat
studies.meaning: This ayah has already appeared once in this surah, word for word, only eight ayat earlier. The Quran repeats things often. But repeating a whole ayah this close is unusual, and nothing changes except what stands in front of it. The first time, it followed sons naming their father's God at a deathbed. This time it follows a claim that those same ancestors belonged to a later community. So one sentence closes both uses of ancestry, the pious one and the one used in argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the surah's Abraham passage, before the surah turns to the change in the direction of prayer. The classical scholars note the exact repeat. They read it as bracketing the argument about who may claim the patriarchs. So the section opens and closes by denying that anyone inherits their record in either direction.

keyTerms.note: From a root that also gives the words for a mother and for one who leads from the front. The lexicographers connect them through origin and direction, a body moving toward something.

A particle of certainty attached to a verb meaning to become empty. The construction states the passing as settled fact, which is what makes the rest of the sentence a matter of accounting rather than of judgement.

The clause is repeated for both parties in the same sentence with the noun stated twice rather than pronouns used. The symmetry is deliberate, and it makes neither side's record available to the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was the central science of that society. Men memorised lines of descent across many generations. Specialists were consulted the way lawyers are now, and standing in a dispute could turn on whose ancestor had done what. A family's line was often the most valuable thing it owned. Being told that an ancestor's record does not transfer was being told that the main asset did not count.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's repeats usually carry some change, a word altered or clauses moved, and this surah has a clear example of that a little earlier. Here there is none. The ayah comes back identical. The only variable is the claim it lands on. That suggests the repeat is aimed at the two different uses, not at the sentence itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Standing that cannot be inherited is a hard teaching in any society built on descent. It applies evenly in both directions. The passage does not say the ancestors were unimportant. It says their record belongs to them. What that leaves a person is a smaller inheritance and a more usable one. It is the only kind still open to addition by the person holding it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical ayah eight earlier, closing a different claim about the same ancestors.
States the positive form of the principle, that honour with God rests on mindfulness rather than on lineage.
Says a person has nothing except what he himself has striven for.

studies.applyIt: Say aloud one thing you are proud of that belongs to someone in your family rather than to you. A profession, a reputation, a story people tell. There is nothing wrong with valuing it. The exercise is only to put it in the right column, since most of us have never separated the two on purpose.
studies.explainEasier: An earlier people came and went. What they earned belongs to them. What you earn belongs to you. You will not have to answer for anything that they did.

studies.title: East And West Both Belong
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted in the future tense. People will say this, and the answer is supplied before anyone has said it. What the reply does is more interesting than what it says. It does not explain the change or give a reason for it. It states that both directions belong to God, which removes the assumption the objection rests on, namely that a direction carries value in itself. What is left is guidance, named in the second half, so a question about the compass is answered by naming who does the directing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It marks the change in the direction faced for prayer, which the classical scholars place in the second year after the migration. The surah returns to the matter at length in the ayat that follow, and the commentaries treat this ayah as the opening of that passage. They note that the objection it expects was entirely predictable. The change was public and daily.

keyTerms.note: A future form. The ayah reports the objection before it has been made, which is why commentators read the passage as an answer prepared in advance rather than a response to something already said.

From a verb meaning to face and to receive. The word names the direction a person turns toward, so it describes an orientation rather than a place, which is exactly the distinction the reply relies on.
From the verb to stand. A straight path in Arabic is one that stands up rather than one that runs without bends, which gives the image a sense of a road that holds its line.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Direction was constantly in mind. Travellers found their way by star and landmark. Herders knew where water lay from any point. Traders held the bearings of distant towns in their heads as ordinary working knowledge. Knowing where you stood in relation to everything else was a daily skill, not an idea. A whole community visibly changing the way it faced each day was impossible to miss.
studies.didYouKnow: The objection in this ayah is put in the future tense, so it is answered before it is raised. Early scholars treat it as one of the clearest cases in the Quran of a reply prepared ahead of a question. The surah then returns to the subject over the following ayat. That suggests the early answer was not the end of the matter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer refuses the premise rather than defending the decision. If every direction belongs to God, no direction is better in itself. A change of bearing cannot then be a change of object. That leaves the matter as one of instruction, not of geography. The second half of the reply says so by naming guidance. The surah makes the same point elsewhere about turning faces east or west.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing earlier in this surah, that wherever you turn there is the face of God.
Continues immediately, explaining what the change was for and naming a community placed in the middle.
Says later in this surah that righteousness is not a matter of which direction you turn your faces.

studies.applyIt: Notice one practice you keep whose form matters to you more than you can justify. A seat you always take, an order you always follow. There is nothing wrong with it. Just check whether you would be unsettled by a change, and whether the unsettling is about the practice or about the form.
studies.explainEasier: People will ask why the believers changed the way they face when they pray. The answer is that east and west both belong to God. He guides anyone He wants onto a straight road.

studies.title: A Community Placed In The Middle
studies.meaning: A community is described as balanced, placed in the middle. The purpose given is testimony: they are to be witnesses before humanity, with the Messenger a witness over them. The passage then explains the earlier prayer direction as a sorting device. It marked off those who follow from those who turn back. It grants that the change was hard. It closes by promising that the prayers already offered facing the old direction were not wasted.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This ayah marks the moment the prayer direction moved from Jerusalem to Mecca. Classical reports place it about sixteen or seventeen months after the migration. The change was publicly awkward. Opponents mocked it, some believers were unsettled, and people asked about those who had died praying the other way. The last clause of this ayah answers that question directly, which early scholars treat as its occasion.

keyTerms.note: Used for the best part of a flock, and for the centre of a valley where the pasture is richest. The word carries excellence and centrality together, not compromise between two positions.
The legal term for someone who testifies to what they saw. A witness is only useful if credible, so the role described carries an implied standard of conduct rather than a privilege.
From a root meaning to face or come toward. It names an orientation rather than a destination, which is why the passage can call the change a test of who was facing the Messenger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The reports say Medina's mosque had to be rebuilt around the change. The people turned where they stood, in the middle of a prayer. Word reached outlying villages by messenger over days. So some prayed one way while their neighbours prayed another. In that town, faith was read off what people did in public. The way a person faced was plain to everyone in the row.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayat around this one form the centre of the surah by count. The word used here for a middle community sits almost exactly at the midpoint of the longest chapter in the Quran. The classical scholars noticed the placement. The mosque in Medina where the change happened is still known by a name recording that two directions were prayed in it on the same day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being appointed witnesses makes the community's role outward-facing. It exists to be seen and testified about, not to keep to itself. The passage also treats a change in practice as a fair test, which grants that obeying is easier when nothing moves. Most striking is the closing reassurance. Worship offered in good faith under an earlier instruction still counts. God is shown as not wasting sincerity that has been overtaken.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction itself, turning the face toward the Sacred Mosque wherever you are.
Repeats the role of witnesses before humanity and ties it to the way of Abraham.
Describes the same community as brought forth for people, and states what makes it so.

studies.applyIt: Think of one change you resisted because of how it would look, not because it was wrong. A new way of working, an apology, a shift in a routine you had defended out loud. Ask honestly which of the two reasons was doing the work. The test described here is not whether change is comfortable. It is whether you follow when it is not.
studies.explainEasier: God calls this a community in the middle, so they can be witnesses for everyone. He changed the direction they pray toward to see who would still follow. The prayers they said before were not wasted.

studies.title: A Face Turned To The Sky
studies.meaning: What is answered here was never asked. The ayah reports a posture: a face turning again and again to the sky. It answers that as though it were a request. The direction granted is described by what will please the one receiving it. Then comes the instruction. The word used means toward the direction of, not toward the building. That is what makes the next clause possible. Wherever you are, turn toward it. The closing lines note that those with earlier scripture know what this is.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It marks the change in the direction faced for prayer, which the classical scholars place in the second year after the migration. The reports on the occasion are widely given and broadly agree. A hope was held without being spoken, and the instruction arrived while the community was gathered. The surah already expected the objection this would cause, two ayat earlier, before describing the change itself.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives the ordinary Arabic word for the heart, which is named from the fact that it turns over. The ayah describes a face doing what the word for the heart already means.
A part or a side of something, so the word names a bearing rather than a destination. That is what allows the instruction to be extended to people standing anywhere on earth.

keyTerms.gloss: you will be pleased with it
keyTerms.note: From the root for settled contentment. The same verb appeared a few ayat earlier for the approval others were offering conditionally, and here the pleasing is granted rather than negotiated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Looking up was how a person waited. Rain was watched for from the horizon upward, the thin new moon that began a month was hunted for at dusk by whoever had the best eyes, and travellers read the hour from which stars had risen. A face repeatedly turned to the sky was a legible posture in that world. It meant somebody expecting something to arrive from above.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for the turning of the face here comes from the same root as the ordinary word for the heart, which Arabic names from its turning over. So the ayah's opening image and the organ of longing share three letters. The link is complete in the original and entirely absent from any translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An unspoken hope is answered, and the answer is framed by what will please the one who held it. That is a striking thing for a scripture to record about an instruction. It makes the granting responsive rather than merely commanding. The second clause then takes away any local advantage from the change. A bearing can be taken from any point on earth. The direction becomes something a person carries rather than somewhere they must be.

crossReferences.why: Explains what the change was for, describing a community placed in the middle as witnesses.
Names the House as the first appointed for people, blessed and a guidance for all the worlds.
Repeats the instruction immediately afterwards, extending it to wherever anyone sets out from.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you have been hoping for without ever putting it into words, and put it into words today, once, to yourself. Not as a request necessarily. Just as a sentence. This ayah answers a longing that was carried in a posture rather than spoken, but saying it plainly is worth doing anyway.
studies.explainEasier: God saw His messenger looking up at the sky again and again. So He gave him a direction he would be happy with. Turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, wherever in the world you are.

studies.title: Every Proof Would Not Suffice
studies.meaning: Three refusals in a row, and the third is the one usually passed over. They would not follow your direction. You are not to follow theirs. And they do not follow one another's either. That last clause says the conformity being pressed for could never have been reached by any single choice. The parties pressing for it did not agree among themselves. The ayah then closes with a condition addressed to the Prophet, put in terms severe enough to show the weight of the matter.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, straight after the change of direction, in a city where several communities each faced a different way. The classical scholars note that conditions of this form addressed to a prophet state how serious a thing is. They are not expectations about him. The Quran uses the same construction elsewhere in the same way.

keyTerms.note: A word of totality attached to an indefinite noun, which makes the supposition complete. Not many signs but every one there could be, which is what turns the sentence into a statement about persuasion itself.
A partitive word meaning a portion of a whole. Repeating it in one clause, portion following portion, is what makes the sentence describe division inside a group rather than between groups.
Definite in the Arabic: not knowledge in general but the particular knowledge that has arrived. The definite article turns it into a specific possession that could be set aside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held several communities, each with its own bearing and its own account of why it was right. Taking up any one of them would have meant turning down the others. Everyone living there could have worked that out. The ayah simply says it aloud. That was a useful thing to hear in a city where the push to fall in line came from more than one side at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The middle clause is easy to read past. It notes that the communities in question did not follow one another's direction either. So no single choice could have met the demand being made. The pressure could not be answered at all. The ayah records that in a handful of words without drawing attention to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two questions that pressure usually merges. One is whether more evidence would persuade. The other is whether the evidence is sound. It answers the first with a flat no and leaves the second alone. That keeps truth from depending on how it is received. It also changes how anyone in such a position should read a failure to convince. The ayah has just said that such failure tells you nothing about the case.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing at greater length, that even angels descending would not settle it for them.
Says every sign would not bring them to belief until they see the painful punishment itself.
Uses the identical phrase about following inclinations after knowledge has come, a few ayat earlier.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have been trying to convince, and ask honestly whether any evidence would change their position. If none would, stop assembling it. That is not a defeat and it is not a judgement about them. It just means the conversation you have been having is not the one that was needed.
studies.explainEasier: Even every proof in the world would not make these people face the way you face. You are not to face their way either. They do not even agree with each other. Going along with them would be wrong.

studies.title: As They Know Their Own Sons
studies.meaning: The comparison is the strongest image of unmistakable recognition there is, and it is chosen on purpose. Knowing your own child is instant and leaves no room for doubt. Then hiding is named in the same breath. The two do not clash. To hide a thing, a person has to have recognised it first. Early scholars differ on what exactly is recognised. It may be the messenger, the revelation, or the direction just described, and they record each reading. The second ayah then turns away from the hiders and speaks to the one receiving.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the passage on the change of direction. The wording again limits the concealing to a group rather than to everyone, which is how the surah has handled such statements throughout. The classical scholars note that the second of these two ayat appears again word for word in another surah, in a different setting. That is why it reads as a general principle rather than a comment on this dispute.

keyTerms.gloss: they recognise him, they know it
keyTerms.note: Recognition of something already encountered, distinct from learning it new. The pronoun is open, and commentators divide over whether it refers to the messenger, the revelation, or the direction.
The comparison chosen for certainty rather than for affection. In a society without written records, knowing a face was the most reliable form of identification anyone possessed.

From a root also used for drawing milk from an animal. Lexicographers connect the two: to wrangle is to keep pulling at something, so this doubt is a repeated drawing rather than a single uncertainty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households were large, and children were raised among cousins in a shared compound. A man might have many small faces around him. Picking out his own took no effort at all. There were no records of any kind, so identity ran entirely through faces and remembered line. That made this recognition the most dependable one anybody had, and so the natural comparison to reach for.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for the doubters at the end of this passage shares a root with the verb for drawing milk from an animal. The early Arabic dictionary writers link them through the idea of pulling at something over and over. So doubt in this word is a hand that keeps returning, not a single moment of uncertainty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The remedy offered for other people's concealing is not exposure and not argument. It is settling your own position, stated in four words with nothing attached to justify it. That puts the burden where it can actually be carried. The passage also treats recognising and hiding as things that go together, not things that clash. So doubt in others tells you nothing about whether they have seen the thing clearly.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same comparison, those given the Book recognising it as they recognise their own children.
Repeats the second of these ayat word for word, in a completely different setting.
Addresses doubt directly, and names the truth as having come from the Lord of the one addressed.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you have been treating as an open question when it is in fact something you have already recognised and would rather not settle. Leaving a matter open is often a way of postponing what follows from it. Name the thing today, without deciding what to do about it yet.
studies.explainEasier: People who were given the Book know this message as surely as they know their own children. Some of them hide it anyway. The truth comes from your Lord, so do not let yourself doubt it.

studies.title: Race Toward The Good
studies.meaning: The difference in directions is granted rather than settled. Every community has one it turns toward. The Arabic can be read as the direction it faces or as the direction it is turned toward, and early scholars record both. Then comes the instruction. The verb is the plain word for running a race. Attention moves away from bearing, where the parties differ and cannot be brought together, to a contest measured in something else. The closing clause explains why that works.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the passage on the change of direction and turns the subject outward. The classical scholars read the ayah as a general principle, not as a comment on any one community. They note that a closely matching statement appears in another surah. There, difference between communities is described as intended, and the same instruction to compete in good works follows from it.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a face. It names the way a person or a community is turned, so the noun describes an orientation rather than a place, which is what allows the ayah to set the question aside.
The ordinary verb for racing. It appears elsewhere in the Quran in its plainly literal sense, of brothers going off to hold a race, so the register here is sporting rather than general.
A definite plural, so what is raced toward is a known field of good actions rather than goodness in the abstract. The plural also means there are many places to gain ground.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Racing was the great public sport of Arabia. Horses and camels ran at the seasonal fairs and after a victory. Single animals were famous and were remembered in verse. The result was argued over for years. An instruction to race landed in a world everyone knew from the inside. A field of runners. A start nobody picks. Ground gained by effort, and a finish decided by someone other than the runners.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as race is used elsewhere in the Quran in a plain, everyday sense. Joseph's brothers use it when they explain that they went off to hold a race. So the word carries no special religious ring. The instruction uses the words of an actual sporting contest.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Granting a difference and then turning the energy elsewhere is a distinct move. The closing clause is what makes it hold together. Everyone is brought to one place, whichever way they faced. So the direction is the part of the question that will not survive the journey. The competition is the part that will. What the ayah leaves people to do in the meantime is not to settle the argument.

crossReferences.why: Says difference between communities was intended, and directs them to compete in good works instead.
Uses the same racing verb, directed toward forgiveness from the Lord and a garden as wide as the heavens.
Repeats the instruction to race, and describes what is being raced toward in the same terms.

studies.applyIt: Pick one good thing you could do more of and treat it as a race for a week, against your own last week rather than against anyone else. Count it. The word in this ayah is the plain word for a contest, and counting is what turns effort into one.
studies.explainEasier: Every group has a direction it turns to face. So race each other to do good instead of arguing. Wherever you are, God will bring you all together in the end. He can do anything.

studies.title: Not Heedless Of What You Do
studies.meaning: The command to face the Sacred Mosque comes three times within a few ayat. Each time it carries a different addition. Here two clauses follow it. The direction is the truth from your Lord. And God is not inattentive to what you do. The first settles the question of who says so. The second moves the subject from geography to being seen. Turning becomes something watched rather than a rule merely obeyed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It falls in the months after the direction of prayer moved from Jerusalem to Mecca. The change was public and contested. The ayat around it record the objections it drew. The early scholars read the repeats as answering different audiences in turn. First the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself. Then the community, at home or travelling. Then those outside it, looking for an inconsistency to press.

keyTerms.note: The word means a part or side of something, and so a general bearing rather than an exact line. It asks for orientation towards the House, which is what a traveller without instruments can actually manage.
Describes someone whose attention has lapsed, not someone ignorant. Denying it of God rules out the gap between an order given and an order noticed, which is where most human authority quietly fails.
