studies.explainEasier: God says this rule about killing saves lives. A fair answer stops a feud from growing. The passage then asks people to leave a fair will for their parents and close family before they die.

studies.title: Whoever Changes What He Heard
studies.meaning: Two situations are handled in turn. Someone who alters a testament after hearing it carries the guilt himself, and the person who made it is left clear. Then a second case: someone who suspects the testament itself was slanted or wrong, and who reconciles the parties instead. The first is charged, the second cleared, and the difference between altering and mending is where the whole passage rests.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following straight on from the instruction about making a will. Such arrangements were spoken, not written, so the witnesses were the record. A witness who changed his account could quietly send an estate elsewhere. The second ayah handles the opposite worry, that a dying person might favour one heir unfairly. The early scholars read the two together as covering both places where the thing can fail.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for putting one thing in place of another. It is the same word used elsewhere for altering scripture, so the offence is framed as tampering with a record rather than as simple theft.

A rare word describing a tilt away from straightness, used of a person who inclines without meaning harm. It is paired here with a stronger word for deliberate wrong, so the ayah covers both the mistake and the intention.
Placed at the end of an ayah about words spoken and then altered, the name is doing specific work. The original wording is described as heard by someone whose record cannot be edited afterwards.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Almost everything in Medina rested on witnesses. Sales, marriages, debts and bequests were spoken in front of people who would be asked to recall them years later. A name as a reliable witness was a kind of wealth. Memory was trained for this. A man known to have shaded his account once was finished. The word for altering carries all that weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used in the second ayah for a leaning that was not meant occurs only here in the Quran. A related form appears just once more, in a different surah. It is paired with a common word for deliberate sin. That lets the sentence cover an honest tilt and a dishonest one in the same clause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guilt is attached to the act, not to the outcome. A person who set something up correctly is not held to account for what others did to it later. That is a precise idea, and it protects the dead as well as the honest. The second ayah then makes room for stepping in. Someone who moves to repair a bad arrangement is cleared. That places mending things between people above carrying out a document to the letter.

crossReferences.why: The instruction being protected here, about making a testament for parents and near relatives.
Asks those settling an estate to imagine their own children left behind, and to speak rightly.
Makes reconciling two parties a concern of the wider community, using the same verb for mending.

studies.applyIt: If you are holding a message that belongs to someone else, something you were told to pass on or a decision you were asked to relay, pass it on this week in the words it was given to you. Not improved, not softened. The distance between what was said and what arrives is where this passage puts the whole problem.
studies.explainEasier: If someone changes a will after hearing it, the blame falls on the one who changed it. The person who made the will is clear. But if a will was unfair and someone steps in to put it right, that is fine.

studies.title: A Practice Older Than This Community
studies.meaning: Fasting is introduced to the believers as something prescribed. The sentence at once places it in a longer history: as it was for those before you. The purpose given is not endurance, or discipline for its own sake. It is becoming aware of God, and the grammar leaves that as a hope, not a guarantee. Early scholars note that the practice is presented as handed down rather than invented. That softens what would otherwise be a heavy new demand.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. The classical accounts place this in the second year after the migration, when the yearly fast was set for the community. The ayat right after it name the month, allow for illness and travel, and say that ease rather than hardship is meant. Early scholars read the sequence as deliberate. The practice is given, then its history, then its purpose, then its exemptions.

keyTerms.note: The root means to hold back, or to come to a standstill. Arabic uses it of a horse that stops and of wind that drops. Fasting is described as stillness, not as going without.
The passive of the verb to write, used across the Quran for what has been decided. The image is of something entered in a register. That is why the same verb covers both instruction and destiny.
From a root meaning to shield or guard against. It describes a watchful care before God rather than fear of Him. Here it is named as the whole point of the exercise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia already knew fasting. Meccans kept a fast on one day of the year. Jewish neighbours in Medina fasted on fixed days. Christian monks along the trade routes were famous for going without. The audience did not need the practice explained, only regulated. Even so, a month of daytime fasting was a clear step up, in a place where the summer heat was severe and water was carried by hand.
studies.didYouKnow: The month is named only once in the whole Quran, two ayat after this one. That single mention is also the only place the Quran names any month at all. The classical scholars noted how singular that is. The reason given there is not the fast itself but the revelation. The month is identified as the one in which the Quran was sent down.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the practice alongside earlier communities makes it a shared human discipline. It is not a badge of difference. That fits the surah's wider argument about one line of revelation. Naming awareness of God as the purpose puts the act itself under an inward result. So the fast is a means. It can be done without reaching anything. The closing hope is put as a chance, not a promise. That keeps the outcome out of the faster's hands.

crossReferences.why: Names the month, gives the reason, and states that God intends ease rather than hardship.
Follows the fasting ayat with the promise of nearness, which early scholars read as connected.
Shows an earlier fast, Mary instructed to vow abstention from speech.

studies.applyIt: Whether or not you are fasting, try skipping one thing tomorrow that you take without thinking, and pay attention to the first twenty minutes after you notice its absence. That gap is where the mindfulness in this line is supposed to appear. You are not testing your willpower. You are finding out how much of your day runs on habits you never chose.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers to fast. He points out that people before them fasted too. The point is not to go hungry. It is to help you think about God and stay careful about how you live.

studies.title: A Counted Number Of Days
studies.meaning: The first phrase limits the whole thing: a counted number of days, not a season. Then two cases are named where the days are moved rather than dropped. A third case has a different provision. The early scholars differ over that third clause. Some read it as an early stage that was later settled. Others read it as covering people who can only fast with real difficulty. The ayah ends by preferring the fast without ordering it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the second year after the migration, when fasting was set for the community. The early scholars record a real difference over this ayah. Some hold that it described a first arrangement, in which a person could choose between fasting and feeding someone in need. The ayah that follows then settled it. Others hold that it always applied to those for whom fasting is a real hardship.

keyTerms.note: A plural form used in Arabic for small numbers, so the word carries a hint of fewness alongside counting. Naming the days as countable is itself a kindness, since a limit is easier to carry than an open one.
The word is used of what redeems a captive, so it names a payment that stands in place of something rather than a penalty for failing. That framing matters: nothing is being fined.

A reflexive form suggesting obedience offered freely, from a root meaning to comply. The same verb appeared earlier in this surah about the two hills, both times marking what someone does beyond what was asked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia was slow and physically hard. A journey to Syria took weeks, and a traveller rationed water against the next well rather than against thirst. Illness, without medicine to speak of, meant weeks of weakness. The two exemptions in this ayah name the two states in which the body has no reserve, and everyone listening had been in at least one of them.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a number of other days appears twice within two ayat: here and in the ayah that follows. The wording is the same both times, and it appears nowhere else in the Quran. Repeating a whole clause at that distance is unusual. The commentaries treat it as a marker that the two ayat are one statement rather than two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure keeps returning to the same principle. Something is asked, and in the same sentence the cases where it cannot be done are named, with an alternative attached. Nobody is left to work out their own exemption or to feel they have failed. The closing preference, stated as better for you rather than as a command, also leaves the reader's judgement engaged rather than replaced.

crossReferences.why: Continues directly, naming the month and stating the principle of ease behind these concessions.
States the general rule these concessions rest on: no soul is charged beyond its capacity.
Uses the same verb for volunteering good, and closes with God described as appreciative.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk to yourself about a day when you could not do what you planned. This ayah names two situations and provides for both without a word of reproach. Try borrowing that tone once this week when something goes uncompleted. Move it rather than adding it to a list of failures.
studies.explainEasier: The fast is only for a set number of days. If you are ill or travelling, the same number of days is made up later. Someone who finds fasting very hard can feed a person in need instead.

studies.title: The Month The Quran Came Down
studies.meaning: The month is named by what happened in it, not by its place in the calendar. Three words describe the revelation: guidance, clear proofs, and a criterion that separates one thing from another. Then the practical clauses repeat. A purpose is stated in several parts, ending in thanks. The famous sentence in the middle states a rule wider than fasting: ease is intended, hardship is not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the second year after the migration. Ramadan already existed as a month in the Arabian calendar. The early Arabic dictionary writers link its name to fierce heat. The classical commentaries tie the descent of the Quran mentioned here to the start of revelation in that month. They record different accounts of what exactly the descent refers to.

keyTerms.note: The only month named anywhere in the Quran. Lexicographers connect the name to scorching heat, from the season in which the pre-Islamic calendar first fixed it, before the lunar year began moving it through the year.
From a root meaning to split or distinguish. It names the revelation by its effect, something that divides truth from falsehood, and it becomes the title of a whole surah later in the Quran.

From a root associated with the left hand and with what comes without strain. Its opposite in the same sentence is built on a root for what is hard to handle, so the pair sets facility against friction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian calendar was lunar and watched by eye. Someone had to see the new crescent and report it. So a month began on a person's word, not on a sum, and cloud could push the start by a day. Fixing a month by sighting made shared time depend on people looking up together at the same hour. They did it from different parts of the same town.
studies.didYouKnow: Ramadan is the only month named in the whole Quran. The sentence about ease and hardship in this ayah is quoted far outside its subject. People use it in settings that have nothing to do with fasting. The classical commentaries already treated it as a general statement rather than one tied to the month.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The month is tied to a book, not to an event in nature or a founding battle. That is unusual among religious calendars. What is being marked is a text arriving. The purpose clauses at the end fall into an order: completing the count, then praising God as great, then giving thanks. So the practice is shown as leading somewhere rather than as an end in itself.

crossReferences.why: Names the night of the descent and describes what happens in it, without naming the month.
Calls it a blessed night in which every wise matter is distinguished, using the same root as criterion.
Repeats the principle of ease directly, saying no hardship has been placed on you in religion.

studies.applyIt: Take the sentence about ease and hardship out of its month for a moment and hold it against something you are making harder than it needs to be: a task you keep restarting, a standard you set for yourself alone. Ask what the easy version would look like. That question is not a concession; it is in the ayah.
studies.explainEasier: Ramadan is the month when the Quran first came down. It gives people guidance and shows them right from wrong. Anyone who is ill or on a journey fasts the same number of days later. God wants things easy for you, not hard.

studies.title: The Answer With No Go-Between
studies.meaning: A question is reported about God, and the reply is unusual in two ways. It drops the usual instruction to the Prophet to say something, and answers in the first person directly. And it does not describe God's location but His nearness, then His response, before asking anything of the questioner. Only after the assurance does the sentence turn to what people should do: answer Him, and trust Him. The order places the promise before the condition.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits among the ayat on fasting, right after the month is named and before the instructions resume. Several classical reports describe a question put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). People asked whether God was near enough to be spoken to quietly, or far enough to need calling out. The reports differ in detail, and early scholars record them without settling which is primary.

keyTerms.note: Used of physical closeness and of kinship, since the related word means a relative. Nearness here is stated flatly, with no qualification. Early scholars contrast it with the distance the questioners assumed.
The noun for one act of calling out, not a general practice. Its use makes the promise specific: an individual call answered, rather than an assurance that God listens in general.
The same verb used a clause earlier for God answering, now turned back on the caller. The repetition makes the relationship two-directional in a single sentence, with the same word on both sides.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to power in that world ran through go-betweens. Approaching a chief meant a relative to introduce you, a client relationship, or a gift. The sanctuary before Islam was full of objects thought to carry a request closer to a god. Asking was a chain of favours. A statement that the call goes straight, and the answer comes straight, removed every link in that chain at once.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the very few ayat where God answers a question about Himself without the usual instruction to the Prophet to say it. Elsewhere in this surah, questions are introduced with that formula again and again. Early scholars point out that the grammar drops it here, exactly where the subject is nearness. The shape of the sentence does what it says.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes asking direct, with nothing in between. That has consequences for how worship is understood: nothing is needed between a person and God at the moment of asking. It also ties God's answer to the caller's response, without making the second the price of the first. The promise is stated first, and without condition. And its place among the fasting ayat suggests hunger is meant to produce asking, not only restraint.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the invitation, call on Me and I will respond, and warns against disdaining it.
States the same nearness physically: closer to a person than their jugular vein.
Asks who answers the desperate when they call, and leaves the question standing.

studies.applyIt: Ask God for one specific thing today, out loud and in your own language, rather than in a borrowed phrase. Name it plainly: the actual worry, with its details. Many people find this harder than reciting, which is itself worth noticing. The promise in this line is attached to calling, and calling means saying what you actually want.
studies.explainEasier: Someone asked where God is. God answered Himself: I am close. When you call Me, I hear you and answer. You do not need anyone else to pass the message on.

studies.title: Until The Threads Can Be Told Apart
studies.meaning: A restriction the community had been keeping is lifted, and the reason given is that they had been straining against it in private. The passage does not scold. It names what happened, says the turning has already been accepted, and moves on. In the middle sits an image of husband and wife as garments for one another. The day's limits are then drawn by what the eye can see.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the second year after the migration. The classical sources broadly agree on what happened. In the first period of fasting the night was more restricted than it later became. Some people found that restriction beyond them. The ayah is reported as the answer. Its opening is unusual, because it admits the difficulty before removing it.

keyTerms.note: The everyday word for what is worn. Applied to two people about each other, it carries covering, warmth, closeness to the skin and the ordinariness of something put on daily without thought.
A reflexive form of the verb for betraying a trust, with the object being the people themselves. It describes a private inconsistency rather than a wrong done to anyone else.
An ordinary word for a thread of cotton. The image asks a person to look east and wait until two strands of colour can be told apart, which is a test anyone can perform without an instrument.

The word for the edge of a piece of land or the blade of a sword, so a line that is sharp rather than vague. The instruction that follows is about not approaching the line, not merely about not crossing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Medina owned a clock. The day was read off the sky: first light in the east, the sun's height at noon, the length of a shadow, the last colour going out of the west. Farmers and travellers knew these signs the way a modern person knows the time without looking. Defining dawn by two threads of colour used a measure everybody already carried.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest ayat in the surah. It moves through four different subjects without a break. The image of two people as garments for each other occurs only here in the Quran. The phrase about the limits of God appears several times across the text. But the instruction not to come near them, rather than not to cross them, belongs to this place alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things happen at once that religious talk often keeps apart. A hardship is admitted, and the admission is not turned into a charge. The answer is a turning and a pardon before anything else. Then the plain closeness of a marriage is given a warm image, inside a passage about holding back. That refuses to treat the body as something merely put up with. The ayah ends by explaining rather than ordering.

crossReferences.why: Describes marriage as tranquillity, affection and mercy placed between two people as a sign.
Uses the same phrase about the limits of God, there with a different instruction attached.
States the principle of ease that this concession puts into practice, a few ayat earlier.

studies.applyIt: Notice the moment today when the light changes and you can first tell colours apart, or the moment it goes. Stand still for it. This ayah measures a whole practice by something you can see with your own eyes, and most of us have stopped looking at the sky for anything except weather.
studies.explainEasier: At night in Ramadan, husbands and wives may be together and may eat and drink. God calls them clothing for each other. The fast starts when you can first tell a white thread from a black one at dawn.

studies.title: Lowered To The Officials
studies.meaning: Two moves are described in one sentence, and the second gives the ayah its bite. Eating up property wrongly is named first. Then comes a specific method: handing some of it to those who decide cases. A larger share can then be taken with a ruling behind it. The last three words close every excuse. The whole thing is described as done knowingly, not by mistake.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the practical instructions that follow the passage on fasting. Medina had judges and arbitrators. Disputes over palm groves, wells and debts were settled by men whose decisions carried weight. Gifts to such men were an ordinary part of the culture. That is what makes the ayah sharp. It names something that looked respectable and calls it eating what belongs to others.

keyTerms.note: The verb describes lowering a bucket into a well. Used of a bribe, it pictures something let down quietly out of sight, which is a precise image for a payment nobody is meant to see.
Names what is void and comes to nothing, the opposite of the word for truth and rightful claim. Property taken this way is described as having no foundation, whatever paperwork supports it.
The plain verb for eating, used across the Quran for taking wealth. It makes the wrong bodily rather than abstract, and the same verb appears twice inside this one sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Medina were settled face to face, before a judge both sides accepted. He was often a man known for good sense rather than someone given the post. His view decided who kept a well or a stand of palms. There were no written records to appeal to and no higher court. So a judgement was final, and whoever swayed it took everything. Hospitality and gifts blurred easily into something else.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for eating up wealth appears at both ends of this sentence. It frames the payment in the middle. The Quran uses eating as its standard image for taking property. The same picture came a few pages earlier in this surah, of those who swallow fire into their bellies.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A legal outcome is denied the power to make a wrong right. The property is called void before the ruling is even mentioned, so the judgement changes nothing about what the thing actually is. That is a claim about the limits of procedure, and it holds even where the process was followed correctly. The final clause locates the offence in knowledge: the person knew, and the knowing is part of the charge.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the warning against consuming wealth wrongly and sets trade by mutual consent against it.
Uses the same image of consuming, there for what is gained by keeping revelation quiet.
Addresses those who judge between people directly, asking that they judge with justice.

studies.applyIt: Look for the smallest place where you use an advantage that is not really yours: a connection who moves you up a queue, a form filled in loosely, a claim you know will not be checked. Pick one and do it the slow way this week. The ayah's last clause is about knowing, and you already do.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people not to take what belongs to others by cheating. He also tells them not to pay judges to hand them a ruling so they can take even more. They know what they are doing.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Approach The Houses By Their Doors
studies.meaning: A question about the moon gets a practical answer rather than one about the stars. The phases are a calendar people can read. Then the ayah turns without warning to a custom of entering houses from behind. It says that goodness is not found there. The early scholars explain the custom as something pilgrims did while set apart for the pilgrimage. The instruction that follows is short and literal: use the door.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the passages that answer questions the community had put. The classical sources describe a practice tied to the state of pilgrimage. A man who had entered it would avoid the doorway of his own house and climb in from behind. He treated the door as something to keep away from. The ayah is reported as an answer to that. It refuses to count the practice as piety.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word for a new crescent, which shares a root with the shout that greeted its appearance. Naming the phases in the plural fits the answer, since it is the sequence rather than any one night that makes a calendar.
From a root for fixing a time or a place, and a related word later names the boundary points where pilgrims enter consecration. It covers scheduled moments rather than stretches of duration.
A broad word for upright conduct, connected to the word for dutiful kindness towards parents. The ayah defines it by removing a candidate first, then by naming awareness of God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabia was timed by the moon: markets, pilgrimages, the truce months when fighting stopped, the due date on a debt. A merchant who lent money counted repayment in moons. A family knew when to expect a caravan by the same count. The crescent was public news. Everybody saw it at once, and nobody needed an expert to read it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a run of ayat in the surah that begin with the words they ask you. The phrase comes up several times in this section, on different subjects. The answer here stands out for not addressing what was asked. The question is about the moon's phases. The reply is about what they are for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of misplacing are corrected in one ayah. The first answers a question about the natural world by giving its use, not how it works. That sets a tone about what revelation is for. The second refuses to let a detour on foot count as devotion. Together they push the same way. Religion is being pulled apart from the decorative and the merely odd.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same construction, denying that righteousness is a direction before defining what it is.
Describes the moon's phases as determined so that people may know the number of years.
Presents night and day as two signs made for reckoning time and seeking provision.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing you do the complicated way for no reason you can name: a route, a routine, a formality. This ayah answers a question about the sky and then, in the same breath, tells people to use the door. Take the direct route once this week and notice whether anything was actually lost.
studies.explainEasier: People asked about the changing shapes of the moon. God says they are there to mark time for people and for the pilgrimage. He also tells them to go into their houses through the front door.

studies.title: The Limit Given With The Permission
studies.meaning: Permission to fight is given with a limit attached in the same sentence. The limit is stated twice: only against those who fight you, and no going beyond. The classical scholars read the second clause widely, covering excess of every kind. They list what it was understood to rule out, including people who were not fighting. The ayah closes with a statement about what God does not love.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the time when the community was allowed to defend itself. They had been driven out of Mecca, and for years before that fighting had not been allowed. The early scholars treat this as among the first ayat on the subject. They note that the limits arrive with the permission, not after it. Reports about the exact occasion differ, and the classical works record more than one.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form describing two sides engaged with each other, rather than a verb for killing. The grammar assumes an opponent already fighting, which is why the following clause names them as those who fight you.
From a root meaning to cross over a boundary. The word covers going beyond in any direction, which is why the commentators read it as reaching well past the battlefield itself.

The clause states a divine disposition rather than a penalty, and the Quran uses this construction repeatedly to mark the outer edge of what is allowed. It closes the sentence without a threat attached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: War in Arabia had few restraints. A raid could take everything a settlement owned, cut down its date palms, and carry off its women and children. The answering raid was expected to be larger. Fighting ran by season and stopped in the truce months. Within those limits the scale was whatever a tribe could manage. A limit stated inside a permission would have sounded strange.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God not loving those who exceed appears several times in the Quran. It always takes the same shape, attached to an instruction just given. Here it closes the first ayah of the surah's passage on fighting. So a limit is the last thing said before anything else is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure matters as much as the content. Every clause that widens is followed by one that narrows. The passage never lets a permission stand alone. That builds restraint into the same sentence, rather than leaving it to conscience later. The closing statement roots the limit in what God is like, not in results. That puts it beyond any sum about what an enemy deserves.

crossReferences.why: States the permission to fight in terms of having been wronged and unjustly driven from homes.
Insists that hatred of a people must not push anyone away from acting justly.
Directs that an inclination towards peace be met with the same inclination, and with trust in God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a conflict you are in, however small, and ask where your limit is. Not whether you are right, since most people can answer that quickly. Ask what would count as going too far, named in advance, before you are angry. This ayah puts the limit in the same sentence as the permission, which is the only moment it is easy to set.
studies.explainEasier: God allows people to fight back against those who fight them. But he sets a clear limit in the same breath. Do not go too far. God does not love people who go past the line.

studies.title: But If They Cease
studies.meaning: Hard instructions are given for a specific conflict, and each is paired with a condition. Expulsion is answered by expulsion, from where the expulsion happened. Fighting near the sanctuary is excluded unless it is begun there. Then the passage ends, twice in three lines, with a way out: if they stop, it stops. The final clause names God as forgiving rather than as victorious.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The passage allowed the community to fight after it had been driven out of Mecca. The early scholars tie the instructions to that one conflict. They name a particular opponent, a particular expulsion, and a sanctuary where fighting had been set aside for generations. The clause about persecution being worse than killing is read as pointing to the pressure that forced them to leave.

keyTerms.note: The root describes testing gold in fire, and the word covers persecution, civil strife and temptation together. Commentators here take it as the pressure applied to make people abandon their faith.
A verb for coming upon someone and getting the better of them, associated with skill and quickness. It describes an encounter in the course of a conflict rather than a search carried out at leisure.
From a root meaning to reach an end, and related to the word for being told to stop. The verb appears at the close of both ayat, and each time it ends the instruction that preceded it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: At the sanctuary in Mecca, weapons had been set aside for as long as anyone could remember. Tribes at war met there and nothing happened. The whole pilgrim trade rested on that promise. A man could see his brother's killer inside the sanctuary and do nothing. That restraint was one of the few things all of Arabia agreed on. It is why the exception here is stated so carefully.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah of this pair is six words long in Arabic. It holds nothing but a condition and two names of God. It is among the shortest ayat in the surah, and it comes straight after one of the harshest. The classical commentaries note that placing as deliberate, not an accident of where the ayat divide.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Even at its hardest, the passage keeps an exit open and states it twice. Cessation ends the matter, and the sentence that describes the ending names God by mercy rather than by power. That places the purpose of the fighting in stopping something rather than in defeating someone. The classical readings hold to that distinction, and it is what keeps the passage tied to its occasion.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same condition: if they desist, what has already passed is forgiven them.
Says nothing prevents kindness and fairness towards those who did not fight you or drive you out.
The ayah immediately before, which sets the limit these instructions operate inside.

studies.applyIt: Notice how hard it is to let something end when you have been wronged and the other person stops. This passage says it twice in three lines, as if it expected the difficulty. Think of one grievance that is technically over and check whether you have actually put it down, or only stopped mentioning it.
studies.explainEasier: This part is about the people who drove the believers out of Mecca. It says fighting back is allowed, even near the holy place, if they start it there. But the moment they stop, it all stops. God forgives.

studies.title: A Sentence That Contains Its End
studies.meaning: A purpose is stated for the fighting described in the preceding ayat, and it is a stopping point rather than a conquest: until the persecution ends and worship is free to be given to God. Then the same condition returns. If they stop, hostility stops, and the exception at the end restricts anything continuing to those still committing wrong. The sentence is built to close itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short passage on fighting that began three ayat earlier. The early scholars read the stated aim as lifting the pressure that had made faith impossible to practise in Mecca. They do not read it as turning anyone to Islam. The surah says a few dozen ayat later that there is no compulsion in religion. Reports on the exact occasion of the passage differ.

keyTerms.note: A particle marking a limit in time, and the whole shape of the ayah depends on it. What follows is the point at which the instruction expires, so the sentence carries its own ending inside it.

The word covers religion, obedience and the settling of accounts. Here the commentators read it as devotion offered freely, so the aim is that worship be possible rather than that anyone be made to offer it.
From the same root as the earlier warning against transgression, so the word is used consistently across the passage. Its repetition ties this ayah's ending back to the limit set at the start.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Arabia belonged to the group, not to the person. Anyone who changed sides lost his family's protection and often his living. The pressure came through relatives, not through any official. The early Meccan converts were boycotted and cut off from marriage and trade. Some were held by their own households. That is the state of things the word for persecution names here.
studies.didYouKnow: The condition about stopping appears in this ayah and in the one before it. Each time it is followed by a limit rather than by another instruction. The word for hostility at the end shares a root with the word for going beyond at the start of the passage. So the whole section opens and closes on the same idea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A stated aim turns an open conflict into a bounded one, because an aim can be reached. What is named is a state of the world, not the defeat of a party. So the instruction ends when that state changes, not when someone surrenders. The closing exception narrows the target once more. By the end of the sentence very few are left inside it.

crossReferences.why: States later in this surah that there is no compulsion in religion, which the commentators read alongside this aim.
Gives the same purpose in nearly identical wording, followed by the same condition about desisting.
Names monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques among what this kind of restraint protects.

studies.applyIt: Ask what would count as done in an argument you are still having. Not winning: done. If you cannot describe the state of affairs that would end it, the argument has no exit and will run until you are tired. This ayah gives its instruction an ending in the same sentence, which is worth copying.
studies.explainEasier: The point of the fighting is to stop people being harmed for what they believe, so they can worship God freely. Once the other side stops, the fighting ends too. Nothing goes on against those who have stopped.

studies.title: In The Same Measure As He Did
studies.meaning: The rule of matching is applied to the sacred months, and then to sanctities in general. What was violated may be answered in kind. The standard is stated as a measure. The same verb is used on both sides, so the response is tied to the size of the first act. Two clauses then pull the other way. They ask for awareness of God and say that he is with those who keep it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources link it to the year the community set out for the sanctuary and was turned back. They also link it to the question of a sacred month in which they had been stopped. The early scholars read the ayah as settling that a violated sanctity does not simply pass. At the same time it ties the answer to the same measure. Accounts of the details differ between the works.

keyTerms.note: The plural of what is set apart and protected: months, places and persons alike. Using the plural widens the sentence beyond the month just named, which is why commentators apply it to sanctities generally.

A word for exact likeness, used in the Quran for correspondence rather than approximation. Placed in the middle of the sentence, it turns a permission into a measurement, since anything beyond the like falls outside it.

From a root meaning to shield oneself, so the word describes someone guarding against harm rather than someone frightened. The closing promise attaches divine company to that guarding, not to the retaliation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Four months of the year were sacred across Arabia. During them fighting stopped, markets opened, and pilgrims travelled roads that were otherwise dangerous. The arrangement was old and kept by everyone, because everyone's trade rested on it. Breaking it was a serious matter. A tribe that did so could expect to be named for it in poetry for generations.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for going beyond appears three times in this one ayah. Twice it describes the response, and once the first act. Arabic uses that kind of repetition to bind two things to the same measure. The classical commentaries note that the second use is called going beyond only because it matches the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The measure is the whole point. Permission is given and at once fixed to the size of the injury. So what is being stopped is the growing of the response, not the response itself. Then the ayah changes tone. Two clauses about awareness of God close a sentence about striking back. The promise of God's company is attached to holding back. What is allowed and what is praised are not the same thing here.

crossReferences.why: Permits a matching response and then says patience is better for those who are patient.
Sets an equal answer beside forgiveness and calls endurance a matter of firm resolve.
Applies the same principle of exact correspondence to a killing, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: The next time you answer something unfair, decide the size of the answer before you give it. Say it to yourself: this much and no more. This ayah permits a response and then spends the rest of its length keeping it small, which is harder than either forgiving outright or escalating.
studies.explainEasier: If someone attacks you in a sacred month, you may answer back in the same way and no more. Match what they did, and stop there. God is with the people who are careful about this.

studies.title: Ruin Carried In Your Own Hands
studies.meaning: Two instructions and a warning sit in one short ayah. What the early scholars discuss is how they connect. Spending is asked for. Then hands are named as the means by which people throw themselves into ruin. Several classical readings are recorded. They include holding back wealth when it is needed, and going into danger unprepared. The ayah closes by asking for excellence and naming what God loves.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage that follows the instructions on fighting. There, spending meant equipping and provisioning people at real cost. The early scholars record more than one reading of the middle clause. One early report has a companion apply it to pulling out of the effort, rather than to recklessness. The classical works keep the range of readings rather than settling on one.

keyTerms.note: An unusual form from a root meaning to perish, and the word occurs only here in the Quran. Its rarity is part of why the classical commentaries discuss this clause at such length.
The phrase adds agency to the warning. Ruin is not described as arriving; it is described as something a person carries and drops, which makes the responsibility explicit without naming the act.
From a root for what is beautiful as well as good. The verb asks for quality in the doing rather than merely for the deed, and the noun formed from it closes the ayah as the thing God loves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Equipping a man for a journey or a campaign was expensive. A mount, water skins, food for weeks and a weapon added up to more than many households held. Those who could pay often paid for others as well. Refusing was easy and invisible, since nobody could see what a neighbour had put aside. The instruction to spend was aimed at a decision made privately at home.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for destruction in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. That single use is one reason the classical commentaries set several readings of the clause side by side. The early reports they keep apply it in more than one direction. One of those is holding back, rather than rashness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to treat giving and looking after yourself as opposites. Both appear in the same sentence, and neither is allowed to cancel the other. What holds them together is the final word, excellence. It names a quality of doing rather than an amount given. That leaves the reader with a judgement to make rather than a line to clear.

crossReferences.why: Describes what spending in the cause of God returns, using the image of a grain and seven ears.
Places a warning against killing yourselves directly after an instruction about handling wealth.
Lists spending in ease and hardship among the traits of those God is described as loving.

studies.applyIt: Give something today that you would notice giving. Not the amount that leaves no mark. Then check the other half of this ayah honestly: whether there is any place where being careful has quietly become the reason you never act. The two warnings in this sentence are aimed at the same person.
studies.explainEasier: God asks people to spend on what is good. He warns them not to throw themselves into ruin with their own hands. And he tells them to do things well, because he loves those who do.

studies.title: Whatever Is Feasible Of Offerings
studies.meaning: The longest ayah in this section works through what happens when a pilgrimage cannot be finished as planned. Someone prevented, someone ill, someone with a complaint of the head: each is given another way. The other ways are graded, so a person with no means still has a path. The phrase that keeps coming back is whatever is feasible. The ayah ends with two clauses. One is about awareness, one about what follows.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources link it to the year the community set out for the sanctuary and was turned back before reaching it. The early scholars read the clause about being prevented against that experience. The detail in the ayah reflects a community learning the rites in practice. Questions came up as they went, rather than being settled in advance.

keyTerms.note: A passive form from a root meaning to be confined or hemmed in. The grammar makes the pilgrim the one acted upon, so the clause covers obstruction from outside rather than a change of mind.
Built on the same root as the word for ease used in the passage on fasting. The phrase recurs twice in this ayah, and each time it lets what is asked follow the person's actual capacity.
From a root meaning to guide or to lead, since the animal is led towards the sanctuary. The same root gives the word for guidance, so the offering is named by its journey rather than by its end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reaching Mecca was a serious undertaking. Pilgrims travelled for weeks in convoy, and an animal brought for offering had to be fed and watered the whole way. Illness on the road was common, and sores and lice on the scalp were a routine misery of long travel. Every situation this ayah names was something a caravan would meet in an ordinary year.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the longest ayat in the surah. It names three separate alternatives for people who cannot complete the rites as expected. The phrase about whatever is feasible occurs twice within it. The word used for the offering shares a root with the word for guidance. The classical commentaries note that link often.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is built around exceptions rather than around the rite itself. That says something about how it is meant to be read. Hardship is treated as normal. The other ways are graded downward until they reach someone with nothing at all. The final clause about what follows sits at the end of all that provision. The classical scholars read the two halves together rather than apart.

crossReferences.why: Describes the call to pilgrimage and the rites, including the offerings and the circuits of the House.
States the principle these graded alternatives rest on: ease is intended for you, and hardship is not.
Describes the pilgrimage as owed to God by those who can find a way to make the journey.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have postponed because you cannot do it properly: the visit, the course, the letter. This ayah spends most of its length on partial versions, graded down until nobody is excluded. Do the smallest feasible version of your postponed thing this week, without upgrading it in your head first.
studies.explainEasier: If you set out on the pilgrimage and something stops you, there is another way to finish it. If you are sick, or need to shave your head, you have a choice. You can fast, feed people, or give an offering instead.

studies.title: The Best Provision To Pack
studies.meaning: The months are named. Then three things are set aside for that stretch of time: coarse talk, wrongdoing, and argument. Argument is the surprising item, since disputes are ordinary and not usually placed beside the other two. Then the register changes. Provisions are mentioned, as they would be for any journey, and the sentence turns the word into something else. The best provision is awareness of God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the run of instructions on the pilgrimage. The classical sources report that some pilgrims travelled without supplies, expecting to be fed along the way. They read the instruction to take provisions against that practice. The three things set aside are read as naming what actually went wrong on crowded journeys, where tempers and close quarters met.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to twist a rope tightly, so the word pictures two parties pulling in opposite directions. It names contention rather than disagreement, which is why it can be set aside without ending discussion.
The ordinary verb for packing food for a journey. Its plainness is what makes the turn work, since the sentence uses a traveller's word and then names the best thing to pack as awareness of God.
From a root meaning to guard or shield. Calling it a provision changes the image: something carried and drawn on rather than a state of mind, and something that can run out if it was not packed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A pilgrim caravan was thousands of people moving slowly in heat. They shared wells and campsites with strangers from tribes they might have fought. Tempers were short, animals went missing, and who went first at the water was a live question every day. Setting aside argument for the season was not a lofty idea. It dealt with the most likely thing to go wrong in the next fortnight.
studies.didYouKnow: The address to people of understanding at the end of this ayah appears once before in the surah. That was in the line about life inside the rule on killing. In both places it closes a passage rather than opening one. The three things set aside here fall in order of how dramatic they are. Argument, the least dramatic, is placed last.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A journey made for God is guarded from the ordinary friction of travel by naming that friction in advance. What is asked for is not extra devotion. It is the removal of three named behaviours, which is a small and doable thing. Then the word for provisions is turned. The passage suggests that what a person carries inside is the supply that really decides how the journey goes.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same address to people of understanding, earlier in this surah.
Names the failures of speech that damage a community: mockery, nicknames, suspicion and backbiting.
Describes servants of the Merciful as those who answer the ignorant with peace.

studies.applyIt: Pick one setting this week where you will not argue: a particular meal, a particular hour, one recurring conversation. Not silence, and not agreement. Just no contention inside that window. This ayah fences off a period rather than a topic, which turns out to be much easier to keep.
studies.explainEasier: The pilgrimage happens in known months. While you are on it, leave out rude talk, bad acts and arguing. Take what you need for the road. But the best thing to pack is a heart that is aware of God.

studies.title: Leave From Where The People Leave
studies.meaning: Two worries are answered. The first is whether trading during the pilgrimage spoils it; the answer removes the blame without praising the trade. The second concerns a group who had kept themselves apart at one of the stations, and the instruction is to leave from where everyone else leaves. Then, immediately, comes a call to seek forgiveness, attached to the very act of standing where others stand.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that some families had held themselves above the general pilgrimage. They stayed inside the sanctuary while everyone else went out to the plain. This instruction placed them back among the crowd. The sources also report a hesitation about whether trade during the season was proper. Both reports are widely recorded, though the details vary between the works.

keyTerms.gloss: you pour forth, you surge out
keyTerms.note: The verb describes water overflowing a vessel. Applied to a crowd leaving a place, it pictures a mass moving together rather than individuals departing, which is why the second ayah's instruction lands as it does.

The word means what is left over and abundant, and the Quran uses it for both divine favour and honest earnings. Using one word for both is what allows trade during the season to be described as seeking from the Lord.
From the same root as the word for the marks of God used earlier in this surah. It names a place by its function as something noticed, which is how the Quran describes several of these stations.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pilgrimage season was also the biggest market of the year. Caravans arrived with goods from Yemen and Syria. Poets competed, debts were settled and marriages arranged. For many families the season's trade was a large part of the year's income. The two purposes could not be pulled apart in practice. So the question the ayah answers was a practical one about making a living.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the verb for pouring forth is used three times across these two ayat. It is the word the Quran uses for pilgrims moving between the stations. The instruction in the second ayah, to leave from where the people leave, is one of the shortest correctives in the surah. It is followed at once by a call to seek forgiveness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Standing apart is treated as something to seek forgiveness for. That is the striking move. The ayah does not argue that the separated group had the rite wrong. It places them back in the crowd and then mentions forgiveness in the next breath. Setting yourself above others, even with a religious reason, is handled here as a problem of the heart rather than of procedure.

crossReferences.why: Grounds honour in awareness of God rather than in lineage, addressing the same instinct to rank people.
Describes pilgrims arriving on foot and on lean mounts from every distant road, answering one call.
Answers another practical question from this same section, also by removing a false form of piety.

studies.applyIt: Find one place where you quietly stand apart: a queue you get around, a room you leave early, a group whose company you accept but do not join. Stay this week. The instruction here asks nothing except that you go out when everyone else goes out, and it treats that as worth saying.
studies.explainEasier: You can still trade while you are on the pilgrimage. God does not blame you for it. And when everyone moves on from the plain, move on with them. Do not stand apart as if you are better.

studies.title: As You Remember Your Fathers
studies.meaning: The comparison is unexpected and precise. Remember God the way you remember your fathers, or more strongly, which takes a habit already fully formed and points it somewhere else. Then a second sentence separates two kinds of asking. One person asks only for this world, and the ayah records what he receives and what he does not, without calling the asking itself wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the close of the pilgrimage instructions. The classical sources describe a practice after the rites, in which men gathered and recited the deeds of their ancestors. They competed in the honours of their line. Poetry contests of exactly that kind are well recorded in the season. The ayah is reported as turning the gathering in a new direction rather than ending it.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for an act of worship, which in the Quran attaches to the pilgrimage in particular. It shares a root with the word for a devout person, so the rites and the character are named together.
The comparative is built on the root for firmness, the same word used earlier in this surah for those stronger in love. What is being asked for is intensity rather than frequency.

An old word for an allotted portion, less common in the Quran than the usual term for a share, and used for a portion in the hereafter. Its rarity gives the closing clause a formal weight, like an entry in a ledger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boasting of ancestors was a public art. After the pilgrimage, men would stand and recite what their fathers had given away, whom they had protected, which disputes they had settled, and a good performance raised a whole clan's standing for the year. Nobody thought this frivolous; it was how reputation was maintained. The ayah takes that scene and asks for the same energy in a different direction.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a share used at the end of this ayah is uncommon. In the Quran it always names a portion in the hereafter that someone does or does not have. The sentence stops without saying what happens to the person described. The classical commentaries note that as deliberate restraint rather than something left out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A comparison is used as a measure. The ayah does not describe what remembrance of God should feel like. It points at something the audience already did with force and asks for that, or more. That is a practical standard rather than an ideal one. The second half does not sort requests into good and bad. It sorts them into narrow and complete, which the next ayah then shows.

crossReferences.why: Gives the complete request that this ayah's narrow one is set against, and states the outcome.
Describes what is given to whoever seeks only this world's harvest, and what is withheld.
Draws the same distinction between those who want the immediate and those who pursue what is beyond.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you talk about with real energy: a team, a project, a family story you tell well. Then notice the difference in your voice when you talk about God. The ayah does not ask you to manufacture feeling. It points at intensity you already have and asks where else it could go.
studies.explainEasier: When the rites are done, remember God the way you talk about your own family, or even more. Some people only ask God for things in this life. They get nothing waiting for them later.

studies.title: Goodness Here And Goodness There
studies.meaning: A second kind of asking is quoted, and it has become the most repeated prayer in Muslim practice. Three requests sit in one line: goodness in this world, goodness in the next, and protection from the Fire. The word for goodness is left undefined, which the commentators note, since it covers whatever is genuinely good rather than a list. The following ayah says these have a share of what they earned.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the pilgrimage section by setting a second prayer against the first. The early scholars record that this became the most repeated prayer in the community. It was said at the circuits of the House and at the close of gatherings. Its shortness is part of the reason. A crowd can say it together without being taught it first.

keyTerms.note: An indefinite noun, so what is asked for is a good rather than the good. Commentators list health, sufficiency, a righteous household, knowledge and forgiveness, and note that the word is left open deliberately.
An imperative from the same root as the word for God-consciousness, which describes shielding oneself. Here the shielding is asked of God, so the two uses of the root face each other.
From a root meaning to set something up in place, as a post is fixed upright. It names a portion assigned rather than won, which sits carefully beside the words about what they earned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayers in Arabia were usually specific: rain, a safe return, a son, victory in a dispute. People asked for the thing they needed by name. A vow often went with it. A prayer that asks for goodness without saying what kind would have sounded oddly open. The early scholars note that its wideness is what let it become the prayer everyone could say.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the most repeated prayer in Muslim practice. It is quoted here as the speech of an unnamed person rather than given as an instruction. The word for goodness appears twice in one line, once for each world. The classical commentaries will not define it, and list possibilities instead of choosing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer refuses the choice between this world and the next. It asks for both in the same breath and treats them as fitting together. That shapes a whole attitude. Comfort here is not made a rival of the hereafter, only not enough on its own. The next ayah ties the outcome to what was earned. So the prayer is not offered as a stand-in for anything a person does.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the narrower request this one is set against, in the immediately preceding ayah.
Asks that the home of the hereafter be sought without neglecting one's portion of this world.
Another supplication quoted in the Quran, asking for what was promised and against disgrace.

studies.applyIt: Say this line once today, in English or in the recitation, and notice how little it specifies. Most of us pray for outcomes we have already chosen. Try one prayer this week that names no particular result, and see whether it changes what you are willing to accept as an answer.
studies.explainEasier: Other people ask God for good in this life and good in the next life, and to keep them safe from the Fire. They get a share of what they have earned. God counts quickly.

studies.title: Two Days Or Three
studies.meaning: Remembrance is asked for during a set of counted days, and then the ayah does something unusual: it gives two options and clears both. Leaving after two days is not a fault, and staying longer is not a fault. A short clause attaches a condition to the whole arrangement, and the commentators read it as tying both choices to the same awareness. Neither option is presented as the better one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on the pilgrimage rites. The days referred to are those spent camped after the main day of the rites. The sources report that pilgrims differed over whether an early departure was a shortfall. The ayah settles that question by refusing to rank the two. The classical works record the practice on both sides without preference.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form of the verb for haste, so the person is described as hurrying himself rather than being hurried. Its pairing with the verb for delaying sets two deliberate choices side by side.
The counterpart verb, describing someone who puts himself later. The two verbs are built on the same pattern, which is how Arabic marks a matched pair rather than a preference and a fallback.
A passive verb used of a crowd driven together from every direction, and used of livestock as well as people. It ends a passage full of crowds moving between stations by naming one more gathering.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The days after the main rites were spent camped in a narrow valley with tens of thousands of others. Water was carried, tents were close, and the return journey ahead was long for anyone from Yemen or the north. Leaving a day early could mean joining a caravan that was setting out, or reaching home before supplies ran short. The choice was practical before it was devotional.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for counted days used here also opens the passage on fasting earlier in the surah. There it describes a different set of days entirely. The clause clearing the person from fault is repeated twice in the same wording, once for each option. That reads as a deliberate refusal to weight one above the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two acceptable options are given without either being praised. That is rarer in religious instruction than it sounds. The condition attached applies to both. So what decides the value of the choice is the state of the person making it, not the choice itself. The closing clause reframes the whole scene. A crowd scattering in every direction will be gathered again into one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about counted days, there opening the passage on fasting.
Names the appointed days of the pilgrimage and what is done and eaten during them.
Handles the earlier stations of the same journey, also by removing a supposed fault.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you keep treating as a test of your seriousness: how long you stay, how early you arrive, how much you take on. This ayah gives two answers and clears both, then attaches its only condition to the person rather than to the choice. Take the shorter option once and see whether anything is actually lost.
studies.explainEasier: After the main day of the pilgrimage, keep remembering God for a few more days. If you leave after two days, that is fine. If you stay longer, that is fine too.

studies.title: Speech That Impresses You
studies.meaning: A portrait is drawn in one sentence. Someone's talk about worldly matters is impressive, he calls God as witness to what is in his heart, and the last three words undo both. The oath is the telling detail: he swears about the one thing no listener can check. The final phrase names him the fiercest of disputants, which places the problem in argument rather than in belief.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars record differing accounts of this portrait. Some say a particular man is described, others that a type is being drawn, and several works give both. The passage sits in a stretch of the surah that sorts people by what they do rather than by which group they belong to. The portrait continues over the next three ayat.

keyTerms.note: The verb describes something that wins admiration, and it is addressed in the singular to the hearer. The reader is placed inside the scene as the person being impressed, rather than watching it from outside.

A superlative describing someone who twists and turns in a quarrel and cannot be pinned down. The root is connected to the side of the neck, suggesting a man who turns his head away rather than yield.

A word for parties in a dispute, used of litigants standing before a judge. It places the description in the setting of argument and claim, which is where the person in this portrait actually operates.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Eloquence was the highest public skill in Arabia. A man who could speak well settled disputes, negotiated for his tribe, and was believed before quieter men. Oaths were the currency of proof, since there were no documents to check, and swearing by God was the strongest thing a person could offer. Both of the tools in this portrait were exactly the tools a respected man used.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one that closes the group both begin with the same phrase, among the people is he who. Together they frame a contrast. The first names someone whose speech impresses. The last names someone who sells himself seeking God's approval, and nothing at all is said about that man's speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the impression a person makes from what they are. It does so without giving the reader any way to tell the difference in advance. That is honest rather than useful. It warns that the tools that make a person believed can be held by anyone. What follows in the next ayat is not a test for spotting such a person. It is a description of what they do once they have power.

crossReferences.why: Continues the portrait directly and then sets its opposite against it in the same construction.
Describes an appearance that impresses and speech worth listening to, attached to the same warning.
Shows the same gap between what is said in a person's presence and what is planned afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you were persuaded by how something was said rather than by what it was. Not tricked, just carried. Try one thing this week: write down the actual claim, in your own plain words, before you agree with it. The gap between the two is what this ayah is describing.
studies.explainEasier: Some people talk in a way that sounds very good. They even swear to God that they mean it. But God says such a person is really the harshest kind of arguer.

studies.title: The Man Who Sells Himself
studies.meaning: The portrait continues and then breaks. The first man, once he has authority, works to ruin crops and offspring, and correction only stiffens him, since pride takes hold of him through the wrong itself. Then, with the same opening phrase, a second person is named: one who trades his own self seeking God's approval. Nothing is said about his speech, and the passage ends on God's kindness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section that sorts people by conduct rather than by which side they are on. The classical scholars record differing accounts of these portraits. Some say particular men stand behind them, and more than one name is given for the second. The reading several works prefer is that two types are set against each other. The listener is to recognise them wherever they appear.

keyTerms.note: Two words covering what is sown and what is born, so between them they name everything that grows. The pair describes ruin reaching the future rather than only the present, since both are next year's food and next year's people.

The word usually names honour and strength, and is used of God elsewhere in the Quran. Here it takes hold of a man through his own wrongdoing, so what could be dignity becomes the thing that stops him hearing.

The verb can carry both buying and selling in Arabic, and here the commentators read it as selling. What is traded is the self, which makes the transaction total rather than a portion of someone's wealth.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruining crops and livestock was how conflicts were actually fought in Arabia. Burning a field, cutting date palms or driving off a herd destroyed a settlement without a battle. The damage lasted for years. The pairing of what is sown and what is born names the two things a community could not quickly replace. Everyone hearing it knew a place emptied that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The two portraits open with the same phrase, among the people is he who, three ayat apart. The first is given three ayat and the second only one. So the passage spends most of its length on the figure it warns about. It closes on the shorter description, with a word about God's gentleness towards his servants.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined here by what it costs rather than by what it feels like. The second figure is described entirely by a transaction, and no claim about his inner state is reported at all. That inverts the first portrait, where the inner state was exactly what was sworn to. The passage suggests that a visible price paid is more informative than any account a person gives of themselves.

crossReferences.why: Opens this portrait, with the oath about what is in the heart that these ayat then answer.
Describes the same transaction from the other side, as God purchasing the selves of the believers.
Promises the final home to those who seek neither superiority on earth nor corruption in it.

studies.applyIt: Notice what your convictions have actually cost you this year. Not what you believe, what it cost. For most people the honest answer is very little, and that is worth knowing rather than being ashamed of. Pick one thing this week where holding to what you say will cost you something small and concrete.
studies.explainEasier: When that person gets power, he wrecks crops and lives, and he will not take correction. Then God describes a very different person. That one gives his whole self away just to please God.

studies.title: Enter It Whole
studies.meaning: One word carries the ayah: wholly, entirely, all of you. The early scholars read it two ways. It may mean entering submission completely, keeping no part of your life outside it. It may mean all of the believers entering together. Both readings are recorded and neither is dismissed. Then the warning about footsteps returns. The second ayah handles what happens if someone slips after clarity has arrived.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to a community that had arrived from different backgrounds and brought its old arrangements with it. The early scholars connect the ayah to believers who kept practices from before. They held parts of their earlier life apart from what they had entered. Reports about the exact occasion differ between the works, and several prefer the general reading.

keyTerms.note: The word covers peace and surrender together, and shares a root with the words for submission and for safety. Reciters differ over its vowelling, and the two readings pull towards peace or towards submission respectively.
The single word both readings turn on. Grammatically it can describe the peace as complete or the people as all of them, and Arabic lets the ambiguity stand without either sense cancelling the other.
The verb for a foot sliding on a smooth surface, not for a deliberate turn. Choosing it makes the failure an accident of footing, which is gentler than the alternatives the sentence could have used.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: New arrivals in Medina brought debts, alliances, feuds and marriages arranged under older rules. None of it disappeared on arrival. A man might have sworn protection to a clan he no longer prayed with. He might hold a grievance his new brothers had no part in. Entering something wholly, in that setting, meant reworking ties that had been settled for years.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the footsteps of Satan appears twice in this surah: here and earlier in the passage about food. Both times it follows an instruction that sounds entirely ordinary. The word the first ayah turns on can be read more than one way in the grammar. The classical commentaries keep both readings side by side rather than choosing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Partial commitment is named as the problem, rather than outright refusal. The enemy is described as working step by step, not by one big temptation. That is a particular account of how people go wrong. It is not a decision but a drift, one step at a time. The second ayah answers a slip with two names of God, not with a threat. That leaves the door where the first ayah left it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same warning about footsteps, there attached to food and to inventing rules.
Repeats the warning twice in one ayah and states what the following of those steps leads to.
Answers the anxiety a warning about slipping produces, addressed to those who went furthest.

studies.applyIt: Find the part of your life you keep in a separate room from the rest: the way you talk with one group of friends, a habit you would not describe out loud, a corner of your work. You do not need to fix it today. Just stop filing it separately, and start seeing it as part of the same life.
studies.explainEasier: God asks those who believe to come into peace all the way, not just part of the way. Do not follow the steps of Satan. If you slip after the truth is clear, God is still strong and wise.

studies.title: Shadows Of Cloud
studies.meaning: A question is asked that expects no answer. Will anything short of the final scene satisfy them. The image given is left bare on purpose. The classical scholars handle it carefully, saying that it comes without saying how. The verb in the middle settles everything: the matter is finished. Its form reports the outcome without naming who brought it about.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the instruction to enter submission wholly. The early scholars read the question as addressed to those who kept asking for one decisive sign. They note that the same demand comes back across the surah. No specific occasion is reported. The image of cloud shadow belongs to a family of descriptions of the final day found in several places across the Quran.

keyTerms.note: The plural of what casts shade, used of an awning and of anything overhead. Paired with cloud, it names the covered light of a heavy sky rather than a bright appearance, which is not what a listener would expect.
From a root meaning to cover or conceal. The word is used in this surah for the cloud that shaded a people in the wilderness, so the same term carries shelter in one place and finality in another.

A passive verb for a matter brought to its conclusion, used of judgements and of debts discharged. Its passive form leaves the settling without a described agent, which fits a sentence that refuses to elaborate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a bank of heavy cloud was the most watched sight of the year. It meant rain, and rain meant the difference between a good year and a hard one, so people read cloud formations the way a sailor reads a sky. A dense cloud approaching drew everyone outdoors. That expectation of something enormous arriving overhead is the feeling the image borrows.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for cloud used here appears in only four places in the Quran. One of them is earlier in this same surah, where it describes the cloud that shaded the Children of Israel in the wilderness. The classical commentaries note the recurrence. The same covering appears once as mercy and once as the end of all matters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers a demand for proof by describing the moment when proof would finally arrive. At that moment nothing remains to be decided. So the demand defeats itself. The evidence being asked for comes only when it can no longer be acted on. The final clause widens from one scene to a general statement: all matters return to God.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for cloud, there describing shade given to a people in the wilderness.
Describes the sky split open with cloud and the angels sent down in streams.
States that faith arriving on that day will not benefit a soul that had not believed before.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you are keeping open until you have more certainty. Some certainties arrive only when the decision has already been made for you. Ask honestly whether the evidence you are waiting for could still change anything by the time it comes. If it could not, choose now on what you already have.
studies.explainEasier: Some people wait for God to come to them in the shade of the clouds before they will believe. By then everything will already be settled. In the end, all things go back to God.

studies.title: Ask Them How Many Signs
