studies.meaning: An instruction is given to ask a question whose answer everyone already knows: how many clear signs were given. The point is the number, and it is left unsaid so the hearer supplies it. Then a general rule follows about altering a blessing after it has arrived. The word for altering is the one used elsewhere in this surah for changing a text. So what is described is swapping, not neglect.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section where the surah keeps turning back to the history of earlier communities. The signs referred to are those told at length in the first part of this surah. They are the sea, the manna, the water from the rock, the covenant at the mountain. The classical scholars read the question as one that expects no answer. It is addressed to the audience through the request rather than answered by anyone.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative used in Arabic for large indefinite quantities as much as for genuine questions. Placed here it works as an exclamation, so the sentence says how very many rather than asking anyone for a figure.

The intensive verb for putting one thing in the place of another, used earlier in this surah of a word that was changed and of a testament altered. It describes replacement, which is more active than simply losing something.
The singular is used, as it is in the earlier promise of a favour completed. Naming it in the singular treats everything given as one gift, so exchanging any part of it touches the whole of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The stories of the earlier communities were not foreign in Medina. Jewish families in the city kept them in detail. Arab tribes had heard them for generations at markets and around fires. The sea, the mountain and the years of wandering were common knowledge. That is why the surah can ask about them without retelling. Everyone in earshot could have answered.
studies.didYouKnow: The order to ask, addressed to one person, opens this ayah. The same build is used elsewhere in the Quran. It introduces a question whose answer the audience already holds. The verb for altering appears in this surah three times: for a word spoken, for a will, and here for a blessing received.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A blessing is treated as something that can be swapped, not merely lost. That is a sharper idea. The failure described is not forgetting but replacing: putting something else where the gift was. That makes ingratitude an act rather than an absence. It also explains why the ayah opens by asking how many signs. The scale of what was given is what makes the swap visible.

crossReferences.why: Describes people who exchanged the blessing of God for ingratitude, using the same idea.
Opens the surah's address to the same community by recalling the favour given to them.
Says they recognise the blessing of God and then deny it, most of them being ungrateful.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing that has been reliably good in your life for years: a person, a place, your health. Say what it is out loud today, in one sentence, to someone. Long-standing gifts are the ones that get quietly swapped for something else, mostly because nobody ever says their name.
studies.explainEasier: Ask the children of Israel how many clear signs God gave them. Some people take what God gave and put something else in its place. God is very hard on them.

studies.title: Made Beautiful To Them
studies.meaning: The verb at the start is passive and no agent is named: the worldly life has been made attractive to them. Then the mockery is reported without a reply. The answer comes as a statement of position rather than an argument. The mindful will be above them on the day of resurrection. The closing clause changes the subject entirely, and says God provides to whom he wills without measure.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars describe a community in which many early believers had little, while those who mocked them held wealth and standing. They read the ayah against that visible contrast. Reports naming particular individuals differ between the works. What is agreed is the situation: people whose position made the poverty of the believers look like a verdict on their choice.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb with no agent named, so the sentence declines to say who did the adorning. The classical commentaries record more than one view on that, and the grammar allows the question to stay open.

A word of physical position rather than of merit. Answering a social ranking with a spatial one is deliberate: the reply uses the same kind of language the mockery did, and simply reverses the arrangement.

The phrase can mean without limit or without being called to account for it. Both senses are recorded, and either way it detaches what a person receives from any calculation the onlookers could perform.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca and Medina was visible in a way it is not now. You could see it in the number of camels a man watered, the guests he fed, the clothes his household wore at the pilgrimage. Poverty was equally visible. In a small town where everyone knew everyone's circumstances, being poor was a public condition, and mockery of it needed no words at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The passive verb that opens this ayah is used across the Quran for things made to look attractive. The one doing the adorning is almost never named. The closing phrase about provision without measure appears several times in the Quran. It always detaches what someone is given from what they appear to deserve.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two separate points are made, and the second is the more unsettling. The first reverses the ranking at a later date. The second says that provision in this life is handed out with no visible measure. That removes wealth from the evidence a person could use about themselves or anyone else. Together they take the whole subject out of what can be read off appearances.

crossReferences.why: Lists what is made attractive to people, and names the better return standing beside it.
Tells the story of two men and two gardens, where the ranking is reversed within a lifetime.
States that God allocates livelihood among people, raising some above others in degrees.

studies.applyIt: Notice one moment today when you measure yourself against what someone else has. Not to feel bad about noticing, just to catch it happening. This ayah answers that comparison. It says the sharing out has no visible measure in it, so the sum you are doing does not work even in principle.
studies.explainEasier: This life has been made to look lovely to people who do not believe, so they laugh at those who do. But on the last day, the ones who kept away from wrong will be above them. God gives to whoever he wants.

studies.title: Humanity Was One Community
studies.meaning: A whole history is compressed into one sentence. People were one community; prophets were sent with news and warning; scripture came to judge between them where they differed. Then the turn: those who differed over the scripture were the very people who had been given it, out of rivalry rather than confusion. The ayah ends with guidance described as given by permission, not achieved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars differ over what the original single community was. Some read it as a time of agreement before division. Others read it as a shared ignorance before revelation. Both readings are recorded and neither is settled in the classical works. The ayah stands in a section of the surah that keeps returning to how earlier communities handled what they received.

keyTerms.note: The first word names a body of people with something in common, from a root connected both to a mother and to a direction. It describes belonging rather than agreement, which is part of why the commentators differ here.

From a root meaning to seek or desire, used for wanting beyond one's due. The word names the motive for the division, and it is placed in the sentence exactly where a reason for confusion might have gone.
The word for permission rather than for power. Placed at the end of a clause about guidance, it makes reaching the truth something granted rather than something the guided party managed on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held several communities reading scriptures they traced to shared beginnings. They lived in the same streets and disagreed sharply. Arab tribes nearby had their own handed-down accounts. Everyone could see that agreement had once existed somewhere back along the line and had not survived. The question this ayah answers was not a theory for anyone hearing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for differing appears three times in this single ayah. Twice it is about the people, and once about the thing they differed over. That repetition is one reason the classical commentaries treat the ayah as the surah's compressed account of religious history. They do not read it as a comment on any one community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division is placed after knowledge, not before it. The cause named is rivalry, not a lack of clarity. That removes the usual excuse in every direction, since nobody can then claim the message fell short. Then guidance is described as given by permission. That stops the ayah from becoming a claim that one party simply reasoned better than another.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing more briefly: people were one community, then they differed.
Names the religion enjoined on the prophets and repeats that division came after knowledge arrived.
Gives the same diagnosis earlier in this surah, calling the disagreement a deep split.

studies.applyIt: Think about a split you are close to: a family, an organisation, a group of friends. Try to describe the disagreement in one sentence both sides would accept. If you cannot, notice that. This ayah says the trouble usually starts after everyone has the facts, and it takes that seriously rather than blaming a misunderstanding.
studies.explainEasier: People used to be one group. Then God sent prophets with good news and warnings, and sent books to sort out what people argued about. But the ones who had the book started arguing anyway, out of envy.

studies.title: When Is The Help Of God
studies.meaning: A question is put to the community, and it is not gentle. Did you expect to enter the garden without what happened to those before you. What follows describes that experience, ending in a sentence spoken by a messenger and the believers with him, asking when the help of God will come. The reply is one short clause, and it does not dispute anything in the description of the hardship.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars connect the ayah to a period of severe pressure. Several works place it around the difficulties of the early Medinan years, though they differ on which. What is agreed is that the ayah quotes earlier prophets and their followers, not the present community. That is what gives the quoted question its weight.

keyTerms.note: A pair the Quran uses together, the first from a root for severity and harm arriving from outside, the second for damage and loss suffered. Between them they cover what happens to a person and what happens to their circumstances.

A doubled root that imitates the movement it names, used of an earthquake. The passive form leaves the shaking as something done to them, and the same word gives its name to a whole surah about the earth being shaken.
The plain interrogative for time. Its bareness is the point: what is quoted is not a complaint or a doubt but a question about timing, and it is placed in the mouth of a messenger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hardship in that world came without cushioning. A siege, a bad harvest or the loss of a caravan meant real hunger within weeks, and there was nowhere to appeal. The communities the ayah refers to had been driven out, imprisoned and killed. For an audience that had left Mecca with nothing, the comparison would have been recognised immediately rather than heard as history.
studies.didYouKnow: The question quoted here is asked by a messenger and the believers with him. That is unusual: the Quran rarely places a question of this kind in a prophet's mouth. The answer that follows is a single short clause. The classical commentaries note that it corrects the timing without disputing the difficulty at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is presented as a normal part of the road, not as a sign that something has gone wrong. That changes the whole experience, and it is done by comparison rather than by argument: this happened to them too. Then a blunt question about timing is voiced by the most trusted speaker there could be. That makes the asking allowed. The answer is about nearness, not about meaning.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether people expected to say they believe and be left untested, recalling those before them.
Puts the same question about entering the garden, there tied to striving and to steadfastness.
States the relation between hardship and ease twice over, in two consecutive short lines.

studies.applyIt: If you are in something hard, write down the question you have actually been asking. Not the polite version. This ayah puts a blunt question about timing into the mouth of a messenger, which means the asking is not the failure. Then notice that the answer it gives is about how near, not about why.
studies.explainEasier: People may think they will get to the garden the easy way. Those before them were shaken hard. Even the messenger asked when God's help would come. The help of God is near.

studies.title: They Asked What, He Answered Whom
studies.meaning: The question asked is about what to give. The answer changes the subject to whom. Five recipients are listed in a fixed order. It starts at the nearest relation and moves outward to the traveller, who has no claim on anyone. The early scholars note the redirection. Nothing is said about amount or kind, and the ayah closes with a general statement covering any good done at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, one of a series in this section that begins with a reported question. Giving in Arabia was governed by kinship, and the obligation ran outward from close family. The list here follows that order and then extends it past where custom stopped, to the poor and the stranded traveller. The commentators read the ordering as deliberate rather than incidental.

keyTerms.note: Literally the son of the road, an idiom for someone whose circumstances are defined by being on a journey. The phrase makes the road itself his family, which is exactly why he has nobody else to ask.

The same word covers goodness and property, and it appears twice in this ayah, once for what is spent and once for what is done. That double use quietly ties giving and good conduct into one category.

From a root meaning to be still or motionless, so the word pictures someone brought to a standstill by need. It names a condition rather than a character, which is why nothing more is asked about them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller in Arabia was truly helpless. Away from his tribe he had no protection and no claim on anyone beyond custom. If his money ran out or his mount died, he could not simply find work. Towns on the caravan roads dealt with stranded travellers all the time. Naming him last widens the circle of duty to someone who will never repay it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of several ayat in this section that open with a question the community had put. It is the one where the answer most clearly declines the question asked. The word for good is used twice within it, once for what is spent and once for what is done. So a single term covers wealth and conduct in one sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Turning the question around is the teaching. A person asking what to give is thinking about the gift. The answer makes them think about people, and about an order of nearness they may have skipped over. The closing clause then widens the subject past giving altogether. The whole matter is folded into a larger one: whatever good you do is known.

crossReferences.why: Names a similar circle of recipients inside its definition of righteousness, earlier in this surah.
Gives the near relative, the needy and the traveller their due, and warns against squandering.
Describes what giving returns, and what talk about it afterwards can undo.

studies.applyIt: Go through the list in order and stop at the first one where you cannot name a person: parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, someone far from home. That is probably where your giving stops. Find one name for that place this week. The ayah answers a question about amount by asking about people, and it is worth answering the same way.
studies.explainEasier: People asked what they should give away. God answered by naming who should get it: parents, close family, orphans, the poor, and anyone stuck far from home. He knows every good thing you do.

studies.title: You Do Not Know What Is Good
studies.meaning: A hard instruction is given and the dislike it will provoke is acknowledged in the same breath. Then the sentence widens into a general principle that reaches far past its occasion: you may hate what is good for you and love what harms you. The final clause explains why, and it is not a comfort about outcomes. It is a statement about the limits of human knowledge, which is left as the last word.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. By then the community faced organised hostility from Mecca and was being told to defend itself. During the Meccan years they had been forbidden to fight. Early scholars describe real reluctance among believers, some of it moral and some of it fear. They read the opening concession as taking that reluctance seriously, not brushing it aside. The ayat that follow deal with specific questions from the same conflict.

keyTerms.note: Not mild dislike. The word covers what is hateful and forced on you against your will. The Quran uses it here of the believers themselves, granting their feeling rather than criticising it.
A particle of hope and possibility. It keeps the two clauses that follow from becoming a rule. The passage says this can happen, not that every dislike hides a benefit.
The comparative and the plain adjective share a form, so the word slides between good and better. What is being contrasted is not pleasure and pain but two assessments of the same thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The emigrants in Medina had left houses, businesses and family behind. They arrived depending on hosts. Conflict with Mecca threatened the caravan trade that many of their relatives still worked in. Fighting meant facing cousins and brothers across a field. Reluctance in that setting was not squeamishness. It was the reasonable response of people who could name, one by one, the men they might meet.
studies.didYouKnow: The two middle clauses of this ayah are among the most quoted lines in Arabic. People use them outside religion too. It is plain comfort after a lost job or a broken engagement. Early scholars already treated the idea as one you could lift from its setting. That is why the wider statement is put as a chance. It is not a claim about every case.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the gap between God and the human being in knowledge, not in power. That is a specific claim. It does not say that everything painful turns out well. It says your judgement is made with less information than you assume. That leaves room for grief to be real while the verdict waits. And by admitting the dislike first, it shows a faith that does not require pretending to want what you do not want.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same principle to marriage: you may dislike something in which God places much good.
Dramatises the point at length, three acts that look wrong until their reasons are given.
Shows Jacob holding hope against every visible sign, and refusing to despair of God's relief.

studies.applyIt: Think of something from five years ago that you did not want and now would not undo. Write down one sentence about it. Then think of something you are resisting now and put the two beside each other, without concluding anything. The point is not to talk yourself into liking it. It is to remember, accurately, that your reading of events has been wrong before.
studies.explainEasier: God says people will be asked to do things they hate. Sometimes you hate what is good for you. Sometimes you love what will hurt you. God knows how things will turn out, and you do not.

studies.title: Weighing One Wrong Against Another
studies.meaning: A question about fighting in a sacred month is answered in two stages. The act is called grave, which concedes the question rather than dismissing it. Then a list is set beside it of things called graver, and the comparison is what the ayah is doing: not excusing the first but placing it on a scale. The passage then describes the aim of the pressure being applied to the community.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report an incident near the boundary of a sacred month. A small party sent out by the community met an opposing group there. The row that followed prompted the question this ayah answers. Accounts of the details differ across the works, but the setting is well attested and the ayah is read against it.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for large, used here of the seriousness of an act. The comparative form of the same word then appears twice for the items set against it, so the whole comparison is built on a single root.
A verbal noun for blocking someone from a path, covering physical obstruction and persuasion alike. It heads the list of graver things and names an act of prevention rather than one of violence.
The verb is used of an animal that swells from eating a poisonous plant and then dies of it. It describes something that looked like growth and turns out to have been the cause of the ruin.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months held Arabian life together. Trade, pilgrimage and safe travel all rested on the promise that fighting stopped. A breach was talked about across the peninsula. Access to the sanctuary was a related promise, and barring someone from it was a serious act with no remedy anyone could seek. This ayah weighs one such promise against another.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative form appears twice in this ayah. Each time it raises something above the act the question was about. The clause about persecution weighing heavier than killing has already appeared a few ayat earlier, in slightly different wording. So the surah states the same weighting twice within a short passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A comparison is used where a denial might have been expected. The ayah does not say the objection was wrong; it says the objection was smaller than what the objectors themselves were doing. That is a demanding form of argument, because it requires both sides of a scale to be named honestly. It also means the concession stands: the act was grave, and saying so is part of the answer.

crossReferences.why: States the same weighting of persecution against killing, in a slightly different wording.
Names the sacred month and the offerings among what is not to be violated, alongside a warning about hatred.
Describes those who bar people from the Sacred Mosque although they are not its rightful keepers.

studies.applyIt: When you next weigh a complaint made against you, try answering it the way this ayah does. Admit the part that is true first, in plain words, before you say anything else. Most arguments lose their heat at that point. The admission is what the other person was actually waiting for.
studies.explainEasier: People asked about fighting in a sacred month. God says that is a serious thing. But stopping people from God's path, and driving them out of the holy place, is worse.

studies.title: They Look Forward To Mercy
studies.meaning: Three groups are named in one line, and the verb attached to them is the surprising part. They hope for God's mercy, and the sentence stops there. Nothing is guaranteed. Those described have believed, migrated and struggled, which is as much as a person could do, and what they are said to have at the end of it is hope. Two names of God close the ayah.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed directly after the hard ayah about the sacred month. The early scholars read that placing as answering the worry the previous passage would have caused. It speaks to those who had taken part in the disputed incident. The people described are the emigrants who had left Mecca. The reports agree on that while differing over the details.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cut off or abandon, so the word carries the severing of ties as much as the journey. It names leaving a place behind rather than arriving somewhere new.

A verb sitting between hoping and expecting, used of someone who anticipates something without holding a guarantee. Placing it after everything these people had done is what gives the ayah its restraint.

The word appears in the construct form, so it is God's mercy specifically rather than mercy in general. What they hope for is not a verdict or a reward but a relation, which is a smaller and a larger thing at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The emigrants had left houses, businesses and graves behind. Most arrived in Medina with nothing. Some had been traders in Mecca and now worked as labourers. Their old property was held by others, and nobody expected to get it back. What this ayah calls migration was, for those hearing it, the memory of one week when they loaded what they could carry.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here is one of hope rather than of certainty, and the classical commentaries pause on it. They note that the people described had done everything asked of them. The sentence still stops short of a guarantee. It ends instead with two names of God, about forgiveness and mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is withheld from the people best placed to claim it, and the withholding is the point. Hope is presented as the correct posture even after a maximal effort, which keeps the relationship from turning into an account settled. At the same time the two closing names make that hope well-founded rather than anxious. The ayah holds both of those together in one line.

crossReferences.why: Asks that God be called on in fear and hope, naming both postures together in one clause.
Describes the hardship these same people had been through, a few ayat earlier.
Names the same three actions and states the rank given to those who took them.

studies.applyIt: Think about something you have worked hard at and now feel entitled to an outcome from. This ayah takes people who had given up everything and describes them as hoping. Try holding your own effort that way for a day: real, costly, and still not a claim. Most people find it lighter rather than heavier.
studies.explainEasier: The people who believed, who left their homes for God, and who worked hard for him, hope for God's mercy. They are not promised it. They hope. God forgives and is kind.

studies.title: Weighed, Not Simply Declared
studies.meaning: Two questions are answered in one ayah. The first is met with a weighing rather than a verdict: both things carry serious harm and some benefit for people, and the harm is the heavier. The second question, about what to give, is answered with a single word the commentators read as what is left over beyond need. The ayah closes by naming reflection as its purpose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the run of ayat answering questions the community had put. The early scholars describe this as one stage in a sequence of passages on the subject. It comes before the later and more decisive ayat in another surah. They read the weighing here as preparing for what followed. The second half continues a question about giving that was answered a few ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for advantage or profit. Its presence is striking: the ayah concedes real benefits rather than denying them, and then places them on the lighter side of a scale.

A comparative rather than an absolute. The sentence is built as a measurement rather than a declaration, which is why the classical works describe this ayah as a stage rather than the end of the matter.
The same root gives the word for pardon and for what is left over easily. Answering a question about giving with this word ties generosity to what a person can spare without strain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices were woven into Arabian social life. Wine circulated at gatherings and was celebrated in poetry, and the arrow game divided a slaughtered camel by lot, with the losers paying and the winners often feeding the poor from the meat. That is the benefit the ayah concedes: real people were fed. Naming it honestly is what makes the weighing land.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places where the Quran answers a question by granting the other side first. It makes its own point after that. The word given as the answer to the second question is a single word in Arabic. The same root produces the word for pardon, so the vocabulary of giving and of forgiving overlap.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A judgement is given as a comparison, and the reader is left holding the scale. That is unusual. The closing clause explains it: the purpose named is thinking, not obedience. It also models a kind of honesty about mixed goods. Something can be truly useful and still not be worth what it costs. The ayah refuses to make the case easier by denying the usefulness.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same two subjects later and states the outcome the classical works read as decisive.
Answers the earlier form of the same question about giving, there by naming the recipients.
Uses the same word for what comes easily and is left over, there about how to deal with people.

studies.applyIt: Take one habit you defend by naming its benefits, and write those benefits down honestly. Then write the cost beside them, in the same detail. This ayah does not tell you the answer comes out one way. It shows you the method, and it names thinking as the point of the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: People asked about wine and gambling. God says there is some good in them, but the harm is bigger. They also asked what to give away. He says: give what you have spare.

studies.title: Then They Are Your Brothers
studies.meaning: A question about orphans is answered in two moves. The first names the standard: whatever improves their situation is best. That leaves the method open and fixes the aim. The second handles a practical worry about mixing households and property. It answers with a word about kinship rather than about accounting. Then a clause notes that God tells apart the one who spoils from the one who repairs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that severe warnings had come about eating up the property of orphans. Guardians then began separating their food and belongings entirely. That made caring for them impractical and left the children cut off. The ayah is reported as the answer to that. The sources broadly agree on the setting even where details differ.

keyTerms.note: From the root for mending what is broken, used earlier in this surah of repairing a testament and of reconciling people. Naming the aim rather than the method leaves the guardian to judge each case.

The verb for blending two things together, used of mixing property and of sharing a household. It describes an intermingling rather than a transaction, which is exactly what the questioners were worried about.
From a root meaning hardship and being brought into difficulty. The clause states what was not done, so the ease of the arrangement is presented as a deliberate restraint rather than an oversight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Orphans in Arabia were common and at risk. Conflict, disease and hard travel left children without fathers. Their property, often a share of palms or animals, passed to a relative to manage. Households were shared: the same cooking fire, the same herd, the same store of dates. Separating an orphan's food completely from the family's meant something close to shutting him out.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah calls orphans in a shared household your brothers, using the ordinary word for a sibling. The clause about God telling apart the one who spoils from the one who repairs is built on two roots. Both are already used across this surah. So the sentence sorts guardians with the same words it has been applying to whole communities.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard given is an outcome, not a procedure. That places the weight on the guardian's judgement. It then names the one who can tell the difference. It is a demanding arrangement. It removes the safety of a rule followed exactly. The clause about not being overburdened suggests that a stricter arrangement was possible and was not chosen. That frames the whole answer as a relief.

crossReferences.why: Warns against substituting the bad for the good and consuming orphans' property along with your own.
Sets out testing orphans before handing over their property, and warns against consuming it hastily.
Puts the same concern in one short line, in a Meccan surah addressed to an orphan.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you help at arm's length: a relative you send money to, a neighbour you check on from the doorway. This ayah answers a worry about getting too involved by naming the person as family. Do one thing this week that mixes your life with theirs rather than keeping the accounts separate.
studies.explainEasier: People asked how to look after orphans. God says: do what is best for them. You can share a home and food with them, because they are your brothers. God knows who helps and who harms.

studies.title: Even If She Pleases You
studies.meaning: Two parallel statements are made, one about women and one about men. The wording is almost the same. Between them sits a comparison that does the work. A believing servant is better than an idolater, however attractive. The ayah is built to set attraction against direction. It gives the reason at the end. One side calls towards the Fire, the other towards the Garden and forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section on households and their arrangements. Marriage in Arabia was an alliance between families as much as a bond between two people. It carried religious weight, since a household's practices followed its arrangement. The classical scholars discuss the scope of the terms used here at length. They record differences over how widely the terms extend.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used a few ayat earlier of speech that impresses a listener. Its recurrence links the two passages: in both, something admirable on the surface is set against what lies underneath it.

The feminine of the word for one who has faith, from a root meaning safety and trust. The comparison applies it to someone in the lowest social position of that time, which is what gives the sentence its force.

The ordinary verb for calling someone towards something. Using it of both sides is deliberate: the passage describes two invitations rather than a threat and a promise, so the difference lies in the destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A marriage in Arabia joined two family lines. It decided which gods a household honoured, which feasts it kept, and which side it took in a dispute. Children followed the arrangement. Marrying across a religious line was therefore not a private matter. Both families would have weighed the alliance for protection, trade and standing before anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The two halves of this ayah mirror each other almost exactly. The same clause about being pleased is repeated for each. That kind of full symmetry is uncommon in the Quran's passages on household arrangements. The comparison in each half reaches for the person of lowest standing in that society and places them above the alternative.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage rearranges a social order without arguing against it directly. Standing, wealth and beauty are not denied. They are simply outweighed by something that society did not rank at all. The closing image reframes the whole subject. What is described is not a matter of status but two directions of travel, with a household moving in one of them together.

crossReferences.why: States a matching principle about who is suited to whom, in the language of good and bad.
Denies that lineage or origin decides rank, and grounds honour in awareness of God.
Handles a related question about households divided by belief, in a later Medinan passage.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of a first impression you form from things you would not defend out loud: appearance, accent, the confidence in someone's voice. This ayah names attraction honestly and then sets it beside something else. Try describing one person this week by what they are pointed at rather than by how they come across.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers not to marry someone who worships idols, even if they attract them. A believing servant is better than a free person who does not believe. One road leads to the Fire. God's road leads to the Garden.

studies.title: A Question Answered With Restraint
studies.meaning: A question is put about menstruation. The answer is kept narrow. It calls the condition a discomfort, not an impurity in the person. It sets apart marital intimacy for as long as it lasts, and nothing more. Then the sentence lifts: God loves those who turn back to Him, and those who keep themselves clean. Early scholars read that closing line as the point of the whole ayah. A matter of the body is turned into a matter of love.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits among a run of ayat that begin with reported questions from the community. The classical sources describe the practice around them. Some neighbouring communities kept a menstruating woman from eating and sitting with the household at all. Other Arabian custom made no distinction whatever. Early scholars read the answer as taking a middle position between two customs the audience already knew.

keyTerms.note: A mild word, used elsewhere for an irritation, a nuisance, or hurtful speech. Early scholars note it is much weaker than the words for defilement available in Arabic, and that the choice is deliberate.
An intensive form, describing people who return repeatedly rather than once. It is paired here with cleanliness, which links an inward habit to an outward one in a single clause.
A reflexive form: the action is done by the person to themselves. The root covers physical washing and inward clearing alike, and Arabic keeps both senses in play at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in Medina were close quarters. Families ate from a shared dish, slept in one or two rooms, and drew water together. A rule of complete separation meant a woman spending several days each month outside her own home. Reports from the period describe exactly that arrangement among some communities in the town. Against that background, an answer that touched only one part of married life was a large narrowing.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a run of ayat in the surah that open by reporting a question to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). That formula occurs about fifteen times across the Quran, and it clusters heavily here. Early scholars use these openings to work out what the first community was actually asking about. It turns out to be mostly practical matters of daily life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to treat a natural function as a stain on the person. The wording carries that refusal. It then attaches God's love to two ongoing habits, not to a state reached once. Repentance and cleanliness are set side by side, as if they were versions of the same movement. What could have been a note about restriction becomes a statement about what God is drawn to.

crossReferences.why: Uses the image of spouses as garments for one another, describing the same relationship at its warmest.
Names tranquillity, affection and mercy as the purpose of the marital bond.
Repeats God's love for those who purify themselves, in an entirely different context.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you speak about bodies, your own and other people's, when something is uncomfortable or awkward. The words chosen here are careful, and the care is the lesson. This week, when illness or a bodily limit comes up in your household, pick the gentler word rather than the blunter one. See whether the conversation goes differently.
studies.explainEasier: Someone asked about a woman's monthly period. God says she is not dirty. It is just something that hurts. Husbands and wives wait a few days before being close again. God loves people who keep themselves clean.

studies.title: Send Something Ahead For Yourselves
studies.meaning: An image from farming is used for the marital relation, and the commentators are clear about its scope: it names the bearing of children, the ground on which the next generation grows. Then the sentence turns without pause to something else entirely. Send ahead for yourselves, and know that you will meet Him. What began as a private matter ends facing a meeting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the run of ayat on households. The classical sources record that a question was raised about a particular matter and that this ayah was the reply. The works differ over the details. What they agree on is the shape of the answer. It gives an image, then an immediate turn to conduct and to answering for what you do. It ends with an instruction to give good news.

keyTerms.note: The word for ploughed land, used earlier in this surah for the crops a corrupter destroys. The commentators read it as naming what grows rather than the standing of the ground, so the image is about offspring.
A verb for sending something in advance of yourself, used of provisions dispatched before a traveller sets out. It moves the sentence from the present into what a person will find waiting for them.
A participle rather than a verb, so it names a settled fact rather than a future event. Placing it here attaches the most private part of a life to the most public reckoning of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming in Medina was the centre of life, and the words of sowing and harvest ran through ordinary speech. A field was tended over seasons, watered, protected and relied on for years. A farmer's bond with his land was long rather than a one-off deal. That is the register the image belongs to. It would have sounded like patience rather than ownership.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for ploughed ground appears earlier in this surah in a completely different setting. There it describes what a corrupter destroys, along with the next generation. The two places are eighteen ayat apart, and both pair the field with offspring. So the surah reuses one image on opposite sides of a contrast.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The turn in the middle of the ayah is the teaching. Something private is named and then at once joined to a meeting with God. That refuses to leave private life outside the account. What is asked for is not restraint but forethought: send something ahead. And the last clause changes who is addressed, ending a passage about the household with good news.

crossReferences.why: Names tranquillity, affection and mercy between spouses as a sign to be reflected on.
Uses the image of a garment for the same relation, earlier in this surah.
Uses the same verb about a soul considering what it has sent forward for tomorrow.

studies.applyIt: Take one relationship you are inside every day and ask what you are sending ahead in it. Not what you are getting. This ayah moves in a single sentence from something private to a meeting, and the move is worth copying: choose one small thing today that the other person will still be glad of in ten years.
studies.explainEasier: Wives are like a field where the next generation grows. Come to them and send something good ahead for yourselves. Keep God in mind, because one day you will meet him. Give the believers good news.

studies.title: An Oath Laid Across The Road
studies.meaning: A specific trap is named. Someone swears by God not to do something, and then finds the oath itself standing between him and doing good, keeping ties, or making peace between people. The ayah does not discuss the technicalities of oaths; it points at what this one is being used for. The construction covers both a genuine bind and a convenient excuse without distinguishing them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the instructions on households and disputes. Oaths were the strongest verbal promise available in a society without documents, and men swore readily and in public. The early scholars record that some treated an oath sworn in anger as grounds for staying apart from a relative. They read the ayah as addressing that. The ayat that follow continue with oaths nobody meant.

keyTerms.gloss: an obstacle, a thing set up
keyTerms.note: The word means something laid across a path, and also something exposed and put on display. Both senses fit here: the divine name is placed across the road, and held up as the reason for staying put.
From the same root as the word for righteousness used earlier in this surah, and applied especially to kindness towards parents. It names the ordinary good that an oath in this case is preventing.

The verb for repairing, appearing here for another distinct time in this surah, after a testament and an orphan's affairs. Each time it names putting something back rather than starting something new.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in Arabia bound a man in public and was expected to hold. Swearing by God in front of witnesses made it a matter of honour, and backing down cost standing. So a quarrel between relatives could be frozen for good by a few words spoken in temper. Neither side could move without looking weak. Everyone knew a family in that position.
studies.didYouKnow: Three good things are named in this one short ayah as what an oath might be blocking. They are doing good, mindfulness of God, and making peace between people. The ayah then closes with two names of God, about hearing and knowing. They sit pointedly at the end of a sentence about words spoken aloud.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A religious promise is described as able to become an obstacle to religion. That is a sharp observation. The divine name is exactly what makes the oath binding, and exactly what is being misused. The passage does not fix this by adjusting the rules about oaths. It names the purpose the oath is serving and leaves the person to see it. The ayat that follow then deal with what oaths actually bind.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately, distinguishing unintended oaths from what the heart actually resolved.
Sets out what is done about an oath deliberately made, rather than leaving it standing forever.
Addresses someone who withheld from a relative, asking whether they would rather be pardoned themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you have taken that you would not take today, and that you are holding because you said it out loud. Not a principle, a position. This ayah is about the moment a commitment starts working against the thing it was meant to protect. Say the harder sentence this week: I have changed my mind.
studies.explainEasier: Some people swear by God and then use that oath as a reason to stop doing good. They use it to stay away from family, or to avoid making peace. God hears and knows.

studies.title: What Your Hearts Have Earned
studies.meaning: A line is drawn between words said with no weight behind them and what the heart actually resolved. Only the second is held against a person. Then a specific case follows: a vow to keep away from one's wife. A waiting period of four months is set. Two endings are possible. Each is met with names of God rather than a verdict, one pair about mercy and one about hearing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section on households. The classical sources describe a pre-Islamic practice in which a man could swear off his wife indefinitely, leaving her neither married in any real sense nor free to remarry. Setting a limit of four months put an end to an indefinite suspension. The commentators are broadly agreed on that background.

keyTerms.note: Names speech with nothing behind it, the filler phrases people use without meaning them. The word is used elsewhere in the Quran for what is absent from the Garden, so it carries a sense of the pointless.

The verb is the ordinary one for earning wages. Applying it to hearts treats an intention as something worked for and acquired rather than as a passing state, which is why it can be held against a person.

A reflexive form describing someone holding themselves in expectation. The same root is used for the waiting period after a separation, so the vocabulary of this whole section is built around suspended time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman in that position had no way out. She could not remarry, her family could not press the matter, and she had no income of her own. An indefinite vow left her in a state that could last years, and it was a known instrument of pressure inside a marriage. Setting a fixed limit turned a permanent condition into a bounded one with a required outcome.
studies.didYouKnow: These three short ayat close with three pairs of divine names in a row: forgiving and forbearing, forgiving and merciful, hearing and knowing. The last pair arrives at the moment a separation is decided. The classical commentaries note that hearing is named there, rather than any word about judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Blame sits in what was actually resolved, not in what was said. That is a claim about how a person is read. Words spoken carelessly do not create duties; the heart's intention does. Then the passage takes an open-ended cruelty and puts a clock on it. What had no end becomes finite, and both possible endings are named without either being condemned.

crossReferences.why: Precedes this directly, naming the misuse of an oath that these ayat then take apart.
Draws the same distinction between idle oaths and deliberate ones, and sets out what follows.
Applies the same principle to an honest mistake, holding a person only to what the heart intended.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between something you said and something you meant, in one conversation this week. Most of our speech is the first kind, and this ayah says it is not being counted against us. Then find the one thing you did mean and have not acted on. That is the part the ayah is actually interested in.
studies.explainEasier: God does not hold you to words you say without thinking. He holds you to what your heart really meant. A man who swears off his wife has four months. Then he either goes back to her or the marriage ends.

studies.title: What God Created In The Womb
studies.meaning: A waiting period is set. Then the most striking clause arrives: what is in the womb may not be hidden. The ayah puts that in terms of belief rather than of procedure, which makes honesty here a matter of faith. Then rights are described as running both ways, in a phrase the early scholars discuss closely. The closing word about a degree is read in more than one way across the classical works.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's passage on divorce. Before this, what happened afterwards was set by custom. It was set by whichever family had more standing. A pregnancy decided who inherited, whose line a child joined, and what the child could claim. So hiding one could change a family's future. The early scholars read the clause about honesty against that. Telling the truth often went against what a woman or her family wanted at the time.

keyTerms.note: A word carrying two opposite senses in Arabic, covering both a monthly period and the interval between them. The classical commentators record both readings, and the difference affects the length of the waiting.

keyTerms.gloss: in what is recognised as right
keyTerms.note: Literally what is known, meaning conduct a community would recognise as decent. The phrase recurs throughout this section, tying the standard to something people can see rather than to a fixed list.

The word for a step or a rank. The classical commentators read it in more than one way, most often of the husband's responsibility for maintenance or of his standing in the matter of return, and they record the range.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A separation in Medina reordered a woman's whole position. It decided where she lived and who supported her. It decided whether she could remarry, and what her children could claim. All of it was settled in front of families with their own interests. A waiting period created a fixed stretch in which nothing could be rushed. It gave a pregnancy time to become known before arrangements were fixed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the waiting period belongs to a small class of Arabic words that carry two opposite meanings. The classical commentaries record both readings without one pushing out the other. The clause about not hiding a pregnancy is stated as a matter of believing in God and the Last Day. It is not stated as a rule of procedure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is placed at the exact point where hiding something would be most useful. It is also the point where nobody could catch it. The ayah answers that by tying the telling to belief rather than to enforcement. That is a pattern the Quran uses again and again. Where checking fails, the standard is raised rather than lowered. The description of rights as running both ways then sets a floor the passage works within.

crossReferences.why: Opens a later surah on the same subject and repeats the concern with counting the period carefully.
Continues directly, setting limits on what may be taken back and calling them the limits of God.
Addresses the same relation and states that women are not to be inherited against their will.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing you know and have not mentioned because mentioning it would cost you something and nobody would ever find out. That is the exact situation this ayah describes. You do not have to announce it publicly. Just tell the one person whose decision actually depends on it.
studies.explainEasier: A woman who has been divorced waits for three cycles. She should not hide it if she is carrying a child. Women have rights just as men do, in a fair way.

studies.title: Retention Or Release, Both Kindly
studies.meaning: A count is set on how far a separation can be reversed. Each stage is given two possible endings, named with the same weight. One is keeping the arrangement decently. The other is releasing it with kindness. The two are set out as equal options, not as a good outcome and a failure. Then a narrow exception is described about what may be returned. The passage closes by naming limits.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources describe a practice in which a man could separate and take back again and again, with no limit. That kept a woman suspended with no end in sight. They report that this ayah set the count. The reports are widely recorded. The passage sits in a long stretch of the surah working through the arrangements a separation produces.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of turning livestock loose to pasture in the morning. The image is of release into open ground rather than of expulsion, and the word carries none of the harshness the English can.
The noun from the verb meaning to do something well and beautifully. Attaching it to the release rather than to the retention puts the higher of the two standards on the harder option.
The word names a boundary line around a piece of ground. The passage repeatedly asks that people stay inside rather than test the edge, and the phrase built on it dominates this whole section.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Repeated separation and return was a known way of controlling a woman without letting her go. She could not remarry. Her family could not step in. The cycle could run for years. Everyone in Medina would have known of a case. Setting a number turned an open loop into something with an end, and the counting is what made the difference.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the limits of God appears four times within this single ayah. That is more than in any other ayah of the Quran. Both of the endings offered are named with a positive word, one about decency and one about kindness. So the language does not mark the separation as the worse outcome.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending something well is treated as an achievement, not as a failure to keep going. The passage gives release its own standard. The warmer of the two words is attached to it, which changes what a person aims at when a relationship ends. The repeated language of limits then frames the whole thing as a marked-out space. Both parties are standing inside it together.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair of options and warns against holding on in order to cause harm.
Uses the same two options in a later surah and adds the calling of two just witnesses.
States that if the two do separate, God will enrich each of them out of His abundance.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are ending or have ended: a job, a friendship, a project. This ayah gives the ending its own standard and uses the warmer of its two words for it. Ask what a good ending would look like in your case, and do one part of it this week rather than letting the thing trail off.
studies.explainEasier: A man can take his wife back after a divorce twice. After that, he either keeps her in a kind way or lets her go in a kind way. He cannot take back gifts he gave her.

studies.title: A Door That Does Not Reopen Easily
studies.meaning: A limit is described that closes the loop the previous ayah opened. After a final separation the arrangement cannot simply be picked up again. The condition stated makes an immediate reversal impossible. A return becomes possible again only under a further condition. The two of them have to think they can keep within the limits. The ayah ends by saying these boundaries are made clear to people who know.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing straight on from the ayah that set the count. The early scholars describe the effect rather than debating the purpose. What had been a reversible cycle becomes final at a set point. The classical works discuss the details of this ayah at length, and much of that discussion belongs to legal writing rather than to a study note.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for entering a marriage. Its use here is what makes the condition substantial, since what is described is a genuine second arrangement rather than a formality arranged for the purpose.

A verb sitting between thinking and being fairly sure, short of certainty. The condition asks for a reasonable expectation rather than a guarantee, which the commentators note as realistic about what anyone can know.

keyTerms.gloss: the two return to each other
keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form, so both parties return rather than one taking the other back. The grammar makes the reunion mutual, which is not how such arrangements had worked in practice before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Words spoken in anger were binding in Arabia. A man could dissolve a marriage in a moment. He could reverse it the next week. Households lived close together, so quarrels were public. The making up was done in front of everyone. A limit that made the third separation final put a cost on a sentence that had been cheap to say.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah closes a passage in which the phrase about the limits of God appears again and again across several ayat. It ends with the words for people who know. That is one of several closing formulas in this section. Each names a different faculty: those who know, those who believe, and those with understanding.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A boundary is placed where reversal would otherwise be unlimited. The effect is to make an easy word expensive. That says something about how the passage understands people. What can be undone cheaply will be done carelessly. The mutual form of the verb for reunion then quietly changes the shape of the arrangement. The return now needs both of them, not one.

crossReferences.why: Sets the count that this ayah completes, and introduces the language of limits it uses.
Continues the passage, addressing pressure applied after a separation has already been made.
Opens a later surah on the same subject and asks that the counting be done carefully.

studies.applyIt: Notice a sentence you say easily when you are angry, and that you then have to take back. This passage works by making a cheap word expensive, which is a strategy rather than a scolding. Choose one such phrase and take it out of your vocabulary for a month. The cost will land somewhere better.
studies.explainEasier: If a man divorces his wife a third time, he cannot just take her back. She would first have to marry someone else, and that marriage would have to end on its own. These are the lines God has drawn.

studies.title: Do Not Hold On To Cause Harm
studies.meaning: The two options return, and this time both are named with the same word, so neither is presented as the better. Then the specific abuse is named: holding on in order to cause harm. The ayah calls that wronging yourself rather than wronging her, which is a deliberate reversal. It closes by recalling what was given and warning against treating revelations as a plaything.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that some men would take a woman back near the end of the waiting period and separate again. That restarted the count, purely to stretch out the suspension. The ayah names that use of the arrangement directly. The early scholars read the warning about treating revelations lightly as aimed at exactly that trick.

keyTerms.note: A form describing mutual or deliberate harm, from the root for damage. Placed as the purpose of the holding on, it names the intention rather than the act, so the same action is right or wrong by what it is for.

The passage does not say he wronged her, which the commentators notice. The construction turns the harm back on the person doing it, a move the Quran uses repeatedly for wrongs committed against others.
The word for something taken as a joke or a toy. Used of revelations, it names the treatment of a protective arrangement as a device, which is a specific kind of contempt rather than open rejection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The waiting period was a woman's protection: a fixed stretch after which she was free. Restarting it again and again turned that protection into a cage. There was no authority she could appeal to. Her family could argue, but the man held the procedure. Naming this in revelation gave the situation a public description it had not had before. That is often the first thing that changes anything.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names three things in sequence at its close: God's favour, the Book, and wisdom, all as things sent down to teach. The same three appear together earlier in this surah in the description of what a messenger does among people. Here they arrive at the end of a warning about manipulating a procedure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The wrong sits in the intention, not in the action. Taking someone back is otherwise exactly what the passage encourages. So the same conduct is right or wrong by what it is for. That is a demanding standard, and one nobody can enforce. And by saying the man wronged himself, the ayah refuses to leave the injury as only the victim's problem.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same two options and the language of limits that this ayah returns to.
Warns against coercion undertaken in order to take back part of what was already given.
Repeats the instruction not to cause hardship in order to constrain someone's choices.

studies.applyIt: Ask what one of your ongoing commitments is actually for. Not what it was for originally, what it is doing now. This ayah judges an identical action by its purpose, which means the audit has to be internal. If you find something you are holding on to in order to make a point, let it go this week.
studies.explainEasier: When the waiting time is nearly over, either keep your wife in a kind way or let her go in a kind way. Do not hold on to her just to hurt her. Anyone who does that only hurts himself.

studies.title: Do Not Stand In Their Way
studies.meaning: The address turns from the two people involved to everyone around them. When a waiting period has run and both parties want to resume, the surrounding family is told not to obstruct it. The verb used describes preventing something by force of position rather than by argument. The ayah ends with a comparative, that this is purer for you, and then plainly: God knows and you do not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report a case in which a man's sister had separated and then wished to return to her husband. Her brother refused, out of anger on her behalf. They report this ayah as the answer. Accounts differ in detail across the works, but the situation described is consistent: a relative blocking a reconciliation both parties wanted.

keyTerms.note: An uncommon verb describing obstruction by someone who has the power to obstruct, and used of a difficult birth. It names blocking rather than advising, and its rarity gives the instruction a precise target.

A reciprocal form of the verb for being pleased, so agreement on both sides is written into the word itself. The condition is that the two are content, which is what makes the outside objection an intrusion.

A comparative from the root that joins cleansing and growth, used earlier in this surah for what a messenger does. Naming the outcome as purer answers the objectors in the terms they cared about, which was honour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage was a family matter, and a brother or father spoke for a woman in the talks. When a marriage failed, the family that had given her felt the insult. Letting her return could look like accepting shame. Honour was a real currency, and refusing was the respectable choice. That is the pressure this ayah is speaking into.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction here is addressed in the plural to the people around the couple, rather than to either of them. That is unusual within this passage. The ayah closes with two comparatives in a row, purer and more decent. Then comes a short clause saying that God knows and you do not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Third parties are named as a real obstacle. That is an honest observation about how relationships actually end. Family honour is not argued with. The ayah simply sets out a different measure of what is cleaner. And the closing sentence puts a limit on the objectors' confidence. The outcome they are guarding against is one they cannot see.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same kind of obstruction from those holding power over a woman's arrangements.
Handles the mirror case, where the husband rather than the family is the one causing harm.
Warns against acting on suspicion, which is usually the material an objection like this is made of.

studies.applyIt: Think of a reconciliation between two other people that you are, quietly, not helping along. Perhaps you heard the story from one side and took it up. This ayah addresses the bystanders, not the couple. Step back once this week from a dispute that is not yours, and say nothing where you would usually add something.
studies.explainEasier: When two people who have divorced both want to get back together, their families should not block them. It is cleaner and better that way. God knows things that you do not know.

studies.title: Neither Parent Harmed Through The Child
studies.meaning: A period is named for nursing. Everything else in the ayah is about protecting the people inside the arrangement. The father provides. Nobody is burdened beyond capacity. Neither parent is to be harmed through the child. The same duty passes to an heir. Weaning earlier is cleared if both agree after talking it through. Hiring a nurse is cleared if payment is fair.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage on separation. Nursing arrangements were exactly what became contested when a household split. In Arabia, infants were often nursed by women other than their mothers. That created lasting bonds, recognised as a form of kinship. The ayah addresses a situation the community faced constantly rather than a rare one.

keyTerms.note: A dual form with an adjective for completeness attached to it. The precision is the point: naming a full term gives both parents something fixed to measure an agreement against rather than a matter of opinion.
A form that carries both harming and being harmed, so the clause covers each parent using the child against the other. Arabic lets a single word do what English needs two separate clauses for.

A reciprocal noun from a root connected to drawing out honey, and so to drawing out an opinion. Requiring consultation alongside agreement means the decision has to be talked through, not merely conceded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nursing was a serious economic arrangement. A wet nurse was paid, and Meccan families often sent infants to be nursed among the desert tribes for the health of the child and the language it would learn. A nursing woman had a claim on the household. When a marriage ended, the question of who paid for what was immediate and could turn bitter quickly.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about no soul being burdened beyond its capacity appears here. It sits in the middle of a passage about nursing. It returns in almost the same words at the very end of the surah, inside the closing prayer. The same principle is stated once as a practical point and once as the ground of a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The whole ayah is arranged around stopping a child from becoming a tool. Both parents are protected by the same clause, in the same word. That refuses to blame either of them in advance. And the call for talking it through makes the decision joint, even after the relationship has ended. A form of partnership stays alive past the point where everything else has been divided.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause about capacity at the very end of the surah, there inside a prayer.
Recalls a mother's carrying and her weaning over two years as grounds for gratitude.
Repeats the instruction about payment for nursing and about consulting one another properly.

studies.applyIt: If you share a responsibility with someone you no longer get on with, look at how decisions get made between you. This ayah asks for agreement and for talking it through. Those are two different things. Do the second one this week. Ask before you decide, even where you could decide alone.
studies.explainEasier: Mothers may feed their babies for two full years. The father pays for the mother's food and clothes in a fair way. No one is asked for more than they can give. Neither parent should be hurt through the child.

studies.title: Four Months And Ten
studies.meaning: A period is set for a widow, and its length is stated oddly precisely: four months and ten. Then the sentence releases her. When the term has run, no blame attaches to anyone for what she does with herself within what is recognised as decent. The clause is addressed to the community rather than to her, which is where the pressure in such situations actually comes from.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before this, a widow in Arabia could be held in mourning for a full year, secluded and set apart, in a custom the classical sources describe as severe. The passage that follows a few ayat later refers to a year of support, and the commentators discuss the relation between the two at length. What is agreed is that a long confinement was shortened.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb from a root meaning to receive something in full. Death is described as a soul being collected rather than as an ending, and the passive leaves the one collecting unnamed in the sentence.

A reflexive form: the women hold themselves in waiting rather than being held by anyone. The same verb is used earlier in this section for a different waiting, so agency stays with the person waiting.
A name of God for one who knows the inside of a matter, from a root connected to testing soil by ploughing it. It closes a sentence about what people around a widow might do or say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A widow's mourning in Arabia before Islam could mean a year in a small hut. She wore the worst clothes she had and touched no perfume. The sources describe the ritual that ended it in unpleasant detail. Neighbours watched and enforced it. A woman's family had a stake in how long she was seen to grieve, since her conduct reflected on them.
studies.didYouKnow: The period given here is four months and ten, not five months, and the classical commentaries note the precision. The clause releasing people from blame is addressed in the masculine plural. So it speaks to those around the widow rather than to her. That is where objections to a woman remarrying actually started.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit on grief is set in both directions. There is a period, so a bereavement is given real time and is not rushed; and the period ends, so nobody may extend it on her behalf. The release is phrased as removing blame from onlookers, which quietly names the actual obstacle. And the closing name for God is one about knowing the inside of things.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same situation a few ayat later, with a year of support and no eviction.
Continues directly, handling what may and may not be said during such a period.
Sets out waiting periods for other circumstances, and promises ease to whoever is mindful of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are keeping someone else's grief on your own timetable: expecting them to be over it, or expecting them not to be. This ayah sets a period and then ends it, and it speaks to the onlookers rather than to the bereaved. Ask the person what they want rather than deciding for them.
studies.explainEasier: When a man dies, his widow waits four months and ten days. After that time is over, she is free to do what she wants in a decent way. Nobody should blame her for it.

studies.title: What You Keep Inside You
studies.meaning: A narrow space is described with unusual care. During a waiting period, an indirect hint of interest is cleared. So is keeping the interest entirely to yourself. Then a line is drawn. There are to be no private promises, and no closing of the arrangement until the term has run. Between the permissions and the limit sits a sentence granting the obvious. People will be thinking about each other.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing from the ayah on a widow's waiting period. The early scholars explain the situation in practical terms. A woman in that period would receive interest, and the question was what could be said. It had to avoid pressuring her or settling the matter before the term ran out. The passage answers by separating indirect speech from a promise, rather than by banning contact.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for approaching a subject from the side rather than head on. The word names indirect speech precisely, and the ayah's whole distinction rests on the difference between hinting and undertaking.
From a root meaning to shelter or house something, which gives the words for a cupboard and for a covering. What is described is not hiding a wrong but keeping a thought in its proper enclosure.
The word for a knot tied in a rope. Marriage is named by that image throughout this section, so what is postponed is the tying itself rather than the intention that precedes it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in a Medinan neighbourhood was known. A visit was noticed. A conversation at a doorway was reported. A woman without a husband was watched more closely than anyone. A widow with property or standing would attract approaches at once, some from men her family had reason to prefer. The line this ayah draws was a real protection from being tied down before she was ready.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah concedes what people will be thinking before it sets any limit, using a clause that begins with God knowing. That order recurs across this section of the surah, where the difficulty is often named before the instruction. Two names of God close the ayah, one about forgiveness and one about forbearance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A thought is separated from a commitment, and only the second is restricted. That is a specific view of the inner life: what passes through a person is not held against them, and the line falls at what they do with it. Then the sentence about God knowing what is inside a person is placed on the other side, so the concession does not become licence. Both halves are needed.

crossReferences.why: Sets the waiting period whose conduct this ayah then describes in detail.
Draws the same line between what is said carelessly and what the heart has actually resolved.
States in one short line that God knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret.

studies.applyIt: Notice a thought you have been treating as a failing simply because you had it. This ayah clears the thought and draws its line at the commitment. Try separating the two this week: let the thought be there without arguing with it, and watch what you actually do next. That second part is what is being asked about.
studies.explainEasier: While a woman is waiting, a man may hint that he is interested. He may also keep it to himself. But he should not make any secret promise, and nothing is settled until the waiting time is over.

studies.title: According To His Means
studies.meaning: A situation is described where nothing was owed and nothing had been settled, and the ayah still asks for something to be given. The amount is not fixed; it is scaled twice, once for the person with room and once for the person without, using the same word for both. That word means capacity rather than obligation. The closing phrase attaches the whole thing to those who do good.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the run of ayat on the arrangements a separation produces. In Arabia a woman leaving a marriage that had barely begun would have nothing. No custom required anything to be given. The early scholars read this ayah as creating a provision where none had existed. They note that it is framed as a due upon those who do good, not as a claim anyone could enforce.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for what is enjoyed and made use of, which also gives the noun for goods and provisions. It asks for something usable rather than a token, and the root recurs across this section.
