studies.theologicalSignificance: Charity is measured here by its effect on the person receiving it, not by the cost to the giver. That reverses the usual accounting. The ayah also puts speech inside the category of charitable acts. So a decent refusal can outrank a grudging gift. The two names of God at the close ground the ethic in His own conduct. He needs nothing and is not in a hurry, and that is what the giver is being asked to be.

crossReferences.why: Shows what the alternative destroys, comparing spoilt charity to soil stripped from a rock.
Instructs a gentle word when you have nothing to give and must turn someone away.
Pairs the provision of the vulnerable with speaking to them kindly, as a single obligation.

studies.applyIt: The next time you cannot give someone what they ask for, spend the thirty seconds you would have spent apologising on something warm and specific instead. Then say nothing about it afterwards. This ayah claims that exchange is worth more than money handed over with a sigh. It is one of the few claims here you can test directly on someone's face.
studies.explainEasier: A kind word, and letting something go, is worth more than money you give and then throw back in someone's face. God is rich. He does not need your money.

studies.title: Rain On A Bare Rock
studies.meaning: A warning is given about what can undo a gift after it has been made: a reminder of the favour, and a wounding word. The comparison that follows makes the point physical. A smooth stone with a layer of soil on it looks like ground until rain arrives, and then it is bare again. What is lost is not the reward alone but the appearance that anything was ever there.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the long passage on giving that runs through this part of the surah. Early scholars read the two failings named as the ordinary pull on a generous person. They are not the faults of an obvious hypocrite. The scholars note that the ayah speaks to believers. The parable in the next ayah is its exact counterpart.

keyTerms.note: From a root for conferring a benefit, which in this form means holding it over someone afterwards. Arabic uses the same root for genuine grace, so the word marks the point where giving turns into a claim.
A slab of bare stone with nothing to hold water. The word is chosen for its surface: soil sits on it convincingly and nothing can root in it, which is the whole comparison in a single image.
An uncommon word for a surface left clean and hard. It is the last word of the image, and it describes not damage but exposure, which is what the parable is actually about.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In that country a sudden downpour was the most testing thing that happened to land. Soil that had blown across rock looked exactly like a field until it rained, and then a farmer discovered what he had. Anyone who had planted in the wrong place knew that discovery. Rain, which everywhere else in the Quran is a mercy, is here the thing that reveals.
studies.didYouKnow: The same word for a downpour appears in this ayah and in the next. Once it strips a surface bare. Once it doubles a garden's crop. The surah sets two parables side by side using the same element. So the difference between them lies entirely in what the rain lands on, not in what arrives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A finished good deed is described as something that can be undone. That is a demanding idea. What undoes it is not a later sin but words spoken about the deed itself. So the giving and the talking about it count as one act stretched over time. The comparison with someone giving to be seen suggests both failings work the same way. In both, the audience has become the point.

crossReferences.why: States the same condition positively: those who do not follow their giving with reminders or hurt.
Gives the matching parable, where the same downpour doubles a garden's produce instead.
Describes those who spend to be seen by people, and pairs it with not believing.

studies.applyIt: Think of a favour you have mentioned more than once to the person who received it. Once is a story; twice is a bill. This ayah is unusually specific about how that undoes the thing. Choose one such favour and decide, deliberately, never to mention it again, then notice how quickly the impulse comes back.
studies.explainEasier: When you give something away, do not spoil it by reminding the person or saying hurtful things. That is like rain washing thin soil off a rock. Nothing is left, and the giver gains nothing.

studies.title: And If Not, Then Dew
studies.meaning: The counterpart parable arrives, and its terms are the same but the outcome inverted. A garden on high ground receives the same downpour and doubles its yield. Then the sentence adds something the first parable had no need of: if the heavy rain does not come, dew is enough. The comparison is not between success and failure but between soil and stone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage on giving. Early scholars note that this ayah names two motives together: seeking God's approval, and strengthening one's own soul. They read the second as the settling that giving produces in the giver. The pairing with the earlier parable is deliberate, since both turn on the same word for the rain that falls.

keyTerms.note: The noun comes from the verb for making something firm, used in the prayer for steady feet earlier in this surah. Giving is described as producing that firmness rather than only expressing it.

keyTerms.gloss: on a rise, on high ground
keyTerms.note: Elevated land, which drains well and catches both rain and dew. The detail is agricultural: a garden placed there is well sited, so the parable's outcome follows from the ground it stands on.
The gentlest form of moisture, what settles overnight without a cloud. Naming it as sufficient changes the parable's claim: good ground does not depend on abundance, only on being what it is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gardens in Arabia were built where water could be managed: on terraces, near a spring, above the flood line. Dew mattered more than a traveller might expect. In some seasons it was all the water a crop got, and farmers built low walls to catch it. The parable's detail about high ground would have read as skill rather than luck.
studies.didYouKnow: The two parables share the same word for a heavy downpour. The difference between them lies entirely in what receives it. This one adds a second, lighter kind of rain that the other has no use for. So the passage ends with the good ground bearing fruit in plenty and in want alike.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The measure of a gift is placed in the giver, not in the amount. A garden on good ground bears fruit in a downpour and bears fruit in dew. That cuts the outcome loose from whatever weather happens to arrive. And by naming an inward strengthening as one of the two motives, the passage treats giving as something that shapes the giver, not only a moving of wealth.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching parable, where the same downpour leaves bare stone behind it.
Opens this passage with the image of a grain producing seven ears of a hundred grains each.
Uses another agricultural image for a good word, a tree yielding its fruit in every season.

studies.applyIt: Give something small this week in a season when you feel you have nothing to give. Not the large gesture when things are going well. This parable's point is that good ground produces in dew as well as in downpour, and the only way to find out which ground you are is to try it when the weather is poor.
studies.explainEasier: People who give to please God are like a garden up on a hillside. Heavy rain makes it grow twice as much. And if the heavy rain does not come, a little dew is enough.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Garden Burned In Old Age
studies.meaning: A question is put rather than a statement made, and it is meant to be answered from inside. Would any of you want this: a garden of palms and vines, every kind of fruit, rivers underneath. Then old age arrives, and weak children, and a fiery whirlwind takes it. The details are stacked so the loss lands at the worst moment, when nothing can be rebuilt.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the run of parables about giving. The classical commentaries record a report that a companion was asked what this ayah meant. He tied it to a man whose deeds were undone at the end of his life. Early scholars mostly read it against the warning just before it, about reminders and hurtful words, rather than as a separate subject.

keyTerms.note: The verb is one of affection and wishing rather than of choosing. Putting the parable as a question in this form invites the listener to answer from feeling before any reasoning arrives.

Literally largeness, used of age as the accumulation of years. Its arrival in the sentence is what makes the loss final, since the same disaster earlier in a life would be a setback rather than an ending.
A wind that turns on itself and lifts what it passes over. The word occurs only here in the Quran, and the fire inside it makes the image specific rather than a general storm.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A garden of palms and vines was the work of decades. Palms take years to bear, irrigation channels are dug and maintained by hand, and a man planted for a son as much as for himself. Fire in a dry palm grove moves faster than anyone can run. Everything in this parable would have been familiar, including the particular horror of losing it late.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the whirlwind in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The parable is built entirely from good things: a garden, fruit, children, long life. The disaster arrives only in the last clause. So a listener has fully pictured owning it before losing it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues by imagination rather than by assertion. Nothing is claimed; a scene is built and the listener is asked whether they would want it. That works because the answer is obvious and the application is not. Placing the parable after the warnings about undoing a gift suggests that a lifetime of good can be arranged so that it is not there at the end.

crossReferences.why: Names the two things that undo a gift, which this parable then dramatises as total loss.
Tells a longer version of the same scene, a garden destroyed and its owner left with nothing.
Describes a garden's owners who planned to withhold its harvest and found it stripped by morning.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are building that could still be undone at the end. Not by disaster, by your own hand. This parable is placed immediately after a warning about spoiling a gift by talking about it. Look at one thing you have built and check whether the way you speak about it is quietly burning it down.
studies.explainEasier: Picture a man with a lovely garden full of fruit. He is old now, and his children are still small. Then a burning wind hits the garden and it all burns down. God asks if anyone would want that.

studies.title: What You Would Not Take Yourself
studies.meaning: Two sources are named for what is given: what you have earned and what the earth produced for you. Then the instruction narrows to quality. Do not aim at the poor part of it, and the reason given is a test anyone can apply, since you would not accept this yourself except with your eyes shut. The ayah closes with two names of God about sufficiency and praise.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage on giving. The classical sources report that some people brought the poorest of their dates to be handed out. They report that this ayah spoke to that practice. The commentaries note that the giving named here covers both trade income and the produce of land. Between them those two covered nearly every household in Medina.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to head for something on purpose. It names a choice rather than an oversight, so what is described is someone selecting the poor portion rather than simply giving carelessly.
The direct opposite of the word for wholesome used at the start of the same ayah. Placing the two in one sentence sets a scale, and the giving described sits at the wrong end of it.
A verb for closing the eyes, used of overlooking a fault in a transaction. It names the exact behaviour of a buyer accepting poor goods to end a negotiation, which is the standard the ayah applies.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date harvests were sorted with care. The best fruit was kept or sold. The middling was eaten. The poorest was dried hard and fed to animals, or held back for lean months. Everyone in Medina could grade dates by sight. Bringing the lowest grade to a public handout was plain to everybody there. The ayah names something people could watch happening.
studies.didYouKnow: The test the ayah offers is a buyer's test, not a moral one: would you take this in a trade. The word for shutting the eyes belongs to the language of a market deal. So the standard for giving is set by what a person would accept in a bargain, not by what they think is generous.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard runs itself. The ayah does not fix a level of quality. It asks a person to use the judgement they already use when they are the one receiving, and nobody can be wrong about that. The closing names then remove the obvious objection. The one it is offered to does not need the gift. So its quality is entirely about the giver.

crossReferences.why: States that virtuous conduct is not attained until you give from what you cherish.
Names another way a gift is spoiled, there by what is said afterwards rather than by what is given.
Describes the one who gives and is mindful, and the ease that is made for him afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you last donated: the clothes, the food, the furniture. Ask honestly whether you would have accepted it. Not whether it was usable, whether you would have taken it. If the answer is no, give one thing this month that you would actually have wanted, and notice how differently it feels.
studies.explainEasier: Give away good things from what you have earned and from what grows on your land. Do not hand over the worst of it. You would not take that yourself unless you shut your eyes to it.

studies.title: Two Promises, Two Directions
studies.meaning: Two voices are set against each other, and each one makes a promise. One promises poverty and pushes you toward indecency. The other promises forgiveness and plenty. The match is exact, and that is the point, since both work by what you expect. Then the second ayah turns to wisdom. It is given to whom God wills, and having it is called much good.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage on giving, where fear of running short was the real obstacle. Early scholars read the first ayah as naming that fear exactly and saying where it comes from. They note that the promise on the other side is not of wealth, but of forgiveness and favour. The second ayah widens the subject and closes the passage's argument.

keyTerms.note: The same verb is used of both sides, which is the ayah's structure in a single word. Arabic uses it for a promise and, with a different construction, for a threat, so the doubling here is exact and deliberate.

From a root connected to a broken spine, so the word names being unable to stand rather than merely having little. What is promised is not modest means but collapse, which is why it works as a deterrent.
From a root meaning to restrain, as a bridle restrains a horse. Naming it here, straight after a contrast between two promises, suggests wisdom is what lets a person tell one from the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poverty in Arabia was not an idea but a set order of losses. The animals go first. Then the stored dates. Then the land. Then a family lives off its relatives. Everyone had watched it happen to someone. A man weighing whether to give away part of his stores was counting against that order, and the counting was reasonable.
studies.didYouKnow: The same verb is used for both promises in the first ayah, so the sentence is built as a matched pair. The second ayah closes with a phrase about those with insight that turns up across this surah. The word it uses for wisdom appeared earlier, in the description of what a messenger teaches a community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear of running short is not brushed off as foolish. It is given a source and set beside another expectation. That treats the sum as real and asks which forecast you are working from. And what is offered on the other side is not a promise of wealth, which would answer fear on its own terms. It is forgiveness and favour, which changes the terms instead.

crossReferences.why: Names another failure in giving, there in what is said afterwards rather than in what is feared.
States that whatever you spend, He will replace it, addressing the same fear directly.
Names the same fear of poverty in another setting, and answers it with a statement about provision.

studies.applyIt: Notice the sentence your mind says when you are about to give something away and hesitate. Write it down in the exact words it uses. This ayah says that sentence is a promise being made to you by something. Reading it back in that form is usually enough to see it for what it is.
studies.explainEasier: One voice tells you that giving will leave you poor, and pushes you to do bad things. God promises the opposite: he will forgive you and give you plenty. He also gives wisdom to whoever he chooses.

studies.title: The Case For Giving Quietly
studies.meaning: The first line says that nothing given or pledged escapes God's knowledge. That sets up the second. Public giving is called good, with no qualification. Then private giving to the needy is called better for you. The comparison is not between right and wrong but between good and better. The reason given is the effect on the giver, not on the person receiving. Hidden giving is said to cover over some of your own failings.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines sit in the long section on spending that runs through the middle of it. The community was raising funds openly for emigrants and expeditions, so public giving was both necessary and easy to see. Early scholars note that the passage does not discourage the public appeal it sits inside. It adds a second track alongside it. No single occasion is agreed for these two lines.

keyTerms.note: A binding promise to God to do something, often conditional on an outcome. Listing it beside ordinary charity brings private undertakings nobody witnessed into the same account as public ones.
Shares a root with the word for truthfulness. The connection is deliberate in Arabic: giving is treated as evidence that a stated commitment is genuine rather than as a separate virtue.
From a root meaning to conceal, the same root that gives the word for denial of faith. Here the covering is God's, hiding a person's failings in the way the giver hid the gift.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving in a town like Medina was almost impossible to hide. Households were close, markets were small, and a sack of dates arriving at a poor family's door would be noticed and talked about. Hiding it therefore took effort. You sent a gift at night, or through a third person who would not name the source. Reports from the period describe both methods, which suggests the instruction was taken practically, not as an ideal.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for covering over the giver's failings is built on the same three letters as the Quran's word for rejecting faith. That word literally means to bury or hide something. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect the two senses through farming: a sower covers seed with soil. The same image sits behind the early Arabic word for a farmer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses the simple rule that hidden charity always wins. It calls the public act good in its own right. That protects communal fundraising from suspicion. It then puts the advantage of secrecy in what it does to the giver, not in the receiver's dignity. The ayat around it handle that separately. God's knowledge is the premise for both. Since nothing is unseen, there is no audience worth performing for.

crossReferences.why: Widens the same point across every setting, spending by night and day, secretly and openly.
States that God is the one who receives charity, which is why the human audience is optional.
Shows giving done wanting neither reward nor thanks from those who receive it.

studies.applyIt: Give something this month that nobody will ever know about, including the person receiving it if you can manage it. Do not tell your family, and do not record it anywhere someone might read. Notice the small urge to mention it, and let it pass unspoken. That urge is precisely what this passage is offering to relieve you of.
studies.explainEasier: God knows every gift you give and every promise you make. Giving in the open is good. Giving quietly, so nobody sees, is even better for you. It helps wipe away some of your bad deeds.

studies.title: Their Guidance Is Not On You
studies.meaning: A burden is lifted before anything else is said. Their guidance is not on you. Early scholars read that against a reluctance to give to people outside the community. Then three statements about spending follow, each starting the same way. What you give is for yourselves. It is sought only for the face of God. It will be repaid in full. The reason for giving moves entirely to the giver.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that some held back from giving to relatives and neighbours who had not joined the community. They hoped that holding back would apply pressure. Those sources report this ayah as the answer. The accounts are widely recorded, though the details differ. The opening clause speaks to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and through him to the practice itself.

keyTerms.note: A phrase of removal: something is being taken off a person rather than added to them. Placing it first means the instruction that follows arrives after the weight has already been lifted.
An idiom for the direction and purpose of an act rather than a description of God. Seeking a person's face in Arabic means seeking them specifically, so the phrase names an undivided aim.
A passive verb from the root for completeness, the same one used of a soul taken in death. It describes a measure filled exactly, and the closing clause rules out any shortfall in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Charity in Medina was local and personal. You gave to the family two doors down, to a cousin, to someone you saw every day. Giving was one of the few levers an ordinary person had. Holding it back from a relative who had not joined the community was an obvious use of that lever. It would have felt principled rather than mean.
studies.didYouKnow: Three clauses in this ayah start with the same wording about whatever you spend, one after another. Each ends differently: for yourselves, for the face of God, and repaid in full. The repeat is one of the passage's clearest cases of a shape the surah uses to build an argument by piling up.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Blame for another person's guidance is lifted, and that stops giving from being used as a tool. Once the outcome is not yours, the giving can only be about the giving. That is why the three clauses that follow all turn back toward the giver. What is spent is described as coming back to the one who spent it. It is never a lever pressed on anyone else.

crossReferences.why: States that there is no compulsion in religion, which this ayah applies to the use of generosity.
Asks whether people would be compelled into belief, and answers that God's will decides it.
Describes feeding the needy and the captive for God's sake alone, wanting neither payment nor thanks.

studies.applyIt: Find one place where you give something with a condition you have not admitted to: attention, money, time, help. This ayah takes the outcome out of the giver's account. Try one act of giving this week where you drop any stake in what it produces.
studies.explainEasier: It is not your job to make other people believe. God guides who he wants. Whatever you give away helps you, and you give it to please God. You will get every bit of it back.

studies.title: You Would Know Them By Their Look
studies.meaning: The recipients of the giving described in the previous ayat are identified, and the description is unusual in that it is almost entirely about what they do not do. They cannot travel to earn. Someone who did not know would take them for people of means, because of their restraint. And they do not press people with their asking. The recognition is left to a look.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars identify these with a group of poor emigrants who had left everything behind. They could not travel for trade, and stayed near the mosque in Medina. The reports differ over the details and agree on the situation. The ayah stands at the end of the long passage on giving, naming who it had been describing all along.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form from the root for chastity and abstaining. It names the effort of holding back rather than a natural reticence, so the dignity described is being achieved rather than simply possessed.
The word for a distinguishing sign, used of a mark placed on livestock. Here it names something readable in a face and a bearing, which the ayah says is available to anyone paying attention.
From a root for wrapping something around, as a cloak is wrapped. Asking in this manner means clinging to a person until they give, which is exactly what these people are described as not doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade was how a person without land made a living, and trade meant travelling. A season with a caravan, a market in another town, a share in someone's goods. A man who could not travel had almost no way to earn. The emigrants in Medina included men who had been merchants in Mecca. Now they had no money to trade with and no way to move. Their poverty was hidden by design.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names its recipients almost entirely by what is not true of them. They cannot travel. They are taken for rich. They do not ask over and over. The only positive mark given is something in how they look. The classical commentaries note that the work of noticing falls on the giver, not on the person in need.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Need is described as something that has to be looked for. The people named are precisely those who will not present themselves, which means the giving asked for requires attention before it requires money. That inverts the usual arrangement, in which help goes to whoever asks loudest. And the restraint of the poor is treated as a quality rather than as an obstacle to be overcome.

crossReferences.why: Discusses giving openly and secretly, in the passage that leads directly into this description.
Names the categories to whom the obligatory charity belongs, in a later Medinan surah.
Describes the poor emigrants driven from their homes and property, seeking favour from God.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know whose situation you have never asked about, because they never bring it up. This ayah describes people who look fine on purpose. Ask one specific question this week rather than a general one. Notice how much easier a specific question is to answer honestly.
studies.explainEasier: This money is for poor people who are held back and cannot travel to earn. They look fine, so you might think they are rich. They do not keep begging. You can tell by looking at them.

studies.title: By Night And Day, Openly And Quietly
studies.meaning: Four settings are named in one clause. Between them they cover every occasion on which giving is possible: the two halves of the day, and the two ways of being seen. The effect is to close every gap in which someone might reasonably wait. The reward is then placed with their Lord, not in the world. The ayah ends with the refrain that removes fear of what is coming and grief over what has gone.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line closes its long treatment of charity, right before an equally long passage on lending at interest. Early scholars note the placement as a deliberate contrast. Several classical reports connect these words to a particular companion who gave a sum in four parts, one at each of the times named. The reports differ, and the scholars record them without insisting on any.

keyTerms.note: The everyday verb for spending money, not a religious term. Its root also gives the word for a tunnel, something that runs out at the far end, so wealth is pictured as passing through.
From the root for a secret kept inside. Placed beside its opposite in the same phrase, it makes the pair exhaustive rather than a preference, since between them the two cover all giving.
From a root meaning to become apparent. The word is used of announcements made so that everyone hears, which is the kind of giving that encourages others and risks pride at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The rhythm of that world made the four categories concrete. Business was done in the cool hours after dawn and before dusk, and travel often at night. A merchant might settle accounts publicly in the market and send something quietly to a neighbour after dark on the same day. Naming night and day together described an actual pattern of life rather than a poetic totality.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing formula about having no fear and no grief appears here for the fifth time in this surah alone. Each time it is attached to a different kind of person. Read in order through the chapter, the phrase gathers up five groups. Those who follow God's guidance, believers of earlier communities, those who surrender to God, those who give without wounding, and finally those who give at every hour.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By covering all four settings, the passage removes the idea that charity has a proper occasion. That quietly dismantles the habit of waiting for the right moment. Placing the reward with God, rather than in visible results, also cuts generosity loose. The giver has nothing to inspect. What is left is a practice tied to time, not to circumstance. And a promise aimed at the two worries that giving usually stirs up.

crossReferences.why: Compares open and concealed giving directly and explains why the hidden kind benefits you.
Lists the same habit, spending secretly and openly, among the marks of those who endure.
Instructs the same spending before a day arrives with no bargaining and no friendship.

studies.applyIt: Pick a time of day rather than an amount. Decide that something small leaves your hands at that hour, and set the reminder now. Most people give when they are asked, which means their generosity is scheduled by other people. This ayah describes a habit measured by the clock, and a habit tied to a time survives moods better than one tied to appeals.
studies.explainEasier: Some people give at night and in the day, quietly and out in the open. God says their reward is waiting with Him. They have nothing to fear and nothing to be sad about.

studies.title: Commerce Is Not Like That
studies.meaning: The passage opens with an image of unsteadiness rather than with a rule, and early scholars read it of a condition at the resurrection. Then the objection is quoted: commerce and this are the same. The reply does not argue the case; it separates the two by naming them differently. What follows is about stopping. Whoever stops keeps what has passed, and his matter is left with God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the last run of instructions in the surah. Lending at increase was standard practice across Arabia and the wider region, and Mecca's economy ran partly on it. Early scholars describe the objection quoted here as a real one that merchants raised, since both arrangements involve money and a return. The ayat that follow deal with debts already owed.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to grow and to swell, which also gives the word for a hill. The name describes the mechanism, and the surah then sets it against a word from a root joining cleansing with growth.

An intensive verb for striking blindly and repeatedly, used of a camel trampling ground without looking. It describes a loss of steadiness rather than a single blow, which is what the image depends on.

A phrase for what went before, used across the Quran when a change is introduced without reaching backwards. It keeps a new arrangement from becoming a retrospective accounting of everything already done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Credit was the machinery of Arabian trade. A caravan was paid for by investors who took a share. Farmers borrowed against a harvest, and a bad season meant borrowing again on worse terms. Debts grew on themselves. A family could lose land, then labour, then freedom, in an order everyone had watched. The objection quoted here came from men who paid for real journeys and carried real risk.
studies.didYouKnow: The objection is quoted in the community's own words before it is answered. The Quran does that at several points in this surah. The passage then uses two words from opposite roots for growth. The one for increase on a loan comes from a root for swelling. The word for charity in the next ayah comes from a root joining cleansing with growth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply works by drawing a line, not by arguing, and that is a particular move. Two things that look alike are given different names and different outcomes. The reason is not spelled out. What is spelled out is the way back. Someone who stops is not made to unpick the past, and his case is placed with God rather than with any human reckoning.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same subject in a later Medinan surah, warning against returns compounded repeatedly.
Contrasts what is given to multiply people's wealth with what is given seeking God's approval.
Continues directly, contrasting what is worn away with what is made to grow.

studies.applyIt: Look at one arrangement in your life where the gain is automatic and requires nothing of you. Not to judge it: to notice how it feels different from money you earned. This passage separates two things that look alike, and the difference it points at is what the arrangement asks of the person inside it.
studies.explainEasier: People who live off interest will stand up confused, like someone driven mad. They say that trading and interest are the same thing. God allowed trading and banned interest. Anyone who stops can keep what he already made.

studies.title: Worn Away And Made To Grow
studies.meaning: Two verbs are set against each other, and both are about size. One thing is worn away, the other is made to grow, and the words are chosen so that the outcome reverses the appearance. Then comes a description of those who believe and give, with the refrain about no fear and no grief. The third ayah asks that what remains outstanding be left, with belief named as the condition.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the last run of instructions in the surah. Early scholars report that leaving what was still owed was hard in practice. The debts had been made in good faith under the old arrangement, and families counted on the return they expected. The ayat that follow deal with exactly that difficulty, and the run is read as one movement.

keyTerms.note: The verb used of the waning of the moon, so it describes something diminishing gradually rather than being destroyed at once. The image is of a thing that looks whole while it is already going.
From the same root as the word for increase on a loan, used here of charity. The pairing is deliberate: what was named as growth is worn away, and what looks like loss is what actually grows.

A plain verb for leaving something alone, with no word of condemnation attached to it. It asks that an outstanding claim simply be released rather than pursued, which is practical rather than a verdict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debts still owed in Medina were not entries on a page. A man knew exactly who owed him, how much, and when it was due. Often the debt was held against a stand of palms or a share in a herd. Letting the rest go meant a real loss to a real household. It would have been talked about openly among families who all knew one another's standing.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs in the first ayah come from roots that both concern size. One is taken from the waning of the moon. The other is shared with the word for increase on a loan. The refrain about no fear and no grief in the second ayah appears several times across this surah. Each time it closes a description of those who act rightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reversal is the argument. What is described as growing is said to be shrinking. What looks like giving away is said to be increasing. That moves the whole reckoning somewhere else. Then the second ayah describes a whole life rather than a deal, setting prayer and giving side by side. The third names belief as the condition, so what follows rests on what a person already holds.

crossReferences.why: Gives the image of increase directly, a grain producing seven ears of a hundred grains each.
Sets the same contrast between what increases in people's wealth and what seeks God's approval.
Continues directly, describing what follows for those who do not leave what remains.

studies.applyIt: Pick one number you watch going up: a balance, a follower count, a streak. Then ask what has been quietly going down while it rose. This passage's whole method is to reverse an appearance of growth. You do not have to change anything today. Just do the second sum as carefully as you do the first.
studies.explainEasier: God takes the good out of money made from interest, and makes charity grow instead. People who believe and give will be rewarded. He asks them to let go of any interest still owed to them.

studies.title: Neither Wronging Nor Wronged
studies.meaning: The sharpest sentence in the section arrives, and the way out is stated in the same breath. If the outstanding claims are not released, notice is given of a war from God and His Messenger, language the Quran uses nowhere else. Then: if you turn back, the capital is yours. The closing clause states the principle in a few words, symmetrical in both directions at once.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, right after the instruction to leave what was still owed. Early scholars note how sharp the wording is. They read it as a mark of how deeply the practice was rooted, not as a description of a real campaign. The rule that the capital may be kept is read as protecting lenders from losing what they had truly put up.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from the root for permission and announcement. It reads as a formal notification, of the kind made publicly before hostilities began, which is what gives the sentence its weight.
Literally the heads of your properties, an idiom for the original sum before any increase. The phrase distinguishes what was actually advanced from whatever was added on top of it.
The first half of a pair, followed immediately by the same verb in the passive. One root states the whole standard in both directions, which is unusual and gives the clause its finality.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A creditor in Medina had a real claim, often held against land. Losing a return he had counted on could strain his own household. Debtors, meanwhile, could be ruined by a debt that kept growing. The clause about keeping the capital speaks to both. Nobody is asked to forget what they lent, and nobody is chased for what grew on top of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a war from God and His Messenger appears nowhere else in the Quran. The closing clause of the ayah is built from a single verb used twice, once active and once passive. So one root states the whole rule in both directions, with nothing added to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sharpness and the way out sit in the same sentence. That is the shape this surah keeps returning to. What is being protected is named at the end, and it runs both ways. Not the interest of one side, but the absence of wrong in either direction. That is a general rule stated at the close of a specific instruction. It is what the whole section has been building toward.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately with what happens when the debtor cannot pay, asking for deferment.
Precedes this with the instruction to leave outstanding claims, which this ayah then presses.
Sets trade by mutual consent against consuming wealth wrongly, in a matching principle.

studies.applyIt: Look at an arrangement where you are getting more than you put in, and where the other party had little choice. This ayah's final clause is a standard that runs both ways: not wronging and not being wronged. Test one arrangement against it this week, honestly, and see which side of the sentence you are on.
studies.explainEasier: If you do not stop taking interest, God and his Messenger are at war with you. If you do stop, you can keep the money you first lent out. Nobody is cheated on either side.

studies.title: Until A Time Of Ease
studies.meaning: Two provisions follow, and they are graded. If the debtor is in difficulty, the payment waits until things ease. Then a second option is named as better: release the debt altogether as charity. The comparative form does the work, since nothing here is required. The closing conditional is short and sharp, if you only knew, which leaves the weighing with the reader.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the instruction about claims still owed. Early scholars note that the ayah speaks to the practical situation head on. A creditor who could no longer claim an increase still had his capital owed to him, and a debtor who could not pay it. The rule allowing delay answers what would otherwise have left both sides stuck.

keyTerms.note: From the root for what is hard to handle, the same one set against ease in the passage on fasting. Its counterpart appears in this very ayah, so the sentence names both ends of one scale.
A noun from the verb for looking and waiting, used in this surah of a respite denied elsewhere. Here it is granted, so the same vocabulary carries opposite outcomes in two parts of one surah.
The verb for giving alms, applied here to cancelling a debt. Naming a release as charity reframes it: what is written off is not lost but counted as something given away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Medina was personal and open to view. Both sides lived in the same streets, and a debtor who did not pay was known to everyone. Pressing a claim against a family in real trouble made real enemies. Dropping it earned real standing. Both options in this ayah could be read by the neighbours, and the second cost more.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a delay comes from the same root as a word denied to another group earlier in this surah. There the punishment was not lightened and no delay was given. The same wording turns up in the two places with opposite outcomes. The classical commentaries sometimes note that.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A hard instruction is followed at once by relief for the person on the other side of it. That keeps the section from favouring either party. Then the better option is named without being required, in a comparative. That is this passage's typical move. And calling a cancelled debt charity changes the reckoning. Nothing has been lost, only moved into another column.

crossReferences.why: Precedes this with the provision that the principal may be kept, which this ayah then softens.
Uses the same pattern, naming an entitlement and then calling foregoing it nearer to piety.
States the relation between hardship and ease twice over, using the same pair of roots.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who owes you something small and cannot easily pay: money, time, a favour returned. This ayah names two options and says which is better without requiring it. Choose one such debt this week and simply tell the person it is finished, then notice how much lighter it makes your own side.
studies.explainEasier: If someone who owes you money is struggling, give them more time to pay. And if you let the debt go and treat it as a gift, that is even better for you.

studies.title: Paid In Full For What It Earned
studies.meaning: One short ayah closes the passage on debt by moving the whole subject somewhere else. A day is named, the return is described, and each soul is paid in full for what it earned. The verb for paying in full is a commercial one, so a section that has been about ledgers ends with the largest ledger of all. The last clause rules out any shortfall.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Several classical reports name this as among the last ayat revealed. Early scholars discuss why it sits here, in the middle of a passage about debt, rather than at the end of the Quran's text. The reports differ over the details. The ayah's shortness and its subject have made it one of the most quoted in the surah.

keyTerms.note: From the root for completeness, and the standard word for settling a debt without shortfall. Using a commercial verb at the end of a section about debt turns the whole passage into one extended comparison.
The ordinary verb for earning wages, used across this surah of what a heart acquires as much as of money. It keeps the accounting language running right to the last clause of the passage.

A passive verb: the returning is done to people rather than by them. That grammatical detail places the movement outside anyone's arrangement, which is the difference between this settlement and the ones just described.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every merchant in Medina understood a settled account. Debts were reckoned at fixed terms. A man who paid in full and on time carried a name worth more than the sum itself. The wording of this ayah is the wording of that world. Here it is applied to something that cannot be haggled over, put off, or written off by agreement.
studies.didYouKnow: Several classical reports name this as among the last ayat of the Quran to be revealed. They note that it was placed inside the passage on debt rather than at the end of the text. The commentaries record differing accounts of how long the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) lived afterwards.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage on lending ends by describing an account that cannot be adjusted. That is not a threat tacked on at the close. It is the frame the whole section has been working inside, now said out loud. And the final clause repeats the one used of the capital a few ayat earlier. A human standard of no wrong in either direction is matched by a divine one.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same clause about not wronging and not being wronged, a few ayat earlier.
States that every soul will receive its recompense in full on the Day of Resurrection.
Describes the same settlement in the smallest possible units, an atom's weight either way.

studies.applyIt: Take the last thing you did today that nobody saw and nobody will ever mention. This ayah says it is on the account. That is not meant as a threat; it answers the ordinary suspicion that unseen effort simply disappears. Do one more such thing tomorrow, and leave it unmentioned deliberately.
studies.explainEasier: Watch out for the day when you go back to God. Every person will be paid in full for what they did. Nobody will be treated unfairly, and nothing will be left out.

studies.title: Write It Down
studies.meaning: The longest ayah in the Quran works through one practical situation in detail. A debt with a fixed term should be written down. A scribe writes fairly. The one who owes dictates. A guardian dictates if he cannot. Witnesses are called. Small sums are not left out. A deal settled on the spot is. Reasons are given at the midpoint, and the last instruction protects the scribe and the witness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the final section of the surah. Few people in Medina could read or write, and most agreements were spoken in front of witnesses. So a written record was a real change for ordinary deals. Early scholars note how much detail there is. They read the ayah as setting up a practice rather than settling a dispute. The reasons it gives are stated openly in the text itself.

keyTerms.gloss: a named term, a stated deadline
keyTerms.note: A fixed and specified time, the phrase the Quran uses elsewhere for appointed spans. Its presence at the start means the instruction attaches to agreements that run forward in time rather than to immediate exchanges.

The verb for dictating to a writer. Placing the dictation with the one who owes is a deliberate arrangement: the person with the obligation states its terms, so he cannot later claim the record was made against him.
A comparative from the root for justice and exact measure. Three comparatives appear together in the middle of the ayah, giving three separate reasons, which is unusual in a passage of instruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Most people in Medina could not write, and a trained scribe was a known figure who charged for his work. Agreements were normally spoken in front of witnesses whose memory was the record. Disputes years later turned on what people recalled. A written note changed that entirely. The instruction that a scribe should not refuse speaks to how few of them there were.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the longest ayah in the Quran. Its subject is not prayer or belief but the recording of a debt. The middle of the ayah gives three reasons for the instruction. Each one is a comparative: more fair, stronger as evidence, and more likely to keep you from doubt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The length is the point. A book that states the nature of God in a few lines spends its longest passage on paperwork. That says something about where the tradition puts religion. The reasons are given out loud rather than assumed, and every one of them is about heading off a future dispute. The closing protection of the scribe and the witness guards the people who make the arrangement work.

crossReferences.why: Continues directly with what to do when no scribe is available, on a journey.
The surah's other landmark ayah, of comparable weight and an entirely different subject.
Asks that testimony be given for God even against oneself, one's parents or one's relatives.

studies.applyIt: Write down one arrangement this week that you would normally leave verbal: what you agreed to do for someone, or what they agreed to do for you. Not because you distrust them. The longest ayah in the Quran gives its own reason, which is to make a future disagreement less likely, and that is a favour to both of you.
studies.explainEasier: When you lend or borrow money for a set time, write it down. Get someone to write it out fairly, and have people watch. Even small amounts should be written down. It keeps everyone clear about what was agreed.

studies.title: If You Trust One Another
studies.meaning: The exception to the previous ayah is given. On a journey with no scribe to hand, something held as security serves instead. Then a further case, and this is where the passage turns. If you trust one another, the arrangement runs on trust, and the one trusted gives back what was left with him. The ayah closes by naming the hiding of testimony as something that reaches the heart.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the passage on recording debts. Travel made written records hard, and a pledge held as security was the standard practice on the roads. Early scholars read the second half as covering the case where two people choose not to write anything down. They note that the surah moves from a procedure to a matter of character inside a single ayah.

keyTerms.note: A security item together with an adjective meaning received or held. The specificity matters: what stands in for a document is not a promise but an object physically in someone's possession.
A passive from the root for safety and trust, the same root that gives the word for a believer. The person is defined by having been trusted rather than by any quality he claims for himself.
An unusual construction placing the wrong in the heart specifically rather than in the person. Concealing testimony is an act of silence, so the ayah locates it where the silence is being kept.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: On a journey nobody carried writing materials. A caravan halted at a well was not the place to find a scribe. Business still had to be done: a share bought, a beast sold, a loan taken to buy food. A pledge left in hand was the usual stand-in. A ring, a cloak, a weapon. Everyone on the road understood the arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage moves from the longest ayah in the Quran, full of procedure, to this one, which ends by naming a heart. The wording places the wrong in the heart rather than in the person, which is uncommon. The classical commentaries pause on it. They note that hiding testimony is an inward act with no outward sign.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Procedure and character are set in a sequence, not against each other. The written record exists because trust can fail. The ayah still describes an arrangement in which two people simply trust each other, and does not call that naive. What holds it together is named at the end. It is not enforcement but the state of a heart that could stay silent and does not.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the full procedure that this ayah then provides the exception to.
Uses the same verb for concealing, there of revelation rather than of testimony.
Asks that trusts be returned to their owners and that judgement between people be just.

studies.applyIt: Think of something someone left with you: a key, a confidence, a task, a piece of information. This ayah calls that person the one who was trusted, and defines him by nothing else at all. Discharge one such thing this week without being reminded, which is the only version of it that counts.
studies.explainEasier: If you are travelling and cannot find anyone to write the deal down, hand over something as a deposit. If you trust each other, the one who is trusted must do what he promised. And never hide what you saw.

studies.title: What Is Inside You Counts
studies.meaning: Ownership of everything is stated first, and the reach of the reckoning follows from it. Whether you show what is in yourself or hide it, God will bring it into the account. Forgiveness and punishment are then both put down to His will, in that order. Early scholars differ over how far the opening claim reaches. They also differ over whether the surah's last ayah lifts it, narrows it, or explains what it always meant.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This ayah stands at the end of the longest surah, straight after its long instructions on debt and written contracts. The classical sources report that it distressed the early community. They understood it to mean they would answer for passing thoughts, and they brought their difficulty to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The two ayat that close the surah follow at once as the answer.

keyTerms.note: The verb for bringing something into the open, used of a desert becoming visible at daybreak. It names disclosure as an act rather than as a state, which is what makes it comparable to concealment.
The word covers the self, the soul and the inner life together. Arabic does not divide them as English does, which is why the ayah can speak of what is in your selves without further specifying.

keyTerms.gloss: He will bring you to account
keyTerms.note: From the root for counting and reckoning, the same word used for arithmetic. It frames judgement as an audit, a going through of the books, rather than as a verdict announced without process.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Two ayat earlier the Quran had given its longest passage on writing down debts. Scribes, witnesses and terms were recorded so nothing could be denied later. This ayah lands on an audience that has just been thinking about ledgers. In a trading society, a disputed deal was settled by what could be produced in writing. An account that includes the unwritten was a startling extension.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the last full ayah before the surah's two closing ones. The early Muslim response to it is preserved in unusual detail. Reports describe companions kneeling and saying they had been given something beyond their strength. It is one of the clearest recorded cases of a community's difficulty with a passage being answered by the next revelation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah says the inner life is not private in the way people assume. That closes the gap between what a person does and who they are. Putting forgiveness before punishment in the sentence matters, and early scholars note the order. What the surah does next matters more. Distress at a demand is met not with rebuke but with relief. That sets a pattern for how the Quran treats a troubled conscience.

crossReferences.why: Answers this ayah directly by stating that no soul is burdened beyond its capacity.
Repeats the same claim about concealing or disclosing what is in your hearts.
States that God knows what a person's soul whispers, and is nearer than the jugular vein.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are carrying inwardly that you have never said to anyone: a resentment, an envy, a fear you are ashamed of. You do not need to confess it to a person. Name it once, honestly, in your own words to God, and ask for it to be dealt with. The ayah says it is already known, which means the only new thing is your willingness to look at it.
studies.explainEasier: Everything belongs to God. He knows what you show and what you keep hidden inside you, and He will ask you about all of it. He forgives who He wants. He can do anything.

studies.title: The Last Two Lines
studies.meaning: The surah ends with a declaration and a prayer. The Messenger and the believers are described believing together, making no division between the messengers. They answer with three things: we hear, we obey, and then a request for pardon. The second line lifts the weight the previous ayah had laid down. No soul is charged beyond what it can hold. Then it supplies the words to ask with: do not hold us to forgetting, do not load us as others were loaded, pardon us.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These two ayat close the longest surah in the Quran and answer the distress the previous ayah had caused. Classical reports describe the community's alarm at the idea of being called to account for what passes through the mind. These two ayat are the reply. Some well-known reports place their revelation during the night journey rather than in Medina, and early scholars record both without forcing a choice.

keyTerms.note: From the root for roominess, the same word used elsewhere of God as all-encompassing. Capacity here is what a soul has room for, so the limit is measured individually rather than set as one standard.
A load that binds and holds you down, used of a covenant that constrains. Early scholars connect it to obligations earlier communities took on themselves, which is what the prayer asks not to repeat.
The verb means to erase, as wind erases tracks in sand. It is the first of three requests that escalate: erase it, then forgive it, then have mercy on us regardless.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pattern of the second ayah would have been recognised as a formal petition. Someone approaching a chief opened by acknowledging his authority, stated his obedience, and only then made the request. The asks climbed from the smallest to the largest. Here the community says it hears and obeys before it asks for anything, and then the requests climb in order. The form was familiar. The one being addressed was not.
studies.didYouKnow: These two ayat hold a distinctive place in practice. Classical reports describe them as a nightly recitation, enough for whoever says them. The prayer in the final ayah is also unusual in being written out in advance. Instead of describing what to ask for, the Quran supplies the exact words. It does that at this length only a handful of times.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing answers a hard passage with mercy, not with argument. It does that by setting a limit on what can be asked. Capacity is named as the boundary. So the demands of religion fit the person, which cuts against both perfectionism and despair. The longest surah ends on a request for pardon, not on a command. That leaves the community standing in the very posture it has been describing.

crossReferences.why: States the difficulty these two ayat answer, that even concealed thoughts are brought to account.
Repeats the principle that no soul is charged beyond its capacity, in a passage of instructions.
Applies the same limit to money, saying God does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it.

studies.applyIt: Memorise the final prayer if you have not already. Use it at the end of a day that went badly, rather than a day that went well. It was given to people who had just been told something they found unbearable. Saying it when you feel the weight, rather than as a routine, puts the sentence back in the situation it was answering.
studies.explainEasier: The believers say they trust God and all His messengers. They say: we hear you and we obey. God promises He will never ask more of you than you can bear.
